title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
應天府鄉試錄序
正德已卯秋寔惟天下舉士
之期應天府臣疏請考試官
上以命侍讀學士臣俊右諭德臣
時既至則同考為教授臣神甫
學正臣鳳教諭臣紀臣竒臣
廷美臣鳴鸞臣汝登監試為御史臣
===
必進臣時通暨內外執事皆聘選
以充而提調則府尹臣宗道府
丞臣庭光焉就試之士凡二千
有竒先是言者請減入塲之
數以省費
上重之詔仍舊而有司之奉行者
不一或嚴取以便簡閱或博

應天府鄉試錄序
正德己卯秋寔惟天下舉士

===

丞臣庭光焉就試之士凡二千
有奇先是言者請减入場之
數以省費
上重之詔仍舊而有司之奉行者
不一或嚴取以便簡閱或博
punctuated:
應天府鄉試錄序

正德已卯秋，寔惟天下舉士之期。應天府臣疏請考試官，上以命侍讀學士臣俊、右諭德臣時。既至，則同考為教授臣神甫、學正臣鳳、教諭臣紀、臣竒、臣廷美、臣鳴鸞、臣汝登；監試為御史臣必進、臣時通。暨內外執事，皆聘選以充。而提調則府尹臣宗道、府丞臣庭光焉。

就試之士凡二千有竒。先是，言者請減入塲之數，以省費。上重之，詔仍舊，而有司之奉行者不一，或嚴取以便簡閱，或博
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn of the jimao year [?] of the Zhengde reign (1519), the time had come to select scholars throughout the realm. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture submitted a memorial requesting Examiners. His Majesty appointed Academician Expositor-in-Waiting Jun and Right Admonisher Shi. After they arrived, the Associate Examiners were Prefectural School Instructor Shenfu, Departmental School Instructor Feng, and County School Instructors Ji, Qi, Tingmei, Mingluan, and Rudeng. The examination supervisors were Censors Bijin and Shitong. These, together with the personnel serving inside and outside the examination compound, were all invited or selected to fill their posts. The Proctors were Prefect Zongdao and Prefectural Vice Magistrate Tingguang.

More than two thousand scholars presented themselves for examination. Previously, those offering counsel had requested that the number admitted to the examination compound be reduced to save expenses. His Majesty attached great importance to the matter and decreed that the existing practice should continue. The responsible authorities, however, implemented this inconsistently: some selected candidates strictly to facilitate assessment, while others broadly…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
收以俟来擇盖皆期于得士
以承
德意費非所計也於是臣等得
竭其駑鈍以從事凡得士一
百三十五人并刻其文之優
者凡二十篇以為錄而
獻焉後既被
===
===
命從舟而南也秋水時至百川
沸盈沿白以泝于衛則見夫
二水之相嚮而馳以赴于海
者若爭先而莫之敢後顧瞻
京邑翼然天表誠足為四方之
極萬世之業也已既而歷汶
濟以達于徐泗之間水之用

收以俟采擇蓋皆期于得士
以承
德意費非所計也於是〔臣〕等得
竭其駑鈍以從事凡得士一

===
命從舟而南也秋水時至百川
沸盈沿白以泝于衛則見夫
二水之相嚮而馳以赴于海
者若爭先而莫之敢後顧瞻
京邑翼然天表誠足爲四方之
極萬世之業也已既而歷汶
濟以達于徐泗之間水之用
punctuated:
收以俟来擇，盖皆期于得士，以承德意，費非所計也。於是臣等得竭其駑鈍以從事，凡得士一百三十五人，并刻其文之優者凡二十篇，以為錄而獻焉。
後既被命，從舟而南也，秋水時至，百川沸盈。沿白以泝于衛，則見夫二水之相嚮而馳，以赴于海者，若爭先而莫之敢後。顧瞻京邑，翼然天表，誠足為四方之極、萬世之業也已。既而歷汶、濟，以達于徐、泗之間，水之用
translation_en:
…accepted candidates to await subsequent selection. All, it would seem, hoped to obtain worthy men and thereby fulfill the Emperor’s gracious intent; expense was not their concern. Thus we, your servants, were able to devote our limited abilities fully to the task. In all, we selected 135 men and had twenty of their finest essays engraved for printing, compiling a record to present to the throne.
Later, having received my commission, I traveled south by boat. The autumn waters arrived in season, and the many rivers surged to overflowing. Following the Bai River downstream and proceeding up the Wei River, I saw the two streams racing toward one another and onward to the sea, as though each strove to lead and neither dared fall behind. Turning to gaze toward the capital, soaring at the edge of heaven, I reflected that it was indeed worthy to serve as the lodestar of the four quarters and the foundation of an enterprise lasting ten thousand generations. Then, passing along the Wen and Ji rivers, I reached the region between Xu and Si, where the force of the waters…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
壯益甚則又見夫黄河之會
渡淮陰入邗溝以臨真揚則
又見夫長江之險江河之經
流于中國殆不下萬里而其
委皆在於南服俊於是得巨
觀焉南望羣山扶輿磅礴廻
翔飛翥若自天而降者蟠而
===
為龍踞而為虎以開
帝王之真宅而我
高皇帝之基命實肇於此夫豈偶
然之故哉東南之人物與其
財賦並稱甲於天下其地產
有固然歟俊未及供事而知
其文章之鉅麗必將大有發

又見夫長江之險江河之經
流于中國殆不下萬里而其
委皆在於南服俊於是得巨
觀焉南望羣山扶輿磅礴迴
翔飛翥若自天而降者蟠而
爲龍踞而爲虎以開
===
帝王之真宅而我
高皇帝之基命實肇於此夫豈偶
然之故哉東南之人物與其
財賦並稱甲於天下其地産
有固然歟俊未及供事而知
其文章之鉅麗必將大有發
punctuated: 壯益甚，則又見夫黄河之會。渡淮陰，入邗溝，以臨真揚，則又見夫長江之險。江河之經流于中國，殆不下萬里，而其委皆在於南服。俊於是得巨觀焉。南望羣山，扶輿磅礴，廻翔飛翥，若自天而降者，蟠而為龍，踞而為虎，以開帝王之真宅，而我高皇帝之基命實肇於此，夫豈偶然之故哉？東南之人物與其財賦，並稱甲於天下，其地產有固然歟？俊未及供事，而知其文章之鉅麗，必將大有發
translation_en: …its force grew still greater, and I then beheld the confluence with the Yellow River. Crossing at Huaiyin, I entered the Han Canal and approached Zhenzhou and Yangzhou, where I beheld the formidable natural barrier of the Yangzi River. The main courses of the Yangzi and Yellow rivers through the Central Lands extend no fewer than ten thousand li, yet their outlets are both in the southern region. Thus I, Jun, witnessed a magnificent spectacle. Looking south, I saw the mountains massed in majestic profusion, wheeling and soaring as though descending from heaven, coiling like a dragon and crouching like a tiger to open up the true seat of emperors and kings. It was here, indeed, that our Emperor Gao first laid the foundations of his Heavenly Mandate. Could this possibly have been mere chance? The southeast’s outstanding people and its wealth and tax revenues alike are acclaimed as foremost in the realm. Might this be inherent in the endowments of its land? Before I, Jun, had even begun my duties, I knew that the grandeur and beauty of its literary compositions would surely give rise to something great…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於其心者既而連叩之以觀
其所應則或鏘然而鳴或幽
然而光或沛然而流若向之
觀于河于江者謂非得於氣
化之全也殆未可乎抑建康
之勝舊矣吳及六朝下逮南
唐皆嘗用之卒偏安于一隅
===
而混一之盛始發於
今日固我
高皇帝用夏驅胡功超千古足以
當夫氣數之隆實又以我
文皇帝移駐于北盡據中國之阨
塞而南嚮以聽治於是
兩都之雄屹然對峙於朝宗之

===
今日固我
高皇帝用夏驅胡功超千古足以
當夫氣數之隆實又以我
文皇帝移駐于北盡據中國之阨
塞而南嚮以聽治於是
兩都之雄屹然對峙於朝宗之
punctuated: 於其心者。既而連叩之，以觀其所應，則或鏘然而鳴，或幽然而光，或沛然而流，若向之觀于河于江者。謂非得於氣化之全也，殆未可乎！抑建康之勝舊矣，吳及六朝，下逮南唐，皆嘗用之，卒偏安于一隅。而混一之盛，始發於今日。固我高皇帝用夏驅胡，功超千古，足以當夫氣數之隆；實又以我文皇帝移駐于北，盡據中國之阨塞，而南嚮以聽治。於是兩都之雄，屹然對峙於朝宗之
translation_en:
…arise from their hearts. Then I questioned them repeatedly to observe their responses: some rang out sonorously, some shone with a secluded radiance, and some flowed abundantly, like what I had earlier beheld in the Yellow River and the Yangzi. Surely one could hardly say that these did not derive from the fullness of the transforming cosmic vital force!

Indeed, Jiankang’s geographical advantages are longstanding. Wu and the Six Dynasties, down to the Southern Tang, all made use of them, yet ultimately secured only a regional refuge in one corner of the realm. The grandeur of complete unification first emerged in our own day. Certainly, our Emperor Gao employed the forces of Chinese civilization to expel the non-Chinese, achieving deeds surpassing those of all past ages and fully matching that culmination of cosmic fortune. Yet it was also because our Emperor Wen transferred his residence to the north, took full possession of the strategic passes of the Central Lands, and faced south to attend to government. Thus the two mighty capitals stood towering opposite one another at the convergence of those coming to pay court …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
會海內帖然以就撫馭籍其
財賦以制用收其譽髦以佐
理所以爲
詒燕之圖者可謂宏且遠矣丙
子之秋俊執事于北見才焉
雄深博大往往有奇氣今兹
之南也見才焉如前所云率
===
皆稱其山川至其尊王而賤
伯崇經而黜子則又未嘗有
二說也盖道德之一而風俗
之同也久矣俊既以得士爲
朝廷賀而於其始進也張之以
昌其志俾其知所生之地所
際之時如是之不偶也他日
alt_text:
會海内帖然以就𢹂馭籍其
財賦以制用收其礜髦以佐
理所以爲
詒燕之圖者可謂宏且遠矣丙
子之秋〔俊〕執事于北見才焉
雄深博大往往有奇氣今茲
之南也見才焉如前所云幸
===
皆稱其山川至其尊王而賤
伯崇經而黜子則又未嘗有
二說也盖道德之一而風俗
之同也久矣〔俊〕既以得士爲
朝廷賀而於其始進也張之以
昌其志俾其知所生之地所
際之時如是之不偶也他日
punctuated: 會，海內帖然以就撫馭，籍其財賦以制用，收其譽髦以佐理，所以爲詒燕之圖者，可謂宏且遠矣。丙子之秋，俊執事于北，見才焉，雄深博大，往往有奇氣。今兹之南也，見才焉，如前所云，率皆稱其山川。至其尊王而賤伯，崇經而黜子，則又未嘗有二說也。盖道德之一而風俗之同也久矣。俊既以得士爲朝廷賀，而於其始進也，張之以昌其志，俾其知所生之地、所際之時，如是之不偶也。他日
translation_en: …at the point where those paying homage converge. All within the seas settled peacefully under imperial governance. Its revenues were drawn upon to meet expenditure, and its outstanding men recruited to assist in government. The plans thus made to secure peace for posterity may indeed be called magnificent and far-reaching. In the autumn of the bingzi year [1516], I, Jun, served in the north and encountered men of talent: vigorous, profound, broad, and expansive, often possessed of an extraordinary spirit. Now, coming south, I have encountered talent of the kind described above; in general, these men all measure up to their mountains and rivers. As for honoring the kingly way and disparaging hegemony, exalting the Classics and subordinating the writings of the philosophical masters, there have never been two opinions. Indeed, moral principles have been unified and customs shared for a long time. Having congratulated the court on obtaining worthy men, I now, at the outset of their advancement, encourage them to enlarge their aspirations, so that they may understand how extraordinary are the place of their birth and the age they have encountered. In days to come…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
效用無違其所言無棄其所
學平時則名檢自飭臨事則
忠義奮發曰
上之人於我乎求佐理焉非苟以
榮其身家而已則於
國家化成之厚山川孕毓之勤
為不負矣是舉之興也適南
===
方有兵事倥偬不給卒獲如
期而集者諸司有貞固之幹
焉苟後之議者曰是科盖得
人為多則俊等皆可以忘其
勞矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
汪俊謹序
alt_text:

忠義奮發曰
上之人於我乎求佐理焉非苟以
榮其身家而已則於
國家化成之厚山川孕毓之勤
爲不負矣是舉之興也適南
===
方有兵事倥偬不給卒獲如
期而集者諸司有貞固之幹
焉苟後之議者曰是科蓋得
人爲多則俊等皆可以忘其
勞矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
汪俊謹序
punctuated:
效用無違其所言，無棄其所學，平時則名檢自飭，臨事則忠義奮發，曰：「上之人於我乎求佐理焉，非苟以榮其身家而已。」則於國家化成之厚、山川孕毓之勤，為不負矣。
是舉之興也，適南方有兵事，倥偬不給，卒獲如期而集者，諸司有貞固之幹焉。苟後之議者曰：「是科盖得人為多。」則俊等皆可以忘其勞矣。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉直大夫汪俊謹序。
translation_en:
…when they enter service, may they neither depart from what they have said nor abandon what they have learned. In ordinary times, may they discipline themselves in reputation and conduct; when affairs demand action, may their loyalty and sense of duty rise to the occasion. Let them say: “Those above seek in us assistance in governing, not merely a means to bring honor to ourselves and our families.” They will then have lived up to the state’s generous work of moral transformation and the mountains and rivers’ diligent nurturing of talent.
When this examination was undertaken, military affairs happened to be troubling the south, leaving us hard-pressed and unable to keep pace. That we ultimately completed it on schedule was due to the steadfast administrative ability of the various offices. If those who assess it in later years should say, “This examination obtained many worthy men,” then I, Jun, and my colleagues may all forget our toil.
Preface respectfully composed by Wang Jun, Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Upright Service.

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
可與言而不與之言失人不可與言而與
之言失言知者不失人亦不失言
踐其位行其禮奏其樂敬其所尊愛其所
親
人皆有所不忍達之於其所忍仁也人皆
有所不為達之於其所為義也
易
===
大觀在上順而巽中正以觀天下
繻有衣袽終日戒
君子上交不諂下交不瀆其知幾乎
坤也者地也萬物皆致養焉故曰致役乎
坤兌正秋也萬物之所說也故曰說言

First Session

Four Books

To fail to speak with someone who is fit to be spoken with is to lose that person; to speak with someone who is unfit to be spoken with is to waste words. The wise lose neither people nor words.

…not all the details were put into effect; moreover, the Han remained content with the habits of rule from horseback and did not devote itself to the Odes and Documents. After our Founding Ancestor had pacified the realm, he personally brought about an age of peace. Regulations and prescribed forms were fully established, and the responsible officials maintained them generation after generation. As for the pronouncements through which he bequeathed instruction, every word and every principle shone as brightly as the Six Classics. Quite a few are scattered among the sayings transmitted and recited by elders and the compilations made by Confucian court officials. You candidates have been among the first to receive the nurturing influence of the sage ruler’s transforming instruction, and have received it for a long time. Answer fully on the basis of what you have studied; you must not use the Han as an analogy.
Question: The Odes says, “Diligently our king orders the four quarters.” The Record of Rites says, “Once the guiding principles of order are set right, all under Heaven is firmly settled.” Thus, those who possess a state cannot dispense with these principles for even a single day. Examining antiquity, we find that Emperor Xuan of Han comprehensively checked performance against professed responsibilities, reliably rewarded merit, and invariably punished wrongdoing; Emperor Taizong of Tang exerted himself rigorously to correct abuses, putting every detail of government into effect; and Emperor Taizong of Song planned deeply and decided boldly, assessed achievements, and exercised care in punishment. It cannot be said that they failed to establish the guiding principles of order. Yet among their successors, some declined because they failed to invigorate these principles, while others sought to invigorate them but instead hastened decline. Why was this?
Our Emperor Taizu Gao expelled the non-Chinese Yuan and unified all within the seas. Correcting abuses and establishing laws, he comprehensively brought together the traditions of the kings of all ages. For a hundred and fifty years, people have known to observe the laws; those above have been secure and those below obedient, living joyfully in great concord. This may indeed be called flourishing rule. Recently, however, judging by prevailing customs, the implementation of these guiding principles seems in some respects no longer what it once was. 不可雜是蓋有說矣可得聞歟劉歆叙
七畧王儉撰七志史記以下皆附春秋
其亦有見歟經史之分始於何人至於
爲學遂有以經稱者有以史稱者若宋
司馬氏王氏其最著也得失之故亦有
punctuated:
飭治振起，以復祖宗之盛，其道何居？昔荀悅作《申鑒》，謂人主致治之術，先屏四患，乃崇五政，固紀綱之說也。其論然歟？抑可行于今歟？五政之中，何者爲最要歟？朱子又謂綱紀在于辨賢否以定上下之分，核功罪以公賞罰之施，於悅之言亦有同歟？請詳著于篇，以爲皇上勵精之助。

問：經以載道，史以載事，固也。然則道與事果有二乎？孔子因魯史作《春秋》，與《易》《詩》《書》《禮》《樂》並爲六經。論者謂聖人述史三焉：《書》也，《詩》也，《春秋》也。三者同出於史，而不可雜，是蓋有說矣，可得聞歟？劉歆叙《七畧》，王儉撰《七志》，《史記》以下皆附《春秋》，其亦有見歟？經史之分始於何人？至於爲學，遂有以經稱者，有以史稱者，若宋司馬氏、王氏，其最著也。得失之故亦有
translation_en:
…to set governance in order and reinvigorate it, thereby restoring the flourishing rule of the imperial ancestors: what is the way to accomplish this? In his Extended Reflections (Shen jian), Xun Yue stated that the ruler’s method for achieving good government was first to eliminate the four afflictions and then to promote the five policies. This was indeed an argument about the guiding principles and ordering bonds of government. Was his argument sound? And can it be put into practice today? Which of the five policies is most essential? Master Zhu further said that the guiding principles and ordering bonds of government lie in distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to establish the respective stations of superiors and inferiors, and in examining merits and offenses to make the administration of rewards and punishments impartial. Does this also accord with Yue’s words? Please set out your views in detail in an essay, to assist His Majesty in his earnest efforts at good government.

Question: The classics convey the Way, and histories record events: this is certainly so. But are the Way and events really two separate things? Confucius drew upon the historical records of Lu to compose the Spring and Autumn Annals, which, together with the Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music, constitute the Six Classics. Commentators say that the Sage transmitted history in three works: the Documents, the Odes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals. All three originated in historical records, yet they cannot be treated indiscriminately. There must be an explanation for this; may we hear it? When Liu Xin arranged the Seven Epitomes (Qi lüe) and Wang Jian compiled the Seven Classifications (Qi zhi), they placed the Records of the Historian and subsequent histories under the Spring and Autumn Annals. Did they, too, have some insight in doing so? Who first distinguished the classics from histories? In scholarship, there subsequently came to be those renowned for the classics and those renowned for history. Among these, the most prominent were the Song scholars Sima and Wang. As for the reasons for their strengths and shortcomings, might there also be …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
可言者歟諸士子學於斯二者久矣其
所得何者爲多請遂言之毋讓
問西漢之士尚經術東漢之士崇節義儒
先有是言矣自今觀之有不盡然者如
直諫守節而淮南寢謀持節虜庭而名
標麟閣借劍尚方折檻大呼職在師傅
不肯就吏或印綬加身輒推不受或安
車再迎堅卧不起却牛衣之言甘心于
繫獄拒蘧氏之譬負直以自斃解釼細
===
故也不從以請退免冠隨俗也堅執以
去官此皆士之著名西漢者也不崇節
義歟篤信好古經爲人師徧習經書剖
析疑異或刪定春秋而號樊侯學或考
論圖緯而嘆吾道東兄弟習魯詩爲學
士所歸父子明左氏爲諸儒所法隱居
教授而名重關西正定五經而學宗當
代此皆士之著名東漢者也不尚經術
歟乃偏言之何也西漢之經術尚矣何

可言者歟？諸士子學於斯二者久矣，其所得何者爲多？請遂言之，毋讓。
問：西漢之士尚經術，東漢之士崇節義，儒先有是言矣。自今觀之，有不盡然者。如直諫守節而淮南寢謀，持節虜庭而名標麟閣；借劍尚方，折檻大呼；職在師傅，不肯就吏；或印綬加身，輒推不受；或安車再迎，堅卧不起；却牛衣之言，甘心于繫獄；拒蘧氏之譬，負直以自斃；解釼細故也，不從以請退；免冠隨俗也，堅執以去官。此皆士之著名西漢者也，不崇節義歟？篤信好古，經爲人師；徧習經書，剖析疑異；或刪定春秋而號樊侯學；或考論圖緯而嘆吾道東；兄弟習魯詩，爲學士所歸；父子明左氏，爲諸儒所法；隱居教授而名重關西；正定五經而學宗當代。此皆士之著名東漢者也，不尚經術歟？乃偏言之，何也？西漢之經術尚矣，何
translation_en:
…can these also be discussed? You candidates have long studied these two fields. From which have you gained more? Please set forth your views without holding back.
Question: Earlier Confucian scholars have said that Western Han scholars esteemed classical learning, whereas Eastern Han scholars revered moral integrity and righteousness. Viewed from the present, this does not seem entirely true. Consider the man whose forthright remonstrance and steadfast integrity caused the prince of Huainan to abandon his plot; the man who maintained his allegiance, bearing the imperial tally at the foreign court, and whose name was honored in the Qilin Pavilion; the man who asked to borrow a sword from the Directorate of Imperial Manufactories and, crying out loudly, broke the balustrade; and the man who, holding office as a tutor, refused to submit himself to the judicial officers. Some, when the seal and ribbon of office were bestowed upon them, immediately declined them; others, twice summoned with a carriage in which they could sit at ease, remained resolutely in bed. One rejected the advice offered beneath an ox-covering and willingly endured imprisonment; another rejected the analogy concerning Qu and, relying on the justice of his cause, brought about his own death. Removing a sword was a minor matter, yet one refused and requested leave to retire; removing one’s cap was customary, yet another held firm and relinquished office. These were all men renowned in the Western Han. Did they not revere moral integrity and righteousness?
There were men of steadfast faith who loved antiquity and taught others the classics, and men who studied the canonical writings comprehensively and analyzed doubtful and divergent interpretations. One edited and established the text of the Spring and Autumn Annals, giving rise to what was called the learning of Marquis Fan; another examined the prophetic charts and apocryphal texts, prompting the exclamation, “Our Way has gone east!” Brothers studied the Lu tradition of the Book of Odes, and scholars flocked to them; father and son elucidated the Zuo Commentary, providing a model for Confucian scholars. One lived in seclusion and taught, earning great renown west of the passes; another corrected and established the Five Classics, becoming the scholarly authority of his age. These were all men renowned in the Eastern Han. Did they not esteem classical learning? Why, then, make such one-sided statements? Classical learning was indeed esteemed in the Western Han; why, then, …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
授易者有持祿之譏擬易者有劇秦之
作博學經書者引申伯以阿鳳洽聞廣
見者獻符命以附新安在乎經術之尚
邪東漢之節義崇矣何有清世之志者
功隳于羣小負王佐之才者身殘于餘
孽破柱戮姦者名陷黨議登車攬轡者
禍及友朋安在乎節義之崇邪夫非經
術無以致用非節義無以勵俗崇之尚
之又各有其弊如此殆難乎其為士矣
===
然則必何如而後可試言之以觀其嚮
問天下之事有不可勝論者聊與爾諸士
子論學術可乎自宋大儒出謂為治必
法三代為學必宗孔孟申韓老莊之說
無所干於其間學者守為家法學術可
謂明矣然枝葉盛而本根隱其弊日滋
顧有病之者乃欲脫畧文字以求徑截
其所立亦或有可觀者徐考其歸乃佛
老之緒餘耳仁義之効遠而難見於是

老之緒餘耳仁義之効遠而難見於是

授易者有持祿之譏，擬易者有劇秦之作，博學經書者引申伯以阿鳳，洽聞廣見者獻符命以附新，安在乎經術之尚邪？東漢之節義崇矣，何有清世之志者功隳于羣小，負王佐之才者身殘于餘孽，破柱戮姦者名陷黨議，登車攬轡者禍及友朋，安在乎節義之崇邪？夫非經術無以致用，非節義無以勵俗，崇之尚之，又各有其弊如此，殆難乎其為士矣！然則必何如而後可？試言之，以觀其嚮。

問：天下之事有不可勝論者，聊與爾諸士子論學術，可乎？自宋大儒出，謂為治必法三代，為學必宗孔孟，申韓老莊之說無所干於其間，學者守為家法，學術可謂明矣。然枝葉盛而本根隱，其弊日滋。顧有病之者，乃欲脫畧文字以求徑截，其所立亦或有可觀者，徐考其歸，乃佛老之緒餘耳。仁義之効遠而難見，於是
translation_en:
…did a teacher of the Changes incur criticism for clinging to his stipend, and an imitator of the Changes compose Criticizing Qin (Ju Qin)? Why did one deeply learned in the classics invoke Shen Bo to flatter Feng, while another of extensive learning and broad knowledge presented auspicious tokens of Heaven’s mandate to attach himself to the Xin dynasty? Where, then, was the esteem for classical learning? Integrity and righteousness were exalted in the Eastern Han; why, then, did one intent on purifying the age have his achievements ruined by a crowd of petty men, and one endowed with the talent to assist a king suffer bodily destruction at the hands of surviving villains? Why was the man who smashed pillars and executed evildoers branded by accusations of factionalism, while the man who mounted his carriage and took up the reins brought disaster upon his friends? Where, then, was the exaltation of integrity and righteousness? Without classical learning, one cannot put learning to practical use; without integrity and righteousness, one cannot encourage good customs. Yet exalting the one and esteeming the other each brings abuses such as these. How difficult it must be to be a scholar! What, then, must one do to act rightly? Set forth your views, so that we may discern your inclination.

Question: The affairs of the world are too numerous to discuss exhaustively. Might we, for the present, discuss learning with you examination candidates? Since the great Confucian scholars of the Song emerged, they have maintained that government must take the Three Dynasties as its model, and learning must take Confucius and Mencius as its authorities. The teachings of Shen Buhai, Han Fei, Laozi, and Zhuangzi were to have no part in it. Scholars upheld this as the inherited discipline of their schools, and the principles of learning could be said to have become clear. Yet the branches and leaves flourished while the roots became obscured, and the resulting abuses grew daily. Some, troubled by this, sought to dispense with written texts and find a direct path. Their teachings sometimes had something worthy of consideration; but on closer examination, their ultimate tendency proved to be merely remnants of Buddhism and Daoism. The effects of benevolence and righteousness take time and are difficult to discern; consequently…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
有專事法術權操切以為治其効亦赫
然有稱徐考其歸則申商之粗迹耳夫
竊而用其似已足以取名而動衆使獲
用其全則舉世慕而趨之矣然儒者必
斥之不小假借亦有其說歟彼之所謂
法所謂術其用盖異也亦嘗考其言歟
儒者亦豈得而盡廢之至若無為無不
為之說則益與吾道幾矣將無同歟秦
嘗用商鞅以收富彊之効漢嘗用黄老
===
以成清淨之化然文具而無惻隱之實
秦以亟亡清談盛而晋衰謂非老莊之
罪不可盍究言之

然有稱徐考其歸則申商之粗迹耳夫
竊而用其似已足以取名而動衆使獲
用其全則舉世慕而趨之矣然儒者必
斥之不少假借亦有其說歟彼之所謂
法所謂術其用蓋異也亦嘗考其言歟
儒者亦豈得而盡廢之至若無爲無不
爲之說則益與吾道幾矣將無同歟秦
嘗用商鞅以收富彊之効漢嘗用黄老
以成清淨之化然文具而無惻隱之實
秦以亟亡清談盛而晉衰謂非老莊之
罪不可盡究言之
punctuated: 有專事法術權操切以為治，其効亦赫然有稱。徐考其歸，則申商之粗迹耳。夫竊而用其似，已足以取名而動衆；使獲用其全，則舉世慕而趨之矣。然儒者必斥之，不小假借，亦有其說歟？彼之所謂法、所謂術，其用盖異也，亦嘗考其言歟？儒者亦豈得而盡廢之？至若無為無不為之說，則益與吾道幾矣，將無同歟？秦嘗用商鞅以收富彊之効，漢嘗用黄老以成清淨之化。然文具而無惻隱之實，秦以亟亡；清談盛而晋衰，謂非老莊之罪不可。盍究言之？
translation_en:
…there are those who devote themselves exclusively to laws, techniques, and the harsh exercise of power [?] in governing; their results, too, are conspicuous and acclaimed. Yet, upon carefully examining where their practices lead, one finds only the crude traces of Shen Buhai and Shang Yang. Merely borrowing and employing a semblance of their teachings already suffices to win fame and sway the multitude; if someone could employ them in their entirety, the whole world would admire and follow them. Yet Confucians invariably reject them, allowing them not the slightest indulgence. Do they have grounds for this? What those thinkers call “laws” and what they call “techniques” presumably differ in their applications. Have you ever examined their statements? How, indeed, could Confucians discard them altogether? As for the teaching of “nonaction, yet leaving nothing undone,” it comes still closer to our Way. Might they actually be the same?

Qin once employed Shang Yang and thereby achieved wealth and strength; Han once employed the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi and thereby brought about tranquil government. Yet Qin possessed the outward forms without the substance of compassion, and consequently soon perished; pure conversation flourished and Jin declined—it cannot be said that Laozi and Zhuangzi bore no blame. Why not examine these matters thoroughly and discuss them?

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
可與言而不與之言失人不可與言而與
之言失言知者不失人亦不失言
潘潢
同考試官教諭陰批文字簡勁而理亦精到
他卷所不逮也
同考試官教授趙批言語最難中節易得有
失此作極其形容而嚴重不苟其知慎於用言者乎
===
考試官右諭德李批論語義善體貼當是作者
考試官侍讀學士汪批是殆可與言者
論人於語默動有所失惟知者能無所失蓋語
默而非其宜不失人則失言矣自非知者豈能
致决於此而兩無所失哉夫子之意蓋謂人之
相與固不能以無言然不可以不擇是故有可
與言者焉有不可與言者焉彼其中虛而能受
初筮而可告此人之可與言者也今乃邈焉而
不啟其端語焉而不竟其說則是道有可傳而

punctuated:
第壹場
四書
「可與言而不與之言，失人；不可與言而與之言，失言。知者不失人，亦不失言。」
潘潢
同考試官教諭陰批：文字簡勁，而理亦精到，他卷所不逮也。
同考試官教授趙批：言語最難中節，易得有失。此作極其形容，而嚴重不苟，其知慎於用言者乎？
考試官右諭德李批：論語義，善體貼，當是作者。
考試官侍讀學士汪批：是殆可與言者。
論人於語默，動有所失，惟知者能無所失。蓋語默而非其宜，不失人則失言矣。自非知者，豈能致决於此而兩無所失哉？夫子之意，蓋謂人之相與，固不能以無言，然不可以不擇。是故有可與言者焉，有不可與言者焉。彼其中虛而能受，初筮而可告，此人之可與言者也。今乃邈焉而不啟其端，語焉而不竟其說，則是道有可傳而
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books

“When someone may be spoken with, failing to speak with him is to lose the person. When someone may not be spoken with, speaking with him is to waste words. The wise lose neither people nor words.”

Pan Huang 潘潢

Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Instructor: “The writing is concise and vigorous, and its reasoning is also refined and exact. Other papers do not measure up to it.”

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Professor: “In speech, achieving the proper measure is most difficult, and mistakes are easily made. This composition describes the matter to the fullest, with gravity and care. Is its author someone who understands caution in the use of words?”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Mentor: “In discussing the meaning of the passage, he grasps it sympathetically and well. He must be an accomplished writer.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “Here surely is someone with whom one may speak.”

The point is that people, in speaking or remaining silent, are continually liable to error; only the wise can avoid all error. For if speech or silence is inappropriate, one either loses a person or wastes words. Unless one is wise, how can one reach a firm judgment here and avoid both kinds of loss? The Master’s meaning is, presumably, that in their dealings with one another people certainly cannot dispense with speech, yet they must exercise discernment. Thus there are those with whom one may speak, and those with whom one may not.

Someone whose mind is open and receptive, who may be instructed when he first seeks divination, is a person with whom one may speak. Yet if one now remains aloof and does not open the subject, or speaks but does not fully explain it, then the Way could be transmitted, yet …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
我自新之志有可繼而我固遺之非失人乎其
或語之而未達或拒之以不受此人之不可與
言者也今乃手携而示之事面命而提其耳則
是諄諄雖切投諸無用之地喋喋雖勤徒為無
益之談非失言乎夫惟知者則不然盖其藻鑑

我自新之志有可繼，而我固遺之，非失人乎？其或語之而未達，或拒之以不受，此人之不可與言者也。今乃手携而示之事，面命而提其耳，則是諄諄雖切，投諸無用之地；喋喋雖勤，徒為無益之談，非失言乎？夫惟知者則不然。盖其藻鑑清明，既别於賢否之辨；權度精切，復審於應接之機。苟其人之可與言也，則與之言，識大之賢、語上之才，皆於我乎收矣，曷嘗至於失人乎？苟其人之不可與言也，則不與之言，傷易之誕、傷煩之支，皆於我乎免矣，曷嘗至於失言乎？是則語黙之間，而得失所係有如此者，君子可不致謹於斯哉？考之夫子，不失言於陽貨，而終日之言獨盡於顔子；孟子不失言於王驩，而好辯之稱，不得已於公都。夫固有攸當也。知柔知剛，知微知彰，所謂知幾其神，而聖賢之妙用存焉，又豈特以知者稱而已哉？

踐其位，行其禮，奏其樂，敬其所尊，愛其所親。
translation_en:
…my resolve for self-renewal can be carried forward, yet I persist in neglecting him [?]. Is this not to lose a person? Some, when addressed, fail to understand; others reject what is said and refuse to accept it. These are people with whom one cannot profitably speak. Yet if one takes such a person by the hand to demonstrate matters, instructs him face to face, and even pulls his ear to impress the lesson upon him, then, however earnest the repeated admonitions, they fall where they can serve no purpose; however assiduous the chatter, it amounts only to useless talk. Is this not to waste words?

The wise alone act otherwise. Their discerning judgment is clear and lucid, enabling them to distinguish the worthy from the unworthy; their weighing of circumstances is precise, enabling them also to assess the right moment for responding to others. If someone can profitably be spoken with, they speak with him. Thus I gather to myself both worthy men who understand great matters and talented men with whom one can discuss higher things. How could I ever lose a person? If someone cannot profitably be spoken with, they do not speak with him. Thus I avoid both extravagant talk arising from excessive facility and rambling talk arising from excessive prolixity. How could I ever waste words?

Such, then, is what success and failure depend upon in speaking and remaining silent. Can the gentleman fail to exercise the utmost care here? Consider Confucius: he did not waste words on Yang Huo, yet it was to Yan Zi alone that he fully expounded his teaching throughout the day. Mencius did not waste words on Wang Huan, while, in addressing Gongdu, he explained that his reputation for fondness for disputation arose from necessity. Each response indeed had its proper occasion. To know the yielding and the firm, the subtle and the manifest—this is what is meant by saying that knowing the incipient signs is spirit-like. Herein lies the marvelous working of sages and worthies. How could they merit merely the designation ‘wise’?

Occupy their positions, perform their rites, play their music, revere those whom they honored, and love those whom they held dear.

text:
楊春芳
同考試官教諭魏批題本正大作者往往極
拾陳言令人厭觀晚得此卷能道人所不能道且詞
旨暢達讀之鏗然有餘韻噫子之所養其殆與人殊
乎
考試官右諭德李批語有所見塲中似此者絕少
考試官侍讀學士汪批其指先王也詞不費而義足
其詳見廟議可考是作盖得其說故錄
承先王之所貽者而仁先王之所厚者此聖人
===
之孝也盖先王之所以貽後人者甚備也既承
其所貽矣而於其所厚者豈容有所薄哉中庸
論武王周公之孝既詳其所制之禮而又結之
如此謂夫聖人之孝繼述為大繼述之善愛敬
為先彼負扆而朝卓乎大觀之在上嚮明而治
巍乎飛龍之在天人見聖人踐天子之位矣不
知垂創本于先王而我則纘其緒者也所踐者
非先王之位而何郊社禘嘗而禮無不具與天
地同其節雲咸韶濩而樂無不備與天地同其

楊春芳

同考試官教諭魏批：題本正大，作者往往極拾陳言，令人厭觀。晚得此卷，能道人所不能道，且詞旨暢達，讀之鏗然有餘韻。噫！子之所養，其殆與人殊乎！

考試官右諭德李批：語有所見，塲中似此者絕少。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：其指先王也，詞不費而義足。其詳見廟議，可考。是作盖得其說，故錄。

承先王之所貽者，而仁先王之所厚者，此聖人之孝也。盖先王之所以貽後人者甚備也，既承其所貽矣，而於其所厚者，豈容有所薄哉？中庸論武王周公之孝，既詳其所制之禮，而又結之如此，謂夫聖人之孝，繼述為大；繼述之善，愛敬為先。彼負扆而朝，卓乎大觀之在上；嚮明而治，巍乎飛龍之在天。人見聖人踐天子之位矣，不知垂創本于先王，而我則纘其緒者也。所踐者，非先王之位而何？郊社禘嘗，而禮無不具，與天地同其節；雲咸韶濩，而樂無不備，與天地同其
translation_en:
Yang Chunfang

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: The topic is inherently upright and grand, yet writers often merely collect stale expressions [?], making their work tiresome to read. Late in the examination I obtained this script. It expresses what others cannot express, and its language and meaning flow freely and clearly. Read aloud, it rings out with a lingering resonance. Ah! Surely what you have cultivated within yourself is different from that of others!

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: These words show insight. Scripts like this are exceedingly rare in the examination hall.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “Their” refers to the former kings. The language is economical, yet the meaning is fully conveyed. The details appear in the deliberations on ancestral temples and can be consulted. This composition seems to have grasped that interpretation; hence its inclusion.

To inherit what the former kings bequeathed, and to treat benevolently those whom the former kings treated generously: this is the filial piety of the sage. What the former kings provided for later generations was indeed comprehensive. Having inherited their legacy, how could one possibly slight those whom they treated generously? In discussing the filial piety of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, the Doctrine of the Mean first details the rites they instituted and then concludes in these terms. This means that, in the filial piety of the sage, carrying on the intentions and undertakings of predecessors is paramount; and in carrying them on well, love and reverence come first.

With his back to the ceremonial screen, he holds court, standing loftily above as a magnificent spectacle; facing the light, he governs, towering like a flying dragon in the heavens. People see that the sage occupies the position of the Son of Heaven. They do not understand that the foundation of this enduring enterprise originated with the former kings, and that I am continuing their work. What position does he occupy, if not that of the former kings? In the suburban sacrifices to Heaven, sacrifices to the soil, the di ancestral sacrifice, and the autumn offering, no rite is lacking; their measured order accords with that of Heaven and Earth. In the Yun, Xian, Shao, and Huo music, no music is lacking; it shares with Heaven and Earth their…

text:
□□先聖人用天子之禮樂矣不知制作出於
□□而我則紹其傳者也其所行者非先王之
□所奏者非先王之樂而何若夫先王之所尊
者祖考也吾獨弛其所尊可乎於是致孝享於
假廟之時嚴對越於昭格之頃修廟陳器而報
本追遠之意不少衰焉設衣薦食而尊祖敬宗
之禮不少替焉是則先王雖往而其尊尊之義
不與之而俱往矣先王之所親者子孫臣庶也
吾獨遺其所親可乎於是惇親睦之情於九族
===
隆手足之愛於羣工序爵序事而禮敬之施無
不備焉逮賤序齒而恩意之推無不周焉是則
先王雖遠而其親親之惠不與之而俱遠矣位
也禮也樂也先王之所貽者自我承之至於尊
也親也先王之所厚者我則篤之而不敢薄焉
則其繼述之善也為何如哉此武王周公所以
為孝之至歟嗟夫人之情所賴乎其後者無貴
賤無大小欲其有所繼述而已故繼志述事謂
之達孝然而克盡其道者其惟聖人乎故特舉

translation_en:
…[?] the sages employ the rites and music of the Son of Heaven, yet it is not understood that these institutions originated with [illegible], and that I merely continue their transmission. Are not the rites [?] they perform those of the former kings, and the music they play likewise that of the former kings? Those whom the former kings honored were their ancestors. Could I alone grow lax in honoring those whom they honored? Thus, on entering the ancestral temple, I offer sacrifices with filial devotion; when the spirits manifest their presence, I attend upon them with solemn reverence. In maintaining the temples and arranging the vessels, the intention to repay our origins and commemorate distant ancestors never diminishes. In laying out garments and presenting food, the rites of honoring ancestors and revering the lineage never fall into neglect. Thus, although the former kings have departed, their principle of honoring the honored does not depart with them. Those whom the former kings cherished were their descendants, ministers, and common people. Could I alone neglect those whom they cherished? Thus I deepen affection and harmony among the nine degrees of kinship and strengthen brotherly love toward all officials. In ordering participants by rank and assigning their ceremonial duties, every expression of ritual respect is fully provided; in extending participation to the lowly and ordering participants by age, every kindness is extended to all. Thus, although the former kings grow distant, their benevolence in cherishing their kin does not grow distant with them.

The throne, the rites, and the music: these are what the former kings bequeathed, and I inherit them. As for honoring and cherishing others, I deepen my devotion toward those whom the former kings treated generously, never daring to slight them. How excellent, then, is such continuation of their purposes and deeds! Is this not why King Wu and the Duke of Zhou exemplify filial piety at its utmost? Alas! In human feeling, what people depend upon their descendants for—whether noble or lowly, great or small—is simply that they continue their purposes and deeds. Hence, carrying forward their intentions and continuing their undertakings is called universally acknowledged filial piety. Yet surely only sages can fully realize this way! Thus, the text especially singles out…

大賢言，人能推其所有，則仁義在是矣。盖不忍不為，仁義之端，人之所必有也。茍能自此而推之，則仁義豈外是哉？昔孟子之意，以為人知仁義之難全，而不知求之為至易，在識其端而推
translation_en:
…and ascribes it to King Wu and the Duke of Zhou. Only a benevolent person can offer sacrifice acceptably to the Lord on High; only a filial son can offer sacrifice acceptably to his parents. Once one understands this teaching, the way of serving Heaven likewise lies within it.

Everyone has things he cannot bear to do; extending this feeling to what he can bear to do is benevolence. Everyone has things he will not do; extending this restraint to what he does do is righteousness.

Wu Huai

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: In discussing “extending,” many examination papers explain it in terms of “filling out,” gravely departing from the original purport. This essay grounds its argument in “extending outward,” fully capturing Mencius’s intention in making this statement. Its wording is concise and apt, and its literary brilliance abundant. The author has evidently devoted thought to seeking benevolence and righteousness; his essay deserves inclusion among those selected.

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: Essays on the meaning of the Mencius are not difficult to write, yet even in the examination hall few are as clear and precise as this one.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: When Mencius speaks of benevolence and righteousness, his words are this plain and grounded. Those who write essays interpreting them, however, commonly err through excessive elaboration and rambling. This essay is precise, closely reasoned, and orderly; it merits attention.

The great worthy says that if people can extend what they already possess, benevolence and righteousness lie therein. For what one cannot bear to do and what one will not do are the beginnings of benevolence and righteousness, which everyone necessarily possesses. If one can extend outward from these, how could benevolence and righteousness lie beyond them? Mencius’s intention was that people recognize the difficulty of fully realizing benevolence and righteousness but do not recognize that seeking them is utterly easy: it lies in recognizing their beginnings and extending…

text:
充之耳是故惻隱形於見聞所及孰無不忍之
心乎不忍者仁之端宜念念之皆仁矣然或拘
於氣稟之偏奪於物欲之蔽而於他事有忍之
者心雖暫忍而其本然之天猶夫故也于焉驗
所感之不殊思所發之頓異推不忍而達之於
所忍使所忍者亦不忍焉則一心之內渾然天
理之周流情得其正而慈惠無窮何往而非仁
邪羞惡著於行己之際孰無不為之心乎不為
者義之端宜事事之皆義矣然或局於稟賦之
===
凡移於私邪之誘而於他事有為之者事雖暫
為而其全體之正未嘗息也于焉審事理之無
二思從違之罔同推不為而達之於所為俾所
為者亦不為焉則萬感之間粹然天德之呈露
心得其職而愧恥常存何往而非義邪是則仁
義之用甚廣而其端之推也其易如此人亦何
憚而不為哉嗟夫戰國之時上下馳騖於功利
知所謂仁義者鮮矣矧能擴而充之邪孟子七
篇之作拳拳於四端之論而此章指言仁義之

punctuated: 充之耳。是故惻隱形於見聞所及，孰無不忍之心乎？不忍者，仁之端，宜念念之皆仁矣。然或拘於氣稟之偏，奪於物欲之蔽，而於他事有忍之者。心雖暫忍，而其本然之天猶夫故也。于焉驗所感之不殊，思所發之頓異，推不忍而達之於所忍，使所忍者亦不忍焉，則一心之內，渾然天理之周流，情得其正而慈惠無窮，何往而非仁邪？羞惡著於行己之際，孰無不為之心乎？不為者，義之端，宜事事之皆義矣。然或局於稟賦之凡，移於私邪之誘，而於他事有為之者。事雖暫為，而其全體之正未嘗息也。于焉審事理之無二，思從違之罔同，推不為而達之於所為，俾所為者亦不為焉，則萬感之間，粹然天德之呈露，心得其職而愧恥常存，何往而非義邪？是則仁義之用甚廣，而其端之推也，其易如此，人亦何憚而不為哉？嗟夫！戰國之時，上下馳騖於功利，知所謂仁義者鮮矣，矧能擴而充之邪？孟子七篇之作，拳拳於四端之論，而此章指言仁義之
translation_en:
…and bringing them to fullness, that is all. Thus, when compassion manifests itself in response to what one sees and hears, who lacks a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others? This inability to bear suffering is the beginning of benevolence; every thought should therefore be benevolent. Yet some people, constrained by the partiality of their endowment of vital force and overcome by the obscuring effects of material desires, can bear suffering in other situations. Though the heart may momentarily bear it, its original Heaven-given nature remains as before. One should then examine how the things that move one are alike and consider why the responses they elicit differ so sharply. Extend the inability to bear suffering to those instances in which one can bear it, so that there too one cannot bear it. Then, within the heart, Heaven’s principle will circulate as an undivided whole; the feelings will attain their proper balance, and kindness and generosity will be inexhaustible. Where could one go without being benevolent?

When shame and aversion manifest themselves in one’s conduct, who lacks a heart that refuses to do certain things? This refusal is the beginning of righteousness; every action should therefore be righteous. Yet some people, limited by the mediocrity of their natural endowments and swayed by selfish and depraved temptations, do certain things in other circumstances. Though they may momentarily do them, the rectitude of their whole nature has never ceased to exist. One should then discern that the principles governing these matters are the same and consider why one follows them in some cases and violates them in others. Extend the refusal to act to those instances in which one does act, so that there too one refuses. Then, amid the myriad things that move one, Heaven’s virtue will manifest itself in its purity; the heart will fulfill its office, and a sense of shame will always remain. Where could one go without being righteous?

Thus, although the workings of benevolence and righteousness are exceedingly broad, extending their beginnings is as easy as this. What should people fear that keeps them from doing so? Alas! In the Warring States period, those above and below alike raced after achievement and profit. Few understood what benevolence and righteousness meant, much less could they enlarge them and bring them to fullness. Throughout the seven books of the Mengzi, Mencius earnestly discusses the four beginnings, and this chapter expressly identifies the beginnings of benevolence and righteousness…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
端尤爲明切下文又獨以義反復言之蓋□□
不仁非義害之也非義絶而後仁可存遏□□
人欲而存天理孟子之功不在禹下者其此類
也夫
易
大觀在上順而巽中正以觀天下
吳淮
同考試官教諭趙批中正雖指九五其實德
也作者不察俱以道言則非矣認理真切而措詞雅
===
實者無踰此篇錄之以釋羣疑
考試官右諭德李批典重不浮是之取爾
考試官侍讀學士汪批簡而明是作易義法
爲觀于上而德足以副其觀此觀之所由名也
盖觀之爲道不徒以其位而貴有其德也即卦
之所具者而觀之則觀之爲觀從可知矣彖傳
以卦之體德釋卦名義如此意謂坤巽合體卦
名曰觀伏羲義豈無所取邪誠以卦體九五一
陽在上四陰仰而觀之則是人君出震繼離興

translation_en:
…the beginnings are explained with particular clarity and precision. In the following text, he again speaks repeatedly of righteousness alone. For □□ inhumanity [?] is caused by what is unrighteous. Only after unrighteousness has been eliminated can humaneness be preserved: restraining □□ human desires and preserving Heaven’s principle. That Mencius’s achievement was no less than Yu’s surely lies in things of this kind!

Book of Changes

“A great exemplar stands above; compliant and yielding, central and correct, he displays himself to all under Heaven.”

Wu Huai 吳淮

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “Although ‘central and correct’ refers to the nine in the fifth place, it actually denotes virtue. Writers fail to discern this and all explain it in terms of the Way, which is mistaken. In its precise grasp of principle and its elegant, substantial phrasing, no essay surpasses this one. It is recorded here to resolve the doubts of all.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: “Dignified and weighty, without superficiality: this is why I select it.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “Concise and clear: this is the method for writing an exposition on the Book of Changes.”

To stand above as an exemplar, with virtue sufficient to match what one displays: this is how the hexagram Guan acquired its name. For the way of Guan does not depend on position alone; what matters is possessing the corresponding virtue. If we examine what the hexagram itself embodies, we can understand why Guan is Guan. In this manner the Commentary on the Judgments explains the meaning of the hexagram’s name through its structure and virtues. Its purport is that Kun and Xun combine to form the hexagram named Guan. Could Fuxi have chosen this meaning without a basis? Indeed, in the hexagram’s structure, the single yang line, the nine in the fifth place, stands above, and the four yin lines look up to contemplate it. This represents the ruler emerging in Zhen and succeeding in Li, rising…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
於大寶羣黎百姓頼之以安養以一人而撫
萬邦也握乾闡坤端拱於南面九州八荒藉之
以統治以四海而仰一人也其位固足以爲觀
矣然使德有未備何以副海内之望邪卦德内
坤外巽爲順而巽是乃積於中者有從容和順
之美施於外者無驕矜凌厲之失溫柔寬裕粹
乎可親其所以爲人之利見者盖不獨其位之
尊矣五居上之中得陽之正是乃無過不及而
建中于民不偏不倚而表正于下齊莊中正儼
===
然可像其所以爲人之瞻仰者盖不但其勢之
崇矣是則位足觀也而必本於德德能觀也而
實資於位卦之德位兼隆如此名之爲觀良有
以哉抑伏羲名卦之義可謂精且盡矣文王繫
辭又有所謂盥而不薦有孚顒若者何邪盖君
者民之表一身之小而四方刑焉使輕於自用
則於觀之道有歉臣下將何所儀法哉此所以
必貴乎有始盥之誠而後觀之道可庶幾也噫
小心翼翼萬邦作孚文王其殆以心身而明易

punctuated: 於大寶，羣黎百姓頼之以安養，以一人而撫萬邦也。握乾闡坤，端拱於南面，九州八荒藉之以統治，以四海而仰一人也。其位固足以爲觀矣，然使德有未備，何以副海内之望邪？卦德内坤外巽，爲順而巽，是乃積於中者有從容和順之美，施於外者無驕矜凌厲之失，溫柔寬裕，粹乎可親。其所以爲人之利見者，盖不獨其位之尊矣。五居上之中，得陽之正，是乃無過不及而建中于民，不偏不倚而表正于下，齊莊中正，儼然可像。其所以爲人之瞻仰者，盖不但其勢之崇矣。是則位足觀也，而必本於德；德能觀也，而實資於位。卦之德位兼隆如此，名之爲觀，良有以哉！抑伏羲名卦之義，可謂精且盡矣。文王繫辭，又有所謂「盥而不薦，有孚顒若」者，何邪？盖君者民之表，一身之小而四方刑焉。使輕於自用，則於觀之道有歉，臣下將何所儀法哉？此所以必貴乎有始盥之誠，而後觀之道可庶幾也。噫！「小心翼翼，萬邦作孚。」文王其殆以心身而明易
translation_en:
…to the imperial throne: the common people rely upon him for peaceful sustenance, and one man thus cherishes the myriad states. Grasping Heaven’s authority and unfolding Earth’s efficacy, he sits facing south with hands reverently folded; the Nine Provinces and Eight Wildernesses depend upon him for orderly government, and all within the Four Seas thus look up to one man. His position is certainly sufficient to make him an object of contemplation. Yet if his virtue were incomplete, how could he fulfill the hopes of all within the seas?

The hexagram’s attributes, with Kun within and Xun without, are compliance and yielding. Thus, what he accumulates within possesses the beauty of composure, harmony, and compliance; what he manifests outwardly is free from the faults of arrogance and overbearing severity. Gentle, generous, and forbearing, he is wholly approachable. The reason people find it beneficial to behold him therefore lies beyond the exalted nature of his position alone. The fifth line occupies the center of the upper trigram and possesses the correctness proper to a yang line. Thus, neither exceeding nor falling short, he establishes the mean among the people; neither biased nor partial, he serves as a standard of rectitude for those below. Reverent, dignified, centered, and correct, he is an imposing model for emulation. The reason people look up to him therefore lies beyond the eminence of his power alone.

Thus, although his position makes him worthy of contemplation, it must be grounded in virtue; although his virtue makes him an object of contemplation, it is indeed aided by his position. With virtue and position alike exalted in this hexagram, there is good reason to name it Guan, or Contemplation! Indeed, the meaning embodied in Fuxi’s naming of the hexagram may be called both subtle and exhaustive. Why, then, does King Wen’s appended statement also say, “Having washed the hands, but not yet presented the offering; possessed of sincerity, with a solemn demeanor”? The ruler is the people’s model: although he is but one person, the four quarters take him as their pattern. If he rashly relies on his own judgment, he falls short of the way of Contemplation. What, then, could his subjects take as their model? This is why he must prize the sincerity present at the initial washing of the hands; only then can he come close to realizing the way of Contemplation.

Ah! “Careful and reverent, he became the trust of the myriad states.” Was it perhaps through his own heart and person that King Wen illuminated the Changes…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
爲之易也歟
君子上交不諂下交不瀆其知幾乎
王守
同考試官教諭趙批不諂不瀆夫人能言之
至知幾處則寂寥數語豈幾微未易形容邪此篇獨
能發揮是可以占子之蘊矣
考試官右諭德李批講知幾處與人異
考試官侍讀學士汪批得旨
大傳即君子交際之審著君子見幾之明蓋交
===
際之間幾之所寓也非君子見之之明抑安能
審所處之各當哉大傳釋豫六二爻義如此且
天下之事未嘗無幾而見幾之明則唯君子盍
於交際觀之乎是故人之所與其交不能無在
上者也上交不諂者鮮矣君子於趨承之間唯
持當行之禮雖曰祗畏之克盡而大節之罔虧
貌當恭也不足恭以取容言當遜也不甘臨以
希悅未嘗至於諂焉人之所接其交不能無在
下者也下交不瀆者寡矣君子於接引之際常

punctuated:
爲之易也歟？

君子上交不諂，下交不瀆，其知幾乎？

王守

同考試官教諭趙批：不諂不瀆，夫人能言之；至知幾處，則寂寥數語，豈幾微未易形容邪？此篇獨能發揮，是可以占子之蘊矣。

考試官右諭德李批：講知幾處，與人異。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：得旨。

大傳即君子交際之審，著君子見幾之明。蓋交際之間，幾之所寓也。非君子見之之明，抑安能審所處之各當哉？大傳釋豫六二爻義如此。且天下之事未嘗無幾，而見幾之明則唯君子，盍於交際觀之乎？是故人之所與，其交不能無在上者也。上交不諂者鮮矣。君子於趨承之間，唯持當行之禮，雖曰祗畏之克盡，而大節之罔虧。貌當恭也，不足恭以取容；言當遜也，不甘臨以希悅。未嘗至於諂焉。人之所接，其交不能無在下者也。下交不瀆者寡矣。君子於接引之際，常
translation_en:
…and so composed the Changes, did he not?

“The gentleman, in associating with those above him, does not flatter; in associating with those below him, he is not disrespectfully familiar. Does he not understand the incipient signs of things?”

Wang Shou

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “Anyone can speak of avoiding flattery and disrespectful familiarity. Yet when it comes to understanding incipient signs, there are only a few sparse words. Is it because such subtle beginnings are difficult to describe? This essay alone can expound them fully; from it one can judge the depth of your understanding.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: “His explanation of understanding incipient signs differs from that of others.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: “Grasps the essential meaning.”

The Great Commentary uses the gentleman’s discernment in his dealings with others to demonstrate his clarity in perceiving incipient signs. For it is within human dealings that these signs reside. Without the gentleman’s clarity of perception, how could he discern the appropriate course in each situation? Such is the Great Commentary’s explanation of the second, yin line of the hexagram Yu (Enthusiasm). Moreover, no affair in the world is ever without incipient signs, yet only the gentleman perceives them clearly. Why not observe this in his dealings with others?

Among those with whom a person associates, there will inevitably be some above him. Few associate with those above them without flattery. When attending upon his superiors, the gentleman adheres only to the propriety that ought to govern his conduct. Although he fully manifests reverence and awe, he does not compromise his fundamental integrity. text:
存禮遇之心雖曰詞色之是假而禮貌之不衰
敬之如賓而簡傲不事也待如長者而惰慢不
施也未甞至於瀆焉若是者不其知幾乎盖上
交貴恭遜恭遜一形而不加察焉諂斯至矣事
在毫忽之間而得失所由分也今於易流之地
乃有特立不移之節非其明炳幾先而燭理之
微者安能不諂邪下交貴和易和易一生而不
知省焉瀆斯蹈矣心在擬議之頃而當否所由
判也今於可忽之時不失當然不易之則非其
===
聰明先物而見事幾之審者安能不瀆邪是則
一交際之間而能知幾若此所貴於君子者有
如是夫抑幾之為說其義廣矣周子曰幾善惡
又曰誠神幾夫子乃獨以交際言之何邪盖事
之最近而幾之易忽者莫如交際苟于斯審焉
則餘可以類推矣然非有安靜之德則亦莫之
能也故曰介于石不終日貞吉有事于知幾者
當自謹德始

存禮遇之心，雖曰詞色之是假，而禮貌之不衰。敬之如賓，而簡傲不事也；待如長者，而惰慢不施也。未甞至於瀆焉。若是者，不其知幾乎？盖上交貴恭遜，恭遜一形而不加察焉，諂斯至矣。事在毫忽之間，而得失所由分也。今於易流之地，乃有特立不移之節，非其明炳幾先而燭理之微者，安能不諂邪？下交貴和易，和易一生而不知省焉，瀆斯蹈矣。心在擬議之頃，而當否所由判也。今於可忽之時，不失當然不易之則，非其聰明先物而見事幾之審者，安能不瀆邪？是則一交際之間，而能知幾若此，所貴於君子者有如是夫！抑幾之為說，其義廣矣。周子曰：「幾，善惡。」又曰：「誠、神、幾。」夫子乃獨以交際言之，何邪？盖事之最近而幾之易忽者，莫如交際。苟于斯審焉，則餘可以類推矣。然非有安靜之德，則亦莫之能也。故曰：「介于石，不終日，貞吉。」有事于知幾者，當自謹德始。

translation_en:
…maintains a disposition to treat them courteously. Though he accords them kindly words and expressions, his respectful demeanor does not diminish. He respects them as guests, never behaving with dismissive arrogance; he treats them as elders, never showing negligence or disdain. He never lapses into undue familiarity. Does not such a person understand the incipient signs of change?

In associating with superiors, respect and deference are prized. Yet once respect and deference take outward form, unless one scrutinizes them, flattery follows. The matter turns on the slightest distinction, but it is there that right and wrong diverge. Now, in circumstances where one can easily drift astray, he maintains an independent and unwavering integrity. Unless his insight illuminates what precedes the first stirrings and penetrates the subtleties of principle, how could he avoid flattery? In associating with inferiors, affability and ease are prized. Yet once affability and ease arise, unless one reflects upon them, one lapses into undue familiarity. The mind is poised at the instant of deliberation, but it is there that propriety and impropriety are distinguished. Now, at a moment when carelessness is possible, he does not lose the constant standard of what is right. Unless his perceptiveness anticipates events and clearly discerns their incipient signs, how could he avoid undue familiarity? Thus, even within social intercourse alone, he can understand the incipient signs to this degree. Such is what we prize in the gentleman!

Yet the meaning of incipience is broad. Master Zhou said, “Incipience: good and evil.” He also said, “Sincerity, spiritual efficacy, incipience.” Why, then, did the Master speak of it solely in terms of social intercourse? Among matters closest to hand, none presents incipient signs more easily overlooked than social intercourse. If one discerns them carefully here, the rest may be inferred by analogy. Yet without the virtue of calm tranquility, no one can accomplish this. Hence it is said: “Firm as a rock; not waiting out the day. Constancy brings good fortune.” Those who apply themselves to understanding incipient signs should begin by attending carefully to their virtue.

乎上天若可逸也然去留無常天命之難諶者
此位也豈可以不謹乎端拱穆清而撫臨乎兆
庶若可肆也然從違靡定而民心之難保者此
位也豈可以不慎乎地平天成已治矣而制治
于未亂者一念不可以自遑焉民給邦乂已安
矣而保邦于未危者一日不容以少間焉於是
帝舜一聞于耳即契于心而應之曰俞盖以非

…before Heaven above, he might seem free to take his ease. Yet whether Heaven’s mandate remains or departs is uncertain: this is the position in which that mandate is difficult to trust. How could he fail to be vigilant? Sitting with hands folded in solemn tranquillity and presiding over the countless people, he might seem free to indulge himself. Yet their obedience or defiance is unsettled: this is the position in which the people’s allegiance is difficult to preserve. How could he fail to exercise care? The earth has been brought to order and Heaven’s work accomplished; good government has already been achieved. Yet to secure order before disorder arises, he must not allow himself repose even for a single thought. The people have enough and the realm is well governed; peace has already been achieved. Yet to preserve the realm before danger arises, he must not permit even a slight lapse for a single day.

Thus, as soon as Emperor Shun heard these words, they accorded with his heart, and he replied, “Yes!” For an extraordinary position entails extraordinary responsibilities, and it is I who truly bear them: are not your words my divining turtle and mirror? Boundless blessings also entail boundless anxieties, and I lack the strength to bear them: is not your counsel my medicine and healing stone? A single careless thought bequeaths sorrow to all within the Four Seas; the admonition to exercise care in one’s position is an excellent plan for securing order. A single careless day brings calamities lasting hundreds or thousands of years; the instruction to exercise care in one’s position is the essential way to preserve the realm. Ah! In the court of Yu, ruler and ministers exchanged their words of praise and assent within a single hall, and what they said never went beyond this. This too can serve as a mirror.

Alas! All under Heaven is a weighty vessel. The sage exercises care in everything; how much more so when presiding over all under Heaven! translation_en:
…□ [illegible]. In everything expressed in his government and manifested in his undertakings, he fears only that it might not accord with the hearts of the people. He abides in nothing but benevolence and acts upon nothing but righteousness: everything embodied in his own person is a standard for all under Heaven. He draws close to every worthy person and invariably dismisses those guilty of wrongdoing: everything he bequeaths to later generations is a plan for enduring rule. With such devotion to doing good, how could he allow himself any complacency? Thus he rises early and retires late, fulfilling every obligation incumbent upon his station, yet still dares not take comfort in his accomplishments. By day he acts; by night he gains further understanding. He attends fully to everything within his power, yet still dares not feel satisfied. Has he failed to preserve benevolence? Has he failed to move toward righteousness? The days and months hasten past as though they would never return. Are there worthy men he has not yet promoted? Are there wicked men he has not yet put at a distance? The years and months pass as though they would not wait for him. If, in doing good, he feels only that the days are insufficient, how could his goodness ever come to an end? Who but an auspicious man could attain this?

Generally, yin and yang, day and night, stand opposed to one another. An auspicious man's devotion to goodness is like an inauspicious man's devotion to evil. Good and ill fortune are outcomes they bring upon themselves, and these terms consequently become designations for the people themselves. Is not the intention of the ancients in handing down this admonition most profound? If an inauspicious man redirected the heart that finds the days insufficient and turned toward goodness, who could stop him? Thus it is said: “If the reckless man can become mindful, he becomes a sage.” Alas, Zhou could not be brought to understand this, and the military expedition at Mengjin could not be halted. How lamentable!

六親之謂孝天倫克盡而爲宗族所稱又有所
謂能孝者矣得於已者之謂德善體諸身而爲
國人所賢又有所謂有德者矣以斯人也使之

translation_en:
… remonstrating ministers who can assist the king—can there be none such? The ability to serve one’s six categories of kin is called filial piety. Those who fully discharge their natural family obligations and win the praise of their lineage are what we call men capable of filial piety. What one attains within oneself is called virtue. Those who embody goodness in their own persons and are esteemed as worthy by the people of the realm are what we call men possessed of virtue. Have such men stand at the royal court and lead the king forward: they will not merely set forth goodness and ward off evil; their pure virtue and admirable conduct will themselves exert a gradual, beneficial influence. Have them dwell in the king’s presence and assist him on either side: they will not merely offer loyal counsel and guide him toward goodness; their demeanor and reputation will themselves transform him imperceptibly. Thus the king’s nature will advance daily toward loftiness and illumination, and his virtue will become truly cultivated; his mind will daily grow broader and more far-reaching, and his person will thereby be set aright.

All our common people who behold the king’s bearing will naturally hasten to take him as their model. The multitudes who look up to his deportment will unanimously emulate it, fearing to fall behind. Those far away look toward him with hope, and those nearby never tire of him. Why do those who admire his kindly and gracious influence follow the same course, near and far alike? Because the king’s goodness gathers together the goodness of the many. There he is not hated; here he is never wearisome. Why do those who aspire to the beauty of his joyous ease share one standard, here and there alike? Because the worthiness of the many becomes the king’s own worthiness. If this is so, he may occupy Heaven’s throne without disgrace and receive Heaven’s emoluments without end, while his royal excursions become ever more splendid. Such is the assistance gained from worthy men. How could I, Shi, dare fail to set this before my king?

Ah! A time of supreme harmony and perfect order is precisely when those above and below should admonish one another. Even amid the flourishing court of Yu, there was Gao Yao …

translation_en:
…Gao Yao’s responsive song. The ancients’ care over the slightest matters was surely never relaxed even a little. King Cheng inherited the legacy of Kings Wen and Wu while still very young. During the excursion celebrated in “Winding Hills” (Juan’e), if the Duke of Shao had not seized the opportunity to admonish him, what purpose would his office as tutor and guardian have served? Thus, having first stirred the king’s aspirations with blessings and emoluments in the preceding stanza, he subsequently spoke to him of an abundance of talented men. His guidance, encouragement, and support were consummate. Thereafter King Cheng appointed the worthy and employed the capable, ultimately becoming an excellent ruler of the Zhou. Can one say that he gained nothing from the Duke of Shao’s admonition?

“Heaven’s mandate descended in watchful scrutiny; the people below held him in reverence. Neither exceeding due bounds nor acting indiscriminately, he dared not idle or take his ease. Heaven charged him with the realm below and firmly established his blessings.”
Zhang Fenglai

Comment by Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor: The Shang people’s praise of the reasons for Gaozong’s restoration of their dynasty is summed up in the single phrase ‘neither exceeding due bounds nor acting indiscriminately.’ Writers who do not understand where their argument should lead become tiresomely prolix and vague. Can many pieces be found that possess the standards and order of this one?

Comment by Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor: The topic is inherently grand and dignified, and writers can generally make an essay of it. Yet they are particularly deficient in bringing out how Gaozong united Heaven and humanity as one. In this essay one can discern an accomplished master.

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: In interpreting a hymn, precision and rigor are prized; this essay alone grasps its purport. Qi [?] is surely skilled in explaining the Poetry.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: This writer, too, is skilled in discussing the relationship between Heaven and humanity.

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
知天之不能外乎民則知聖人之所以得天
盖天因於民得民斯得天矣然則高宗受天命
之隆者豈無自而然哉此商人祀高宗之樂歌
謂我高宗之中興也外服遠夷內懐諸夏天實
命之而致此者豈無其道乎誠以仰瞻彼天蒼
蒼之表有予有奪而每鑒觀乎萬方者非自用
其聰明也惟民是託焉耳冥冥之中有禍有福
而每照臨乎下土者非自役其視聽也惟民是
寄焉耳是則俯視斯民其微若可忽矣而天實
===
在焉可忽之而不敬乎其近若可狎矣而天實
寓焉可狎之而不畏乎我高宗知其然賞一人
也必民心之所共好奉天之命何有於僭差然
尤不敢以自怠焉罰一人也必民心之所共惡
致天之討何有於濫及然尤不敢以自遑焉由
是克享天心集此大命合人心於已離而天下
為之大定保佑之命方申而無窮也振王綱於
既墜而商業為之再興隆昌之運自是其有永
也謂之大建厥福信乎其福之無以加矣吁上

知天之不能外乎民，則知聖人之所以得天。

盖天因於民，得民斯得天矣。然則高宗受天命之隆者，豈無自而然哉？此商人祀高宗之樂歌，謂我高宗之中興也，外服遠夷，內懐諸夏，天實命之，而致此者豈無其道乎？誠以仰瞻彼天，蒼蒼之表，有予有奪，而每鑒觀乎萬方者，非自用其聰明也，惟民是託焉耳；冥冥之中，有禍有福，而每照臨乎下土者，非自役其視聽也，惟民是寄焉耳。是則俯視斯民，其微若可忽矣，而天實在焉，可忽之而不敬乎？其近若可狎矣，而天實寓焉，可狎之而不畏乎？我高宗知其然，賞一人也，必民心之所共好，奉天之命，何有於僭差？然尤不敢以自怠焉。罰一人也，必民心之所共惡，致天之討，何有於濫及？然尤不敢以自遑焉。由是克享天心，集此大命，合人心於已離，而天下為之大定，保佑之命方申而無窮也；振王綱於既墜，而商業為之再興，隆昌之運自是其有永也。謂之大建厥福，信乎其福之無以加矣。吁！上
translation_en:
To understand that Heaven cannot be separate from the people is to understand how the sage wins Heaven’s favor.

Heaven follows the people: win the people, and one thereby wins Heaven. Could the abundance of the mandate that Gaozong received from Heaven, then, have come about without a cause? This sacrificial hymn sung by the people of Shang in worship of Gaozong speaks of our Gaozong’s restoration of the dynasty. Abroad he brought distant foreign peoples into submission; at home he won the allegiance of the various Xia states. Heaven indeed ordained this. Yet could there have been no proper way by which he accomplished it?

For when we look up toward Heaven, beyond its azure expanse it grants and takes away, constantly surveying the myriad regions. It does not exercise its perceptiveness on its own authority: it entrusts this solely to the people. Within its unseen depths lie calamity and blessing, and it constantly shines upon and oversees the earth below. It does not employ its sight and hearing independently: it lodges them solely with the people. Thus, looking down upon these people, their lowliness might seem to permit neglect; yet Heaven is truly present among them. Can one neglect them and fail to show reverence? Their familiarity might seem to permit overfamiliar treatment; yet Heaven truly dwells among them. Can one treat them slightingly and fail to stand in awe?

Our Gaozong understood this. Whenever he rewarded someone, that person was necessarily one whom the people’s hearts alike approved. In carrying out Heaven’s command, how could there be any improper or mistaken bestowal? Yet he dared all the less to grow remiss. Whenever he punished someone, that person was necessarily one whom the people’s hearts alike detested. In executing Heaven’s chastisement, how could punishment extend indiscriminately to others? Yet he dared all the less to allow himself repose.

Thus he succeeded in pleasing Heaven’s heart and securing this great mandate. He reunited the people’s hearts after they had become estranged, and through this brought profound peace to all under Heaven; Heaven’s charge to protect and aid him was being renewed without end. He restored the ordering principles of kingship after their collapse, and through this the enterprise of Shang flourished anew; from this time onward its era of prosperity would endure. To call this “greatly establishing his blessings” is fitting indeed: nothing could have added to those blessings. Ah! Heaven above…

translation_en:
…Heaven takes the people as the basis for its mandate, while Gaozong, by attending to the people, gained Heaven’s favor. How subtle is the relationship between Heaven and humanity! Consider, moreover, how the Duke of Zhou composed “Establishing Government” to admonish King Cheng, saying: “Be able to put your armies in order, so as to manifest your radiant glory and proclaim your great achievements.” Such is the indispensability of military force. How much more so for rulers who restore a dynasty after decline and disorder: none has succeeded without martial virtue, as exemplified by Gaozong of Yin and King Xuan of Zhou. Yet the Odes praise Gaozong’s achievements and ultimately sum them up in the single phrase, “neither unwarranted rewards nor excessive punishments.” Thus his use of military force must also have accorded with the Way. Those of later ages who devote themselves solely to exhausting their resources in wanton warfare surely cannot lightly invoke him as their justification!

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The duke joined men of Qi, Song, Chen, and Cai in attacking Wei.” 〔Fifth year of Duke Zhuang〕
“The king’s man, Zitu, came to the aid of Wei.” 〔Sixth year of Duke Zhuang〕
Xie Yinglong

Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments: “Interpretations of the Spring and Autumn Annals prize care and rigor. This essay makes its judgments of approval and disapproval clear, and its arguments bristle with sharpness. Other papers are left staring after it, far behind.”
Examiner Li, Right Mentor, comments: “Only the Sage could determine departures from the usual conventions of the Spring and Autumn Annals. This essay makes that evident.”
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “It achieves the requisite care and rigor of style.”

The feudal lords sided with evildoers, and the Spring and Autumn Annals stripped them of their ranks in its wording to convey censure; the king’s minister showed concern for those in distress, and the Spring and Autumn Annals designated him…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
以致褒此可見聖人予奪之公不以諸侯之
貴而少狥不以王人之卑而有遺也且春秋何
為而作也為正名分而作也為正名分而作則
尊卑之叙宜無所苟矣魯莊公即位之五年嘗
會齊宋陳蔡之君以伐衛四國諸侯也聖人書
經侯之公之可也乃各以人稱何邪盖衛朔以
麀聚之孽構二兄之禍簒居其位而見逐於國
人出奔於外而獲罪於天子是當以王命絶之
矣魯力不能誅遠之可也今乃連四國之師為
===
納朔之舉興兵動眾肆意於抗王拂義亂常甘
心於黨惡天理絶而人心亡故聖人於四國各
削其爵以稱人人諸侯所以人莊公也其義何
嚴乎明年王人子突救衛子突下士也聖人書
經人之名之可也乃獨以字稱何邪盖黔牟之
立出於天王之命諸侯無故興師而欲墟其國
納亡助虐而敢放於周是盖天討之所必加矣
子突雖微王命所能申也于是提一旅之師赫
然為救亂之舉誅逆朔之惡而宗社是圖摧五

punctuated:
以致褒。此可見聖人予奪之公，不以諸侯之貴而少狥，不以王人之卑而有遺也。且《春秋》何為而作也？為正名分而作也。為正名分而作，則尊卑之叙宜無所苟矣。魯莊公即位之五年，嘗會齊宋陳蔡之君以伐衛。四國諸侯也，聖人書經，侯之、公之可也，乃各以人稱，何邪？盖衛朔以麀聚之孽，構二兄之禍，簒居其位而見逐於國人，出奔於外而獲罪於天子，是當以王命絶之矣。魯力不能誅，遠之可也。今乃連四國之師，為納朔之舉，興兵動眾，肆意於抗王，拂義亂常，甘心於黨惡，天理絶而人心亡。故聖人於四國各削其爵以稱人，人諸侯所以人莊公也。其義何嚴乎！

明年，王人子突救衛。子突，下士也。聖人書經，人之、名之可也，乃獨以字稱，何邪？盖黔牟之立出於天王之命，諸侯無故興師而欲墟其國，納亡助虐而敢放於周，是盖天討之所必加矣。子突雖微，王命所能申也。于是提一旅之師，赫然為救亂之舉，誅逆朔之惡而宗社是圖，摧五
translation_en:
…to confer praise. Here one can see the impartiality with which the Sage grants and withholds approval: he shows no indulgence on account of the feudal lords’ exalted status, nor does he overlook a royal officer because of his low rank. Moreover, why were the Spring and Autumn Annals written? To rectify titles and the distinctions of status. Since they were written for this purpose, the ordering of high and low ought to admit of no carelessness. In the fifth year after Duke Zhuang of Lu took the throne, he joined the rulers of Qi, Song, Chen, and Cai in attacking Wei. These were the feudal lords of four states. When writing the Classic, the Sage could properly have called them marquises or dukes; why, then, did he designate each merely as a “man”? Shuo of Wei, the offspring of a union in which father and son shared a woman like deer sharing a mate, contrived the disaster that befell his two elder brothers and usurped the throne. Expelled by the people of his state, he fled abroad and incurred the condemnation of the Son of Heaven. He therefore ought to have been excluded from the succession by royal command. If Lu lacked the strength to punish him, it could at least have kept its distance. Instead, it joined the armies of four states in an undertaking to restore Shuo. Raising troops and mobilizing the multitude, they recklessly defied the king; flouting righteousness and disrupting the constant moral order, they willingly sided with evil. Heavenly principle was severed and the human moral heart lost. Thus the Sage stripped the rulers of all four states of their titles and called them “men.” To call these feudal lords “men” was thereby to reduce Duke Zhuang to a “man” as well. How stern is the judgment conveyed!

The following year, the royal officer Zitu came to Wei’s rescue. Zitu was a lower-ranking serviceman. When writing the Classic, the Sage could properly have designated him simply as a “man,” or used his personal name; why, then, did he instead accord him his courtesy name? Qianmou had been installed by command of the Heavenly King. Yet the feudal lords raised armies without cause and sought to lay his state waste. Restoring an exile and abetting tyranny, they dared to act wantonly against Zhou. This surely demanded Heaven’s punishment. Though Zitu’s rank was low, he could give effect to the royal command. Thus he led a brigade of troops and resolutely undertook to rescue the state from disorder, punishing the wickedness of the rebel Shuo and seeking to preserve the ancestral temples and altars of state, to crush the five …

公會齊侯、宋公、鄭伯、曹伯、邾人于檉，僖公元年。齊侯、宋公、江人、黃人會于陽穀，僖公三年。遂伐楚，次于陘。楚屈完來盟于師，盟于召陵，僖公四年。

translation_en:
…defeating the forces of □ [?] and upholding royal law. Although his undertaking did not succeed, his purpose merits esteem. Thus the Sage made a special departure from his usual practice and recorded his courtesy name. Commending the king’s representative was a means of commending the king’s command. How subtle its meaning! When the warning against siding with evil is made clear, the world will have no ministers who betray the common good; when achievements in relieving distress are recorded, people will aspire to act for righteousness. How profound was the Sage’s intention in bequeathing instruction and establishing moral teachings!
Nor is this all. When Shuo recovered his state, the text records his personal name and says that he “entered”; when Duke Zhuang returned to Lu, it records his “arrival.” The great principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals is that All under Heaven belongs to the public, and that the worthy and able should be selected for office, without being bound by the ritual convention of hereditary succession among great men. Even obtaining a state by rightful means is not in itself esteemed—how much less so in the case of one who killed his elder brother and defied the command of the Son of Heaven? Thus the wording both before and after exposes Shuo’s wickedness, imposing an awe-inspiring judgment like execution by the axe, from which there can be no escape. Earlier Confucian scholars said that none but a sage could have composed the Spring and Autumn Annals. How true!
“The duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and a representative of Zhu at Cheng.” First year of Duke Xi.
“The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and representatives of Jiang and Huang met at Yanggu.” Third year of Duke Xi.
“They thereupon attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to the army to make a covenant; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling.” Fourth year of Duke Xi.
Yang Chunfang
Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: “Profound deliberation and scrupulous observance of ritual were the strengths of Duke Huan of Qi in securing peace within and repelling threats from without. You bring these out through your writing, so vividly that Duke Huan and Guan Zhong seem to be deliberating within its pages. Reading it makes one leap with excitement. Such is your extraordinary talent!”

春秋有予於伯國，其制外也有謀，其服外也有禮。甚矣，楚之未易帖也！自非桓仲制之有謀，而服之有禮，其何以成攘外之功哉？僖公之初，楚始書人，浸強也。幸而齊桓主伯，管仲佐之，君臣合謀，力以遏楚。夫伯圖方新，何往不利？桓仲意以楚勢方盛，難以直擣，念苟不深，則不足以語好謀而成者。於是乎大會于檉，動鄭人之救，以□中國之威；再會陽穀，結江黃之心，以懷遠國之信。□□不欲遂逞哉？蓋威未振，則不足以褫其尚往之志；遠不交，則不足以奪其右援之力。是故檉大會焉，陽穀再會焉，則厚集者可舉，而掎角者可恃矣。其念之深至於如此，楚將謂吾中國之有備，而不容以輕肆其力也，如之何其敢抗？此桓仲之才識優於制楚者，不亦可取乎？夫伯謀既定，何功不克？桓仲又以楚勢可屈，猶慮有變，禮苟不謹，則不足以語臨事而懼者□
translation_en:
Examiner Li, Right Admonisher, comments: “The facts are sound and the deliberation thorough; it captures the meaning of the commentary.”
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “The purport is fully developed and the language vigorous—beyond the reach of an immature writer.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals accords approval to hegemonic states: they employ strategy in restraining outsiders and ritual propriety in bringing them to submission. How very difficult Chu was to subdue! Had Duke Huan and Guan Zhong not employed strategy to restrain it and ritual propriety to secure its submission, how could they have accomplished the task of repelling outsiders? Early in Duke Xi’s reign, Chu first began to be designated in the Annals by the term ‘men’ (ren); its power was gradually growing. Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi assumed the hegemony, with Guan Zhong assisting him. Ruler and minister planned together and strove to check Chu. With their hegemonic enterprise newly launched, where could they have gone without success? Yet Duke Huan and Guan Zhong considered that Chu’s power was then at its height and that a direct assault would be difficult. Without deep deliberation, they could not merit the description ‘fond of planning and successful in execution.’ Thus they held a great assembly at Cheng, initiating assistance for the people of Zheng [?] so as to [illegible] the might of the central states. They assembled again at Yanggu, winning the allegiance of Jiang and Huang so as to gain the trust of distant states. [Two illegible characters] did not wish to press ahead and prevail? Until their might had been displayed, they could not strip Chu of its determination to advance; without establishing relations with distant states, they could not deprive Chu of the strength of its supporting allies. Thus, with the great assembly at Cheng and the further assembly at Yanggu, the substantial forces gathered could be mobilized, and those providing support from different directions could be relied upon. Such was the depth of their deliberation. Chu would recognize that our central states were prepared and that it could not recklessly unleash its strength. How, then, would it dare resist? Were not the superior abilities and judgment that Duke Huan and Guan Zhong displayed in restraining Chu worthy of approval? Once the hegemonic strategy was settled, what undertaking could fail? Duke Huan and Guan Zhong further considered that, although Chu’s power could be brought low, unforeseen changes remained a concern. Without scrupulous attention to ritual propriety, they could not merit the description ‘apprehensive when confronting an undertaking’ [illegible]…

translation_en:
…The feudal lords attacked Chu but halted at Xing specifically to prepare the wording of their formal declaration. When Qu Wan graciously came to them, they withdrew their encampment to Shaoling to conclude the rites of assembly and covenant. Did Duke Huan not wish to give his power full rein? Yet he considered that, unless his declaration was properly prepared, it would not suffice to awe Chu into sincerely acknowledging its guilt; unless the ritual settlement was concluded, it would not suffice to reassure Chu in its earnest submission to righteousness. Thus they halted at Xing and covenanted at Shaoling: the rightful grounds for their action were vindicated on their side, while the wavering were settled on the other. Such was his care for ritual propriety. Chu would recognize the cultural refinement of our central states and could not but rest content in its own uncultivated condition [?]. How could it fail to submit? Was not this excellence in the ability and judgment of Duke Huan and Guan Zhong in securing Chu’s submission worthy of approval? Nevertheless, had they preserved this disposition and advanced in goodness, Duke Huan could have become a true king, and Guan Zhong a king’s worthy assistant. After Shaoling, however, seizures and punitive campaigns in Chen followed in profusion [?]. Proud in purpose and complacent in spirit, they could advance no further. Here the gentleman deeply regrets the inadequacy of their capacity and breadth of mind.

Record of Rites

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Its sympathetic grasp of the subject is subtle and meticulous.”
Only when one knows how to serve those above can one preside over those below. Those above and those below each have their proper way, yet the subordinate role is difficult and the superior role easy. Unless one has experienced the difficulty, how can one fully fulfill the Way as a superior? In dealings between people, why should anyone who wishes to fulfill the Way seek elsewhere? One need only draw upon oneself. Within the household, the relationship between father and son rests chiefly on affection. As a son, I exert all my strength to fulfill every duty incumbent upon me, yet I also have certain expectations of my father. When I then become a father, I need not look beyond myself to discover what to require of my son. The sincerity once expressed in gentle remonstrance will emerge as instruction in righteousness; the ritual attentiveness of settling one’s parents at night and inquiring after them in the morning will take shape as the loving care bestowed on a child. Could any part of the father’s Way remain unfulfilled?
Outside the household, the relationship between ruler and minister rests chiefly on righteousness. As a minister, I have devoted my sincerity to everything my station requires, yet there are also things for which I depend upon my ruler. When I then become a ruler, I need not look beyond myself to discover what to require of my ministers. The loyalty expressed in correcting faults and remedying failings will become the sagely wisdom of accepting remonstrance; the reverence expressed in supporting and furthering the ruler’s good intentions will emerge as steadfast trust in those entrusted with office. Could any part of the ruler’s Way remain unfulfilled?
As for the young serving their elders, this ordered relationship cannot be abandoned. I can humble myself in serving others, act with care and stand in awe of righteousness, and understand the difficulty of serving others. When I then…

以役于我，則所求乎人者，又豈遠於我而哉？是必隨器而使，不責其所不能；因材而□，不強其所不及。使人之道有不盡乎？吁！道盡於下，而後可以爲人上。如此，則夫欲善世子者，其教豈有要於斯哉？大抵天下之事，豫則立，不豫則廢。教世子，爲天下之豫也；蚤諭教，教世子之豫也。然則子其父之豫，臣其君之豫，少其長之豫乎？周公相成王，抗世子法於伯禽，欲令知父子、君臣、長幼之義，而記者有發於此，其知聖人之用豫矣。吁！旨哉！
臣儀行不重辭，不援其所不及，不煩其所不知，則君不勞矣。
盧淮
