考試官侍讀學士汪批：能悉見可而進之義。
translation_en:
…when employing others in my service, how could what I require of them be far removed from myself [?]? Surely one must employ them according to their capacities, without demanding what they cannot do; one must [illegible] according to their talents, without forcing them beyond their abilities. Would this not fully realize the proper way of employing others? Ah! Only after fully practicing the Way as a subordinate can one stand above others. If so, for anyone wishing to make the heir apparent good, could any teaching be more essential than this? Generally, the affairs of the world succeed through preparation and fail without it. Educating the heir apparent is preparation for governing the realm; instructing him early is preparation for his education. Thus, is being a son preparation for being a father, being a minister preparation for being a ruler, and being a junior preparation for being a senior? When the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng, he held up the rules for the heir apparent in educating Boqin, wishing him to understand the duties between father and son, ruler and minister, and senior and junior. The recorder elucidated this point and thus understood the sage’s use of preparation. Ah, how profound!
“When a minister makes his conduct exemplary and does not place weight on words, does not reach for what lies beyond his abilities, and does not trouble himself with what he does not understand, then the ruler will not be wearied.”
Lu Huai
Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, School Instructor: “Other essays, in explaining the passage about the ruler not being wearied, are either vague or forced. None equals this essay in the precision and aptness of its principles or the clarity and purity of its expression. Print it as a model for those studying the Book of Rites.”
Comment by Examiner Li, Right Mentor: “The writing gives full expression to what is to be said. Worthy of selection.”
Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “It fully brings out the meaning of advancing when one sees that it is appropriate to do so.”

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人臣知所以事君則君逸於上矣蓋人臣事君
之道在乎忠也忠則易知而君有不逸者哉緇
衣載孔子之言如此謂夫下難知則君長勞固
矣誠使爲人臣者道積厥躬而形於外者公正
不頗偉然德行之可尊善有諸巳而見諸事者
純明有執凝然丰範之可則容色足以消其逸
志而所以正乎其君者不規規於諫諍之間聞
望足以弭其邪心而所以匡乎其上者不拘拘
於言詞之末君之力所能及也則因其所及者
===
而輔之不擾其所不及而彊之使從君之智所
能知也則就其所知者而導之不煩其所不知
而勉之使聽夫然則凡有所行者行無偽行覩
之而易知凡有所言者言無虛言聆之而可信
心有感通之誠事無扞格之患謨無不明弼無
不諧展轉反覆所以疑乎其臣者可無矣政有
可託安然其自適也諫焉而行言焉而聽疲神
焦思所以憂乎其治者可免矣臣有可憑憇然
其自遂也夫君不勞由於臣之易知如此然則

punctuated: 人臣知所以事君，則君逸於上矣。蓋人臣事君之道在乎忠也，忠則易知，而君有不逸者哉？緇衣載孔子之言如此，謂夫下難知，則君長勞，固矣。誠使爲人臣者道積厥躬，而形於外者公正不頗，偉然德行之可尊；善有諸巳，而見諸事者純明有執，凝然丰範之可則。容色足以消其逸志，而所以正乎其君者不規規於諫諍之間；聞望足以弭其邪心，而所以匡乎其上者不拘拘於言詞之末。君之力所能及也，則因其所及者而輔之，不擾其所不及而彊之使從；君之智所能知也，則就其所知者而導之，不煩其所不知而勉之使聽。夫然，則凡有所行者，行無偽行，覩之而易知；凡有所言者，言無虛言，聆之而可信。心有感通之誠，事無扞格之患，謨無不明，弼無不諧。展轉反覆，所以疑乎其臣者可無矣；政有可託，安然其自適也。諫焉而行，言焉而聽，疲神焦思，所以憂乎其治者可免矣；臣有可憑，憇然其自遂也。夫君不勞，由於臣之易知如此，然則
translation_en: When a minister knows how to serve his ruler, the ruler enjoys ease in his exalted position. For the way a minister serves his ruler lies in loyalty. If he is loyal, he is readily understood; how, then, could the ruler fail to enjoy ease? The “Black Robes” (Ziyi) chapter records Confucius’s words to this effect: when those below are difficult to understand, their ruler is bound to toil. Suppose, indeed, that a minister has cultivated the Way within himself, so that what appears outwardly is impartial and upright, without bias, and his imposing moral conduct commands respect; that he possesses goodness within himself, so that what appears in his actions is pure, enlightened, and steadfast, and his dignified bearing provides a model to follow. His countenance and demeanor suffice to dispel his ruler’s inclination toward indolence, and his means of rectifying the ruler are not narrowly confined to remonstrance. His reputation and prestige suffice to quell the ruler’s wayward thoughts, and his means of correcting his sovereign are not restricted to the mere details of verbal expression. In matters within the ruler’s power, he assists him on the basis of what he can accomplish, without troubling him over what lies beyond his ability and forcing him to comply. In matters within the ruler’s understanding, he guides him on the basis of what he knows, without burdening him with what he does not know and pressing him to heed it. Thus, whatever the minister does contains no false action: one observes it and readily understands him. Whatever he says contains no empty words: one hears it and can trust him. There is sincerity through which their hearts respond to and understand one another, and their affairs suffer no obstruction. Every counsel is clear, and every act of assistance harmonious. The ruler can be free of the grounds for doubting his minister that would otherwise make him turn matters over again and again in his mind. With someone to whom he can entrust government, he rests content and at ease. Remonstrances are acted upon, and words are heeded; he can avoid the exhausting strain and anxious thought occasioned by concern for his government. With a minister on whom he can rely, he rests at ease and accomplishes his purposes. Such is the way in which a ruler’s freedom from toil results from his minister’s being readily understood. If so, then…

translation_en:
…one who would bring ease to his ruler [?]—can he fail to know what he should devote himself to? Generally, the distinction between minister and ruler is as strict as that between the steps and the raised hall, and the feelings of those above and below easily grow distant. Unless a minister is loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and honest, maintaining integrity, candor, loyalty, and steadfastness, suspicions and resentments spring up like hedgehog bristles; few rulers then escape toil in their lofty position. Among the ancients, Yi Yin in his service to Tai Jia and the Duke of Zhou in his service to King Cheng may be said to have fully realized this Way. In later ages, men sought to discharge their duties merely through their lips and tongues: how superficial! The Book of Changes says, “There is sincerity in the Way.” Ah! Only by being thus can one be without shame in fulfilling the Way of the minister!

Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Instructor: The movement of the brush in this paper is full and vast, flowing powerfully like great rivers. It twists and turns, assuming myriad forms in an instant, yet ultimately hastens toward the sea without departing from its proper course. On seeing this composition, one can understand the bow with lowered head before Dongye; I should be the first to bow before you upon hearing of your reputation.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Professor: The two terms “harmony” and “conformity” are exceedingly difficult to expound. Those who lack understanding let their brushes run unchecked, producing vague writing that reaches no conclusion; those with some grasp of principle become constrained and cannot advance. This essay rises and falls, pauses and turns, its waves surging freely, yet it has ample depth of principle and meaning. Reading it leaves one exhilarated and forgetting oneself. The Southern Metropolitan Region certainly has many scholars, but would any dare place himself before you?

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官右諭德李批述經叙理曰論豈容槩以浮詞
敷衍簡而盡直而不肆如此作者决非時文之士所能到
也
考試官侍讀學士汪批此卷初塲文義精到特然迥
出及得此論快讀數過猶天馬行空不施控馭而步驟不
凡疾徐中度意所欲徃無不能達似非止南畿之竒才而已
擢冠多士當愜輿論
君子之處人也有道亦惟不以己與之而已夫
人亦我也我亦人也人我一致廓然大公而惟
===
理是視夫安徃而不和是故以之爲己則順而
祥以之爲人則愛而周以之爲天下國家則無
所處而不得其當嗚呼此和也非同也彼以己
與之者知有己而已以人而狥己曰彼於我有
合也以己而附人曰我於彼有合也其意自以
爲和之道在是矣然而曰同可也曰和不可也
君子和而不同聖人之辨嚴矣哉且和同之名
何始乎書曰同寅恊恭和衷哉禮曰樂文同則
上下和和同之名立而未始分也自晏子遄臺

punctuated:
考試官右諭德李批：述經叙理曰論，豈容槩以浮詞敷衍？簡而盡，直而不肆，如此作者，决非時文之士所能到也。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：此卷初塲文義精到，特然迥出。及得此論，快讀數過，猶天馬行空，不施控馭，而步驟不凡，疾徐中度，意所欲徃，無不能達。似非止南畿之竒才而已，擢冠多士，當愜輿論。

君子之處人也有道，亦惟不以己與之而已。夫人亦我也，我亦人也，人我一致，廓然大公，而惟理是視，夫安徃而不和？是故以之爲己，則順而祥；以之爲人，則愛而周；以之爲天下國家，則無所處而不得其當。嗚呼！此和也，非同也。彼以己與之者，知有己而已。以人而狥己，曰：「彼於我有合也。」以己而附人，曰：「我於彼有合也。」其意自以爲和之道在是矣。然而曰同可也，曰和不可也。「君子和而不同」，聖人之辨嚴矣哉！且和同之名，何始乎？《書》曰：「同寅恊恭和衷哉！」《禮》曰：「樂文同，則上下和。」和同之名立，而未始分也。自晏子遄臺

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: Expounding the classics and setting forth principles is what constitutes a discourse. How could one permit it to be padded throughout with empty phrases? Concise yet exhaustive, straightforward yet unrestrained by no bounds—writing such as this is certainly beyond the reach of those versed merely in contemporary examination prose.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: The meaning and composition of this script’s first-session essays were refined and penetrating, standing far above the rest. When I came to this discourse, I read it eagerly several times. It is like a celestial horse coursing through the sky: without the restraint of reins, its paces are extraordinary, its speed and slowness perfectly measured, and wherever its intent would take it, it can reach. The writer seems to be an exceptional talent not merely within the Southern Metropolitan Region. Placing him first among the candidates should accord with general opinion.

The gentleman has a Way in his dealings with others: it consists simply in not imposing his own self upon them. Others are selves just as I am; I too am another person to them. When others and oneself are understood as one, with expansive impartiality and attention directed solely toward principle, where could one go without achieving harmony? Thus, applied to oneself, this brings accord and well-being; applied to others, it brings love and comprehensive care; applied to all under Heaven, the state, and the family, it ensures that whatever one deals with receives its proper treatment. Ah! This is harmony, not conformity. Those who impose themselves upon others recognize only their own selves. They make others accommodate them and say, “He agrees with me.” They attach themselves to others and say, “I agree with him.” In their own minds, they suppose that the Way of harmony lies here. Yet this may be called conformity; it cannot be called harmony. “The gentleman harmonizes but does not conform”: how exacting is the sage’s distinction!

Furthermore, where did the terms “harmony” and “conformity” originate? The Book of Documents says, “Be united in reverence, joined in respect, and harmonious at heart!” The Book of Rites says, “When the forms of music are shared, those above and below are in harmony.” The terms harmony and conformity were established, but initially no distinction was drawn between them. Beginning with Yanzi’s exchange at Chuantai …

興不敢用其私怨也夫惟不以己也而後能用
其情非情也理也聖人以其情而為和常人以
其情而為同此無他公□□□□□□□□□□
punctuated: 之對，始有其辨矣。曰：「五味之相濟，五聲之相成，和也；以水濟水而不可食，琴瑟之專一而不可聽者，同也。」其說幾矣，然而未盡也。夫天下之情萬殊，理則一而已。君子求同於理，而不求同於人之情。是故天下有公是焉，人之所是，君子亦是之；天下有公非焉，人之所非，君子亦非之。吾何異於人哉？可謂和矣，而非同也。彼人之所同是者，或未當於理歟？君子以一人而非天下之所是者，有之矣。人之所同非者，或未當於理歟？君子以一人而是天下之所非者，亦有之矣。非求異於人也，求同於理而不求同於人之情耳，亦何害其為和哉？君子之不求同於人之情者，非獨於人為然也，於己亦然。是故聖人之喜，以物之當喜；聖人之怒，以物之當怒，不以己為喜怒也。堯老而舜禪，不敢用其私愛也；鯀殛而禹興，不敢用其私怨也。夫惟不以己也，而後能用其情。非情也，理也。聖人以其情而為和，常人以其情而為同。此無他，公私□□□矣。夫小人以
translation_en: …only with that reply did the distinction begin to be drawn. It said: “The five flavors complementing one another and the five tones completing one another constitute harmony; adding water to water so that it cannot be eaten, or playing only a single note on the qin and se zithers so that they cannot be listened to, constitutes sameness.” This explanation came close, but did not exhaust the matter. Human feelings throughout the world differ in myriad ways, yet principle is one. The gentleman seeks agreement with principle, rather than agreement with people’s feelings. Thus, where there is something universally right, the gentleman too approves what others approve; where there is something universally wrong, the gentleman too condemns what others condemn. How am I different from others? This may be called harmony, but it is not sameness. Might what people unanimously approve sometimes fail to accord with principle? There are indeed occasions when the gentleman, standing alone, condemns what the whole world approves. Might what people unanimously condemn sometimes fail to accord with principle? There are also occasions when the gentleman, standing alone, approves what the whole world condemns. He does not seek to differ from others: he merely seeks agreement with principle rather than with people’s feelings. How could this impair his harmony? In refusing to seek agreement with human feelings, the gentleman applies this not only to others but also to himself. Thus the sage rejoices because something merits rejoicing, and grows angry because something merits anger; he does not make himself the basis of joy or anger. When Yao grew old and Shun received the throne through abdication, Yao did not dare act on his private affection. When Gun was put to death and Yu was raised to office, Yu did not dare act on his private resentment. Only by not taking oneself as the basis can one then give effect to one’s feelings. These are not mere feelings: they are principle. The sage uses his feelings to achieve harmony; ordinary people use theirs to achieve sameness. There is no other reason for this: public-mindedness and selfishness [three illegible characters]. Now, as for the petty man, by [?]…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
烏足以及此所比則為同所惡則為異以一己
之好惡帥天下以一己之同異為是非彼視理
為何物是烏得而和哉君子以其一心之和布
而為天下之和施於其家則父子親兄弟宜而
孝弟之實著焉施於其鄉則長幼序鄰里睦而
任恤之行成焉施于朝廷上大夫則誾誾下大
夫則侃侃同列則濟濟而禮讓之風行焉日月
之所以明江河之所以流者此和也天地之所
以變化草木之所以蕃育者此和也彼徒知以
===
同為和者視此何如哉易曰同人于野亨又曰
同人于宗吝君子之和于野之同也小人之同
于宗之同也雖同為同而其所以為同者不同
公私之間而已矣大抵天理人欲同行異情愛
人一也君子為周小人為比自樂一也君子為
泰小人為驕與人一也君子為和小人為同世
之儒者未嘗從事於克己之學而每竊其近似
以自名而不自知其卒陷于小人之歸也可不
戒哉

于宗之同也雖同爲同而其所以爲同者不同
公私之間而已矣大抵天理人欲同行異情變
人一也君子爲周小人爲比自樂一也君子爲
泰小人爲驕與人一也君子爲和小人爲同世
之儒者未嘗從事於克已之學而每竊其近似

punctuated:
烏足以及此？所比則為同，所惡則為異，以一己之好惡帥天下，以一己之同異為是非。彼視理為何物？是烏得而和哉？君子以其一心之和，布而為天下之和。施於其家，則父子親，兄弟宜，而孝弟之實著焉；施於其鄉，則長幼序，鄰里睦，而任恤之行成焉；施于朝廷，上大夫則誾誾，下大夫則侃侃，同列則濟濟，而禮讓之風行焉。日月之所以明，江河之所以流者，此和也；天地之所以變化，草木之所以蕃育者，此和也。彼徒知以同為和者，視此何如哉？
易曰：「同人于野，亨。」又曰：「同人于宗，吝。」君子之和，于野之同也；小人之同，于宗之同也。雖同為同，而其所以為同者不同，公私之間而已矣。大抵天理人欲，同行異情。愛人一也，君子為周，小人為比；自樂一也，君子為泰，小人為驕；與人一也，君子為和，小人為同。世之儒者，未嘗從事於克己之學，而每竊其近似以自名，而不自知其卒陷于小人之歸也，可不戒哉？
translation_en:
…how could he possibly attain this? Those with whom he forms partisan attachments he treats as like-minded; those he dislikes he treats as different. He would lead all under Heaven according to his own likes and dislikes, and make his own agreements and disagreements the standard of right and wrong. What does he take principle to be? How could this amount to harmony? The gentleman extends the harmony of his own heart to bring harmony to all under Heaven. Applied within his family, it brings affection between father and son and fitting relations between brothers, making filial devotion and brotherly respect manifest in practice. Applied within his community, it brings order between elders and juniors and concord among neighbors, establishing the practice of mutual assistance and relief. Applied at court, it makes him frank yet respectful with senior grand masters, composed and forthright with junior grand masters, and dignified with his peers, so that a spirit of ritual propriety and deference prevails. It is this harmony that makes the sun and moon shine and the rivers flow; it is this harmony that enables Heaven and Earth to transform and plants and trees to flourish. How do those who know only to take conformity for harmony measure up to this?
The Book of Changes says: “Fellowship with others in the open country: success.” It also says: “Fellowship with others within the clan: regret.” The gentleman’s harmony is fellowship in the open country; the petty man’s conformity is fellowship within the clan. Though both are called fellowship, the grounds of their fellowship differ: it is simply the distinction between public-mindedness and private interest. In general, heavenly principle and human desire may issue in the same conduct but differ in their underlying disposition. Both love others, but the gentleman is inclusive, while the petty man is partisan. Both are content with themselves, but the gentleman is at ease, while the petty man is arrogant. Both associate with others, but the gentleman seeks harmony, while the petty man seeks conformity. Scholars of the present age have never devoted themselves to the learning of self-mastery, yet repeatedly appropriate its outward semblances to claim a reputation for themselves. They do not realize that they will ultimately fall into the ranks of petty men. Can one fail to take warning?

translation_en:
Model congratulatory memorial by the assembled officials on the completion of the newly established court ritual music of the Great Tang〔Second year of Zhenguan〕
Wu Tinghan
Associate Examiner Tang, School Instructor, comments: In memorial composition, the clever pursue startling novelty, while the boastful indulge in empty generalities; the proper form is lost. Dignity and classical propriety, embodying principle and the Way in parallel prose—this composition achieves these.
Examiner Li, Right Mentor, comments: Resonant and attuned to the pitch standards—should a memorial on court ritual music not be just like this?
Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting, comments: Rich, elegant, and properly formed: it approaches a work of grand classical refinement.
On a certain day of a certain month in the second year of Zhenguan, we, your servants, humbly observe that the newly established court ritual music of the Great Tang has been completed. Truly delighted and truly joyful, we bow our heads to the ground and kowtow as we submit this memorial.
We humbly consider that your sagely virtue matches Heaven and Earth, splendidly manifesting the transforming influence of civilized enlightenment; as the heavenly king, you uphold the great unity of the realm and extend far and wide the establishment of institutions. Since the work of good government has been accomplished, it is fitting that musical sounds should be rectified. Spirits and human beings alike rejoice; all within the seas share in the joy.
We, your servants, venture to reflect that court ritual music derives its meaning from Heaven, and its Way is bound up with government. When feelings emerge, they differ as delight, anger, sorrow, and joy; when stirred by external things, they vary between sharp and dwindling sounds and broad and leisurely ones. punctuated:
而變生，變成方而音著。聖人博采風俗，協比律聲，流動精神，消融邪穢，表萬物之理，動四氣之和。舜制箭韶，斯道大闡，奏極九變，鳳凰來儀；克諧八音，百獸率舞。嗣是以後，代有作興，雖義意之相因，各名稱之不襲，莫不事與時並，名與功偕。慨三代之既還，遭嬴秦之絶學，王風載熄，聲器斯淪。漢魏繼興，亦勤脩制，芝房寶鼎之什，昭武正世之歌，雖曰徒事鏗鏘，猶知希踪雅頌。及夫晉季，大雅云亡，陳競後庭，詞流侈靡；齊倡伴侣，人事淫哇，祗以導欲增悲，安能移風易俗？隋常釐正，訖無成功。盖分裂之既深，宜中和之難復，是不能不有待于今日也。
欽惟德性夙成，聰明天授，民安物阜，協氣薰洽于兩間；治盛功隆，化澤涵濡于九有。
translation_en:
…and transformations arise; when these transformations form patterns, musical tones become manifest. The sages gathered widely from local customs and harmonized the pitch standards and sounds, setting the vital spirit in motion, dissolving depravity and impurity, expressing the principles of all things, and stirring the harmonious energies of the four seasons. Shun established the music called Jian-Shao [?], and this Way was greatly revealed. When its performance reached the ninth variation, phoenixes came in stately bearing; when the eight classes of instruments were brought into harmony, all the beasts danced together. Thereafter, successive dynasties created and revived music. Although they inherited its meaning and intent, each gave it names distinct from those of its predecessors: in every case, the undertaking accorded with its age, and its name matched its achievement.
Alas, once the Three Dynasties had passed [?], learning was severed under the Qin of the Ying house. The civilizing influence of the kings died away, and musical sounds and instruments fell into decline. The Han and Wei rose in succession and likewise worked diligently to restore musical institutions. Their compositions, such as the Mushroom Chamber and Precious Tripod, and their songs, such as Manifest Martial Power and Rectifying the Age, may have concerned themselves merely with resounding instruments, yet they still knew to aspire to the standards of the Odes and Hymns. By the final years of the Jin, however, the great classical music had vanished. Under the Chen, people vied in singing Rear Courtyard songs, their lyrics descending into extravagance and decadence; under the Qi, they promoted Companion [?], and people pursued licentious, vulgar music. These served only to incite desire and deepen sorrow: how could they transform prevailing customs? The Sui attempted to set matters right but ultimately achieved no success. Since political division had become so profound, it was indeed difficult to restore balance and harmony. Thus this task necessarily awaited the present day.
We reverently consider that Your Majesty’s virtuous nature matured early, and that Heaven bestowed your intelligence and discernment. The people are at peace and all things flourish; harmonious energies pervade the space between Heaven and Earth. Your government flourishes and your achievements are exalted; the beneficence of your transforming influence bathes all the nine regions…

translation_en:
…Your voice serves as the pitch standard and your person as the measure; when you lead, all proceeds, and when you act, all is harmonious. The seven celestial luminaries shine brilliantly, and the three spiritual powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—are profoundly at peace. You extend King Xuan of Qi’s love of music and regard Emperor Wen of Han’s lack of leisure for it as inadequate. You devote yourself earnestly to institutions and give your attention to rites and music. Above, you carry forward the late emperor’s intentions; below, you select officials from among your attendants, allowing them ample months and years to investigate and settle these matters.

Your servant Xiaosun took the twelve months as the standard for the method of rotating the tonal center. Your servant Wenshou harmonized the twelve pitch standards and tuned the sounds of the five bells. He made the altered gong tone into the clear gong tone, and the altered zhi tone into the regular zhi tone. Taking the annual cycle as the model, they fixed the name as “Harmony.” There are forty-eight pieces, with changes of mode totaling eighty-four sections [?]; their beginnings and endings succeed one another, and the greater and lesser are all distinct. Gong is weighty and shang light, thereby displaying the distinction between ruler and minister; yu is clear and zhi deep, thereby manifesting the functions of affairs and things. The winds of the eight directions follow the pitch standards without deviation; the five colors form patterns without disorder. Perfect in goodness and beauty, the notes follow one another like threaded pearls. Pure and distinct, the music fills the ears in abundant fullness. It sweeps away the habits of Qi and Liang and entirely dispels the musical styles of Wu and Chu. Presented at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, it delights the spirits; performed at court, it elicits a response from Heaven and humanity. The musical institutions of this dynasty are established, and the systems of a hundred kings cannot surpass them. Formerly, Confucius heard with his own ears…

There is a definite reason for leaving the Han outside the discussion. You have been able to articulate it; moreover, your language is classically elegant, and your talent and discernment are exceptional. Having obtained a scholar like this, we can report back in fulfillment of His Majesty’s command.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: All five policy essays answer well, offering historical precedents and reasoned discussion. In particular, his ability to expound the greatness of our Sagely Founder’s achievements and virtue with powerful language and vigorous writing, leaving nothing out, reveals his learning and discernment. This essay is specially included as representative of the others.

I have long maintained that a sage’s virtue has no fixed form, whereas its operation leaves visible traces. What has no fixed form is difficult to name, while what leaves traces is readily seen. Those skilled in observing a sage use what can be seen to give a name to what cannot be named; thus they may approach some semblance of him. Confucius said: “How lofty! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone modeled himself upon it.” He also said: “How lofty were his achievements! How brilliant were his cultural accomplishments!” Yet achievements and cultural accomplishments cannot encompass all that Yao was, just as the sun, moon, and stars cannot encompass …

…exhaust what Heaven is; yet those who know how to contemplate Yao and Heaven can perceive their greatness through these manifestations. Understanding this, we see that there is much to say about our Sagely Progenitor’s magnificent achievements in pacification, his grand plans for founding the dynasty and handing it down, and his great instructions for ordering the realm. Allow me, in response to your discerning question, to set these forth in praise.

Since the Three Dynasties, commentators have held that Emperor Gao of the Han acquired All under Heaven in the most legitimate manner. This was because he destroyed the tyrannical Qin and chastised the rebel Xiang Yu, while his generosity, benevolence, and magnanimity sufficed to lay the foundations for four hundred years of rule. Yet although the main guiding principles were sound, omissions among the myriad particulars remained inevitable. His call to righteousness had a worthy name, but he merely borrowed it as a pretext to justify his actions. As for other matters, he never abandoned the habits of horseback conquest throughout his life, and the law against possessing books was abolished only in the second generation. His descendants, moreover, willingly contented themselves with the shortcomings of mixing hegemonic practices into their rule. If the precedents bequeathed at the very foundation of the dynasty were like this, what could one still expect of succeeding rulers who inherited the throne and preserved its achievements?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with divine sagacity, appeared at the juncture when an old cycle ended and a new one began. Responding to Heaven and following the wishes of the people, he transformed barbarian ways through Chinese civilization, cleansed a defilement unprecedented since the beginning of the world, and recovered the land upon which emperors and kings had established themselves. In rising to kingship and undertaking his enterprise, he had already surpassed the deeds of Tang and Wu. As for his arrangements and plans embodied in his sagely government, these were sufficient to serve as standards for ten thousand generations. To mention just the principal examples: he compiled the Duties of the Various Offices to establish the designations of official posts, and revised the Great…

translation_en:
…Ming Code, to correct the excesses of statutory provisions. Before his honorific title had been presented, the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain were already established; while military affairs were still pressing, schools were promptly founded. All the manifestations of his sagely government throughout the realm embraced both fundamentals and particulars and addressed matters great and small; they certainly cannot be enumerated in just one or two examples. Their essential purpose was to provide a foundation for ordering the enduring human relationships and making ritual propriety and righteousness clear, restoring the cardinal bonds and constant norms after their decline and reinstating the nine principles of government after their abandonment. The grandeur and far-reaching scope of his design already rivaled the flourishing rule of Tang and Yu and the Three Dynasties. How could the comparatively insignificant Han even merit comparison!
As for the words he uttered to transmit instruction, whether expressed in discussions, proclaimed in edicts, or committed to writing in his works, every statement and principle shone as brightly as the Six Classics. Thus, in expounding the hexagram The Family, he elucidated the way of sincerity and dignified authority, bringing to light the profound meaning of Fuxi and King Wen. In annotating the chapter The Great Plan, he disclosed the mysteries of the august standard and the enduring human relationships, making manifest the categories transmitted by Jizi to King Wu. His single edict Inaugurating the Dynasty embodied the same stern distinction as the Spring and Autumn Annals, which treated the Xia as insiders and the Yi as outsiders. The three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements embodied the same warmth and generosity as the Zhou announcements and the Shang chapter Pan Geng.
Elsewhere, discussing rites and music, he said: “Rites guide reverence; music gives expression to harmony. Without reverence and harmony, how can there be good government?” Even Youzi’s discussion of rites and music could not surpass these words. Discussing schools, he said: “Among the essentials of government, moral transformation through instruction comes first; moral transformation through instruction…”

…in the way of moral instruction, schools are the foundation.” Even Mencius’s discussions of kingly government could offer nothing to supersede these words. Discussing the rise and fall of former dynasties, he said: “The source of ruin and disorder lies in arrogance and self-indulgence.” Discussing the present vastness of the realm, he said: “With so extensive a territory and so numerous a people, we ought precisely to be vigilant and apprehensive.” This, too, is an admonition to remain cautious and diligent, attentive to the times and to the first stirrings of events. If what he harbors within is not the mind of Yao and Shun, yet he wishes to achieve the government of Yao and Shun in his administration, this is utterly impossible.” How great are these imperial words! Even the teachings transmitted by the divine sages of Tang and Yu, and their earnest injunctions beginning ‘Ah, you,’ amounted to no more than this. Here we may reverently perceive the subtlety of the sage’s method of cultivating the mind, which reaches back to renew a tradition left untransmitted for thousands of years.
Through the subtlety of this method of cultivating the mind, he has continued the transmission of the divine sages; thus, all that he harbors is the mind of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. Accordingly, his words become a canon: they are the very words of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. His actions become a model: they are the very governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. What he hands down to his sage sons and divine grandsons to inherit and carry forward is, in every respect, the government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. text:

甚矣天下之大也非法以維之則無以一
眾心統萬事而將有渙散潰亂之憂有其
法而無人以持之則徒法不能以自行抑
何以收治平之効也哉紀綱者維天下之
法也而常藉于人人君者主天下之治也
而必資于法有其法而又有人以持之則

房

維天下之勢存乎法，持天下之法存乎人。

甚矣，天下之大也！非法以維之，則無以一眾心、統萬事，而將有渙散潰亂之憂。有其法而無人以持之，則徒法不能以自行，抑何以收治平之効也哉？紀綱者，維天下之法也，而常藉于人；人君者，主天下之治也，而必資于法。有其法而又有人以持之，則治之成也無難矣。請試陳之。

紀綱之說，其來尚矣，見於《五子之歌》，詠於《棫樸》《假樂》之詩。一家有一家之紀綱，一國有一國之紀綱，天下有天下之紀綱。存之則治，失之則亂。如天之有日月星辰，地之有山岳河海，所以經緯乎上下，不可一日而亡者也。韓愈氏曰：「善醫者，不視人之肥瘠，察其脉之病否而已矣；善計天下者，不視天下之安危，察其紀綱之理亂而已矣。」嗚呼！紀綱之理亂，而天下安危隨之。然則有國者可忽
translation_en:
Fang [?]

Holding together the configuration of power in the realm depends on laws; upholding the laws of the realm depends on people.

Vast indeed is the realm! Without laws to hold it together, there would be no means to unite the hearts of the multitude or coordinate all affairs, and there would be cause to fear fragmentation, collapse, and disorder. If laws exist but there is no one to uphold them, laws alone cannot put themselves into effect. How, then, could orderly and peaceful government be achieved? The governing framework is the body of laws that holds the realm together, yet it always depends on people. The ruler presides over the government of the realm, yet he must rely on laws. When laws exist and there are also people to uphold them, achieving good government presents no difficulty. Allow me to explain.

The idea of a governing framework has a long history. It appears in the “Songs of the Five Sons” and is celebrated in the poems “Luxuriant Oaks” (Yupu) and “Admirable Happiness” (Jiale). A household has its own governing framework; a state has its own governing framework; the realm has its own governing framework. Preserve it, and there is order; lose it, and there is disorder. It is like the sun, moon, and stars in heaven, or the mountains, rivers, and seas on earth: it provides the warp and weft of all above and below and cannot be absent for even a day. Han Yu said: “A skilled physician does not look at whether a person is fat or thin, but merely examines the pulse for signs of illness. One skilled in planning for the realm does not look at whether the realm is secure or imperiled, but merely examines whether its governing framework is in order or disarray.” Alas! Among rulers of the realm in antiquity, Emperor Xuandi of the Han comprehensively examined whether performance matched professed responsibilities, made rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, and reinvigorated the governing order. Thus he achieved the glory of a dynastic restoration. Yet how was it that, from Emperor Xiaoyuan onward, governmental commands gradually weakened, eunuchs acted without restraint, and imperial in-laws monopolized power, until, under Emperors Ai and Ping, able and worthy men were estranged and dismissed, and the governing order deteriorated? It did not deteriorate of itself: there were causes that brought about its deterioration. Emperor Taizong of the Tang exerted himself rigorously to correct abuses, attending to every detail of government. Once the governing order was established, he attained the good government of the Zhenguan era. Yet how was it that, from Emperors Su and Dai onward, government favored indulgence, measures were ill judged, and regional military governors defied the court, until, under Emperor Yizong, the hierarchy between sovereign and ministers declined and the governing order collapsed? It did not collapse of itself: there were causes that brought about its collapse. Emperor Taizong of the Song planned deeply and decided brilliantly, assessed merit and exercised caution in punishment. His governing order may be said to have surpassed that of recent antiquity; his descendants could well have preserved it generation after generation. Yet how was it that Emperor Shenzong deemed the established institutions too limited, recklessly sought sweeping changes, and employed unworthy men? Once the New Policies were implemented, all within the seas was thrown into turmoil, ultimately bequeathing the calamity of the Jingkang era. It was not that the governing order had not been reinvigorated, but that the proper way to reinvigorate it had been lost. How, then, could the dynasty’s decline occasion surprise?

text:
輦轂以及海徼由王公以逮甿庶事為之制
人為之防可謂至精至密而無以復加矣
百五十年來人知法守海內晏然俗美風
醇臻于至治有由然矣承平既久人懷玩
愒法弛弊生執事謂紀綱有失其舊者愚
不敢謂其無也昔荀悅著申鑒論政治之
術有曰先屏四患乃崇五政所謂四患者
一曰偽二曰私三曰放四曰奢五政者興
農桑以養其性審好惡以正其俗宣文教
===
以章其化立武備以秉其威明賞罰以統
其法悅之意以為偽亂俗私壞法放越軌
私敗制四患不除則五政不行故亟去之
去之誠是矣愚則以為紀綱風俗相因者
也紀綱弛于上斯風俗敝于下四患風俗
也五政紀綱也能行五政則四患自除而
何先後之云朱子謂綱紀在於辨賢否以
定上下之分核功罪以公賞罰之施固悅
審好惡明賞罰之說也自今觀之孰有要

昔荀悅著《申鑒》，論政治之術，有曰：「先屏四患，乃崇五政。」所謂四患者，一曰偽，二曰私，三曰放，四曰奢。五政者，興農桑以養其性，審好惡以正其俗，宣文教以章其化，立武備以秉其威，明賞罰以統其法。悅之意，以為偽亂俗，私壞法，放越軌，私敗制，四患不除，則五政不行，故亟去之。去之誠是矣，愚則以為紀綱、風俗相因者也。紀綱弛于上，斯風俗敝于下。四患，風俗也；五政，紀綱也。能行五政，則四患自除，而何先後之云？朱子謂：「綱紀在於辨賢否以定上下之分，核功罪以公賞罰之施。」固悅審好惡、明賞罰之說也。自今觀之，孰有要
translation_en:
…the imperial capital and out to the maritime frontiers, from princes and dukes down to the common people, regulations were established for every undertaking and safeguards set for every person. These may be called supremely refined and thorough, beyond any further improvement. For a hundred and fifty years, people have known to abide by the laws, and all within the seas has been tranquil. Customs have been good and public morals sound: there is good reason that the realm attained the height of good government. Yet prolonged peace has made people complacent and idle; laws have grown lax and abuses have arisen. You, honored examiners, say that the guiding principles and institutional order have lost something of their former condition. I would not venture to deny it.
When Xun Yue wrote Extended Reflections (Shenjian), he said in discussing the art of government: “First eliminate the four afflictions; then promote the five measures of government.” The four afflictions are, first, deceit; second, selfishness; third, license; and fourth, extravagance. The five measures are to promote agriculture and sericulture to sustain the people’s lives; to scrutinize what is favored and disfavored so as to rectify their customs; to spread literary and moral instruction so as to make its transforming influence manifest; to establish military preparedness so as to uphold authority; and to make rewards and punishments clear so as to maintain the rule of law. Yue’s meaning was that deceit disorders customs, selfishness corrupts laws, license transgresses proper bounds, and selfishness [?—the text repeats this term where “extravagance” is expected] undermines institutions. Unless the four afflictions are removed, the five measures cannot be put into effect; hence his insistence on eliminating them urgently. Eliminating them is certainly right. In my humble view, however, institutional order and popular customs act upon one another. When discipline grows lax above, customs deteriorate below. The four afflictions concern customs; the five measures concern institutional order. If the five measures can be implemented, the four afflictions will disappear of themselves. Why, then, speak of what must come first and what afterward? Master Zhu said: “Institutional order lies in distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy in order to determine the respective places of superiors and inferiors, and in examining achievements and offenses in order to make the application of rewards and punishments impartial.” This is precisely Yue’s teaching about scrutinizing what is favored and disfavored and clarifying rewards and punishments. Viewed from the present, what could be more essential…

實善無不顯惡無不彰而民志平矣賞罰

而國法立矣由是農桑可興文教可宣武

上而照臨之愚之所謂存乎人者此也執

于二者乎？盖好惡審，則聽言責事，舉名察實，善無不顯，惡無不彰，而民志平矣。賞罰公，則賞不僭，刑不濫，善知所勸，惡知所懲，而國法立矣。由是農桑可興，文教可宣，武備可立，紀綱振而民風善，尚何政治之不成邪？雖然，朱子又嘗言之矣：「紀綱之所以振，則以宰執秉持而不敢失，臺諫補察而無所私，人主又以大公至正之心恭己于上而照臨之。」愚之所謂存乎人者，此也。執事倘于經幄一陳焉，則所以復祖宗之舊而臻至治之風者在是矣，豈非宗社無疆之休哉！

吳淮
同考試官教諭趙批：經與史本一道，此策歴歴能言，其於治經作史者之得失，剖析明備。非胷中會經史於一貫者不能。噫！脫穎而出者，子其人乎？
translation_en:
…than these two? When likes and dislikes are judiciously determined, statements are heard and performance exacted, and reputations are considered and checked against reality. No good remains unrecognized and no evil remains unexposed, and the people's minds are at peace. When rewards and punishments are impartial, rewards are not improperly bestowed and punishments are not excessive. The good know what encourages them and the wicked know what deters them, and the laws of the state are firmly established. Thus agriculture and sericulture can flourish, civil instruction can spread, and military preparedness can be established. With governing discipline reinvigorated and popular customs improved, what could remain unaccomplished in government?
Nevertheless, Master Zhu also once said: “Governing discipline is reinvigorated because the chief councilors uphold it without daring to let it lapse, and the censors and remonstrance officials remedy deficiencies and scrutinize affairs without partiality. The ruler, moreover, with a mind of utmost impartiality and rectitude, maintains a reverent bearing above and watches over them.” This is what I mean when I humbly say that it depends upon people. If you, sir, would present this once at the imperial lectures, herein would lie the means to restore the ancestral precedents and attain the conditions of perfect governance. Would this not be an everlasting blessing for the imperial ancestral temples and the altars of soil and grain?
Third Policy Question
Wu Huai
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: The Classics and the histories are fundamentally one Way. This policy essay explains this point distinctly, analyzing clearly and thoroughly the successes and failures of those who study the Classics and compose histories. Only someone who has united the Classics and the histories in his mind through a single guiding principle could accomplish this. Ah! Are you the one whose talent stands out from the rest?

史於經而經史之名未立經史之名立而

論經史於未分之前，而天下之學一；論經史於既分之後，而天下之學二。盖古者寓史於經，而經史之名未立；經史之名立，而二者始分矣。此古之學者所以出於一，而後之學者不免岐而二之歟？執事發策京闈，而舉此以下詢承學，此正愚生朝夕之所誦習、今日之所抱負而來試者也，其敢無辭以對？盖經以載道，史以載事，昔人嘗有是言矣。然天下未嘗有道外之事，而經即史也；亦未嘗有事外之道，而史亦經也。二者固未始不合而一也。孔子因魯史以作春秋，與易、書、詩、禮、樂並為□

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: From this candidate’s papers for the first two sessions, his □□ were already apparent [?]. His policy essays are all composed and rich in implication, without indulging in flights of fancy. His response on the classics and histories is especially refined and sound. He is an excellent scholar. How could those who reject ornament and esteem substance fail to select him?

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: This candidate’s papers in all three sessions are pure and proceed entirely from what is correct [?]; their brilliance, like that of gold and jade, cannot be concealed. His self-cultivation is profound indeed. The final few remarks in his policy essay also show no small confidence in his own abilities. An excellent scholar! An excellent scholar!

Consider the classics and histories before they were divided, and learning throughout the realm was one; consider them after their division, and learning throughout the realm was twofold. In antiquity, history was embodied in the classics, and the designations “classics” and “histories” had not yet been established. Only when these designations were established did the two begin to diverge. Is this why the learning of ancient scholars proceeded from a single source, while later scholars could not avoid branching off and dividing it into two?

You, honored examiners, have issued policy questions in the examination precincts of the capital, raising this matter to inquire of us students. This is precisely what I, an unworthy student, recite and study morning and evening, and what I have come to this examination today hoping to expound. How could I dare offer no words in reply?

The classics convey the Way; histories record events: men of earlier times have said this. Yet there have never been events in the world outside the Way, so the classics are themselves histories. Nor has there ever been a Way apart from events, so histories are also classics. The two have indeed always been united as one. Confucius drew upon the history of Lu to compose the Spring and Autumn Annals, which, together with the Changes, Documents, Odes, Rites, and Music, constituted □ [?]…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子謂聖人述史三焉其述書也帝王之制
備故索焉而皆獲其述詩也興衰之由顯
故究焉而皆得其述春秋也邪正之跡明
故考焉而皆當此三者同出於史而不可
雜也故聖人分焉蓋以尚書紀言春秋紀
事而詩明得失之故雖均為史而其體有
三者之異故曰不可雜者此也是固然矣
然而書者二帝三王之史也詩者周與列
國之史也春秋者東遷以降列侯五伯之
===
史也是其紀載之跡又有不同者焉斯時
也固未嘗有經史之名而亦安有所謂經
史之學哉故劉歆叙七畧王儉撰七志史
記以下皆附春秋蓋亦不為無見是則漢
魏以前經史猶未分也其後荀勗分四部
史記舊事入丙部阮孝緒七録經典録六
藝紀傳録史傳而經與史至是始分矣後
之以學名者遂有二者之異若王安石以
經學稱司馬光以史學著是以三經字義

punctuated: 子謂：「聖人述史三焉。其述書也，帝王之制備，故索焉而皆獲；其述詩也，興衰之由顯，故究焉而皆得；其述春秋也，邪正之跡明，故考焉而皆當。此三者同出於史，而不可雜也，故聖人分焉。」蓋以《尚書》紀言，《春秋》紀事，而《詩》明得失之故。雖均為史，而其體有三者之異，故曰不可雜者，此也。是固然矣。然而《書》者，二帝三王之史也；《詩》者，周與列國之史也；《春秋》者，東遷以降列侯五伯之史也。是其紀載之跡，又有不同者焉。斯時也，固未嘗有經史之名，而亦安有所謂經史之學哉？故劉歆叙《七畧》，王儉撰《七志》，《史記》以下皆附《春秋》，蓋亦不為無見。是則漢魏以前，經史猶未分也。其後荀勗分四部，《史記》舊事入丙部；阮孝緒《七録》，經典録六藝，紀傳録史傳，而經與史至是始分矣。後之以學名者，遂有二者之異。若王安石以經學稱，司馬光以史學著，是以三經字義
translation_en: …the Master said: “The sage compiled history in three forms. In compiling the Documents, he fully set forth the institutions of emperors and kings, so that all who seek there find what they need. In compiling the Odes, he revealed the causes of rise and decline, so that all who investigate there gain understanding. In compiling the Spring and Autumn Annals, he made clear the traces of wrongdoing and rectitude, so that all who examine them arrive at sound judgments. These three alike derive from history, yet they cannot be mingled; therefore the sage distinguished them.” This is because the Book of Documents records words, the Spring and Autumn Annals records events, and the Odes elucidates the reasons for successes and failures. Although all are histories, their forms differ in these three ways. This is what is meant by saying that they cannot be mingled. That is certainly so. Yet the Documents is the history of the Two Emperors and Three Kings; the Odes is the history of Zhou and the various states; and the Spring and Autumn Annals is the history of the feudal lords and Five Hegemons from the eastward relocation of the capital onward. Thus the historical particulars they record also differ. At that time, the designations “classics” and “histories” did not yet exist; how, then, could there have been what we call the study of classics and the study of history? Thus, when Liu Xin arranged the Seven Summaries and Wang Jian compiled the Seven Treatises, they placed the Records of the Grand Historian and subsequent works under the Spring and Autumn Annals. This was surely not without insight. Thus, before the Han and Wei periods, classics and histories were still undivided. Subsequently, Xun Xu established four divisions, placing the Records of the Grand Historian and accounts of earlier events in Division C. In Ruan Xiaoxu’s Seven Records, the Record of Classical Texts covered the Six Arts, while the Record of Annals and Biographies covered histories and biographies. Only then did classics and histories become separate. Among those who subsequently gained renown for scholarship, these two distinctions accordingly arose. For example, Wang Anshi was acclaimed for classical scholarship, and Sima Guang was renowned for historical scholarship. Hence the meanings of the Three Classics and of characters [?]…

作於介甫，而通鑑編年成於温公，豈非各因其學之所長以自見歟？然王雖以經學稱，而所行亦何得於經？假周官經世之名，以文管商功利之術，而又擯斥忠讜，引用凶邪，卒以開宣和之釁。宋之不競，議者至今有遺憾焉。司馬雖以史學著，而所得不專在於史。吾觀其平生所行，不外一誠，救焚拯溺，勞瘁不懈，卒成元祐之治。宋之不遽亡，識者以為猶有賴焉。則其人品之高下，又豈待較而明哉？執事又欲聞諸生之所得者，晚生末學，豈足以及此？然竊嘗聞之：善學者必本之經，以究作史之原；參之史，以廣明經之用。使考事者必據經以為之權衡，窮理者必觀史以驗其實迹，則經學不失之迂，而史學不失之陋矣。愚也有志，願學而未能，方趨下風而有請焉。執事以為何如？

第四問
translation_en:
…were written by Jiefu, while the chronologically arranged Comprehensive Mirror was completed by Lord Wen. Was this not because each gave expression to the particular strengths of his learning? Yet although Wang was renowned for his learning in the Classics, what in his conduct actually derived from them? He borrowed the name of ordering the world through the Offices of Zhou to embellish the techniques of Guan Zhong and Shang Yang, aimed at achievement and profit. Moreover, he rejected loyal and forthright men and brought in the wicked and corrupt, ultimately opening the way to the calamities of the Xuanhe era. Commentators to this day retain a sense of regret over the Song dynasty’s weakness.

Although Sima was renowned for his historical learning, what he had gained was not confined to history. When I consider his conduct throughout his life, it never departed from sincerity alone. He rescued those in flames and saved those drowning, toiling tirelessly, and ultimately brought about the good government of the Yuanyou era. Discerning men believe that his legacy still helped keep the Song from perishing immediately. Thus, surely the relative heights of their moral character are apparent without any need for comparison!

You further wish to hear what we students have gained from our learning. How could a junior of such scant learning as myself be equal to this? Yet I have heard that those who study well must take the Classics as their foundation to investigate the sources of historical writing, and consult history to broaden the practical application of their understanding of the Classics. If those who examine events invariably use the Classics as their standard of judgment, and those who investigate principles invariably consult history to verify their concrete manifestations, then classical learning will not lapse into impracticality, nor historical learning into narrowness. Foolish though I am, I have the aspiration and wish to learn, but have not yet attained this. I now humbly approach you to seek instruction. What do you think of this?

Fourth Question

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
楊春芳
同考試官教諭魏批經術節義策場中士子
博者失於斷制狹者拘於所聞是篇識見卓偉抑揚予
奪曲中事理且歸重於節義而又要以至當之論子殆經
術中之有節義者歟
考試官右諭德李批評隲兩漢諸子得失皆為確
論蓋有得於春秋之學者是可以知子之所嚮矣
考試官侍讀學士汪批此卷前二場超然不羣策皆
善答而此篇尤贍整有條其學識之最優者乎
===
談經者貴有明道之功勵節者貴能見幾
之審見道不明則誦說雖勤徒事佔畢而
無益于實用知幾不審則忠憤雖切徒騰
論議而無補于國家持此可以論兩漢之
士矣請條陳之夫三代之後漢稱得士西
漢自武帝表章六經一時之士爭尚經術
然秉操履正以節義自勵者亦不能無焉
觀汲黯數好直諫而淮南為之寢謀蘇武
持節虜庭而匈奴以之奪氣朱雲借劍尚

同考試官教諭魏批：經術節義策，場中士子，博者失於斷制，狹者拘於所聞。是篇識見卓偉，抑揚予奪，曲中事理，且歸重於節義，而又要以至當之論。子殆經術中之有節義者歟！

Yang Chunfang

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: On the policy essay concerning classical learning and moral integrity: among the candidates in the examination hall, those of broad learning fall short in judgment, while those of narrow learning are confined by what they have heard. This essay displays outstanding insight. Its praise and blame, approval and disapproval accord with the principles of affairs in every particular. Moreover, it places chief importance on moral integrity, while taking perfectly balanced judgment as its ultimate standard. Are you perhaps one whose classical learning is joined with moral integrity?

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: Your assessments of the merits and failings of the various worthies of the two Han dynasties are all sound judgments. You have evidently gained an understanding of the learning of the Spring and Autumn Annals; from this one can discern the direction of your aspirations.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: This candidate’s work in the first two sessions stands far above the ordinary. All the policy questions are well answered, and this essay is especially rich, well composed, and orderly. Might he be the foremost in learning and discernment?

Those who discuss the classics are valued for their achievement in illuminating the Way; those who cultivate integrity are valued for discerning the first signs of change accurately. If their perception of the Way is unclear, then, however diligently they recite and expound, they merely pore over texts without contributing to practical use. If their discernment of incipient change is imprecise, then, however fervent their loyal indignation, they merely stir up debate without benefiting the state. By these standards we may assess the scholars of the two Han dynasties. Allow me to set out the matter point by point.

After the Three Dynasties, the Han was renowned for obtaining worthy men. In the Western Han, from the time Emperor Wu honored and promoted the Six Classics, scholars competed in esteeming classical learning. Yet among them there were also men who maintained principled conduct, acted uprightly, and spurred themselves on through integrity and righteousness. title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
方攀檻大呼蕭望之職居師傅不肯就吏
印綬加身輒推不受龔勝耻事乎二姓安
車再聘堅卧不起薛方自託于巢由王章
却其妻牛衣之言抗疏下獄蓋寬饒拒友
人蘧氏之喻上書自殞解劍無傷也雋不
疑則曰君子武備以衞身請不解而退免
冠隨俗也貢禹則曰冠一免安復可冠願
不免以去官之數子者清風勁節蓋凛凛
乎其不可犯矣人惟見夫仲舒京房匡衡
===
更生之流懷經挾術所在霧滃遂以經術
歸之不知經術豈足以盡西漢之士邪東
漢自光武率興教化一時之人競崇節義
然負笈抱策而經術是事者亦未嘗少焉
觀伏湛之篤信好古經為人師桓譚之徧
習五經剖析疑異樊儵刪定公羊嚴氏春
秋章句世號曰樊侯學鄭玄因考論圖緯
請益辭歸其師嘆曰吾道東矣弟習魯詩
而為學士所推者則魯恭魯丕父子明左

方，攀檻大呼；蕭望之職居師傅，不肯就吏；印綬加身，輒推不受，龔勝耻事乎二姓；安車再聘，堅卧不起，薛方自託于巢由；王章却其妻牛衣之言，抗疏下獄；蓋寬饒拒友人蘧氏之喻，上書自殞。解劍無傷也，雋不疑則曰：「君子武備以衞身。」請不解而退。免冠隨俗也，貢禹則曰：「冠一免，安復可冠？」願不免以去官。之數子者，清風勁節，蓋凛凛乎其不可犯矣。人惟見夫仲舒、京房、匡衡、更生之流，懷經挾術，所在霧滃，遂以經術歸之，不知經術豈足以盡西漢之士邪？

東漢自光武率興教化，一時之人競崇節義，然負笈抱策而經術是事者，亦未嘗少焉。觀伏湛之篤信好古，經為人師；桓譚之徧習五經，剖析疑異；樊儵刪定《公羊》《嚴氏春秋章句》，世號曰「樊侯學」；鄭玄因考論圖緯，請益辭歸，其師嘆曰：「吾道東矣！」弟習《魯詩》而為學士所推者，則魯恭、魯丕；父子明左
translation_en:
…from the imperial armory, clinging to the balustrade and crying out loudly. Xiao Wangzhi held office as an imperial tutor and would not submit to the judicial officials. When seals and ribbons of office were placed upon him, Gong Sheng repeatedly pushed them away and refused them, ashamed to serve two ruling houses. Twice summoned with a carriage in which he could sit comfortably, Xue Fang remained firmly reclining and would not rise, claiming for himself the example of Chao Fu and Xu You. Wang Zhang rejected his wife’s words about their days beneath an ox’s coverlet, submitted a remonstrance, and was imprisoned. Gai Kuanrao rejected his friend’s analogy concerning Qu Boyu, submitted a memorial, and took his own life. Removing one’s sword would have done no harm, yet Jun Buyi said, “A gentleman maintains military preparedness to protect himself,” and requested leave to withdraw without removing it. Removing one’s cap would have conformed to prevailing custom, yet Gong Yu said, “Once the cap is removed, how can it be worn again?” He preferred to leave office without removing it. These men’s pure conduct and steadfast integrity were indeed so awe-inspiring that none could violate them. People see only the likes of Zhongshu, Jing Fang, Kuang Heng, and Gengsheng, cherishing the Classics and possessing scholarly learning, gathering like thick mist wherever they were, and consequently characterize Western Han scholars in terms of classical learning. They do not realize: how could classical learning alone encompass all the scholars of the Western Han?

In the Eastern Han, after Guangwu took the lead in promoting moral instruction, men of the age competed in honoring integrity and righteousness. Yet those who carried book satchels and held written texts, devoting themselves to classical learning, were also far from few. Consider Fu Zhan, steadfast in his convictions and devoted to antiquity, who taught others the Classics; Huan Tan, who studied all Five Classics and analyzed doubtful and divergent interpretations; and Fan Shu, who edited and established the texts of the Gongyang Commentary and Master Yan’s Chapters and Sentences on the Spring and Autumn Annals, known in his day as “Marquis Fan’s learning.” Zheng Xuan studied and discussed the prophetic charts and apocryphal writings, sought further instruction, and took leave to return home. His teacher exclaimed, “My Way is going east!” Those who studied the Lu tradition of the Odes and were esteemed by scholars were Lu Gong and Lu Pi—the reference to brothers here is garbled [?]; the father and son who mastered the Zuo …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
氏而為羣儒所宗者則鄭興鄭衆絳帳設
教生徒千人馬融名重于關西正定五經
刻石太學蔡邕儒崇于靈帝之數子者博
古名家蓋彬彬乎其盛矣人唯見夫八俊
八顧八及八厨之輩危言激論所在風生
遂以節義許之不知節義豈足以盡東漢
之士邪經術所以致用明易如張禹藉經
飾詐來持禄保位之譏擬易如揚雄畏禍
取容有劇秦美新之作谷永欲阿王鳳則
===
引申伯以稱其忠劉歆欲附新莽則獻符
命以逢其惡數子非不經術之是究也然
出口入耳無講學明道之功繪句摛章乏
體驗擴充之實是以諛佞成習風節罔聞
規避苟安士氣掃地豈經術之罪哉節義
將以建功有清世之志如陳蕃幾事不密
而功隳羣小負王佐之才如王允氣溢志
驕而身殘餘孽李膺破柱戮姦其事偉矣
無何而名陷黨議范滂登車攬轡其志雄

氏而為羣儒所宗者，則鄭興、鄭衆。絳帳設教，生徒千人，馬融名重于關西；正定五經，刻石太學，蔡邕儒崇于靈帝。之數子者，博古名家，蓋彬彬乎其盛矣。人唯見夫八俊、八顧、八及、八厨之輩，危言激論，所在風生，遂以節義許之，不知節義豈足以盡東漢之士邪？
經術所以致用。明《易》如張禹，藉經飾詐，來持禄保位之譏；擬《易》如揚雄，畏禍取容，有《劇秦美新》之作。谷永欲阿王鳳，則引申伯以稱其忠；劉歆欲附新莽，則獻符命以逢其惡。數子非不經術之是究也，然出口入耳，無講學明道之功；繪句摛章，乏體驗擴充之實。是以諛佞成習，風節罔聞，規避苟安，士氣掃地，豈經術之罪哉？
節義將以建功。有清世之志如陳蕃，幾事不密，而功隳羣小；負王佐之才如王允，氣溢志驕，而身殘餘孽。李膺破柱戮姦，其事偉矣，無何而名陷黨議；范滂登車攬轡，其志雄
translation_en:
…the Zuo tradition, becoming authorities whom the assembled scholars revered, were Zheng Xing and Zheng Zhong. Teaching behind crimson curtains, with a thousand students, Ma Rong won great renown west of the passes. Correcting and establishing the texts of the Five Classics and having them engraved on stone at the Imperial University, Cai Yong was honored as a scholar by Emperor Ling. These men [?], eminent masters versed in antiquity, constituted a splendid flourishing of cultivated learning. People see only how the Eight Eminent Ones, Eight Models, Eight Exemplars, and Eight Providers spoke uncompromisingly and argued vehemently, stirring enthusiasm wherever they went, and consequently commend them for integrity and righteousness. Do they not realize that integrity and righteousness alone cannot encompass the scholars of the Eastern Han?
Classical learning is meant to be put into practice. Zhang Yu, who understood the Book of Changes [?], used the classics to cloak deceit, inviting criticism for clinging to his stipend and safeguarding his position. Yang Xiong, who composed a work modeled on the Book of Changes, feared calamity and sought acceptance, producing his Denunciation of Qin and Praise of Xin. When Gu Yong wished to flatter Wang Feng, he invoked the Earl of Shen to praise Wang’s loyalty. When Liu Xin wished to attach himself to Wang Mang of the Xin dynasty, he presented auspicious tokens of Heaven’s mandate to gratify Wang’s wicked ambitions. It was not that these men failed to investigate classical learning. Yet their learning merely passed into their ears and out of their mouths: they had done no work of discussing learning and illuminating the Way. They embellished phrases and composed ornate passages, but lacked the substance of personal realization and further development. Thus flattery became habitual, and nothing was heard of principled conduct. They evaded difficulties and sought precarious ease, utterly degrading the spirit of scholars. Could this be the fault of classical learning?
Integrity and righteousness are meant to establish meritorious achievements. Chen Fan aspired to purify the age, but failed to keep a crucial undertaking secret, and his achievement was undone by petty men. Wang Yun possessed the ability to assist a sovereign, but grew overbearing and arrogant, and was killed by the surviving remnants of the villains. Li Ying broke open a pillar and executed an evildoer—a magnificent deed! Yet before long his reputation became entangled in accusations of factionalism. Fan Pang mounted his carriage and took up the reins; his resolve was heroic…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
亡未幾而禍及友朋數子非不節義之是
崇也然圭角炫露既昧處困之方勇徃直
前又失亨屯之道是以撩蛇踐虎毒流縉
紳噓枯吹生殃遺黎庶豈節義之過哉夫
經術者學問之功也節義者天資之美也
有天資而又加以問學則行無不周施無
不利出則行道以濟時處則隱居以求志
不幸而際非其時則殺身以成仁斯無媿
于士矣善乎張子有曰昔之儒者學問素
===
充其施于用隨時著見不蘄於立節而其
節不可奪不蘄于徇名而其名隨之嗚呼
盡之矣兩漢之士其有歉于是乎此所以
千載之下不能無遺憾也雖然天地之正
氣賦于人而為節義孟軻氏曰其為氣也
至大至剛以直養而無害則塞于天地之

之道有未盡然能維持漢祚而賴以不墜

punctuated: 亡，未幾而禍及友朋。數子非不節義之是崇也，然圭角炫露，既昧處困之方；勇徃直前，又失亨屯之道。是以撩蛇踐虎，毒流縉紳；噓枯吹生，殃遺黎庶。豈節義之過哉？夫經術者，學問之功也；節義者，天資之美也。有天資而又加以問學，則行無不周，施無不利。出則行道以濟時，處則隱居以求志；不幸而際非其時，則殺身以成仁，斯無媿于士矣。善乎，張子有曰：「昔之儒者，學問素充，其施于用，隨時著見。不蘄於立節，而其節不可奪；不蘄于徇名，而其名隨之。」嗚呼，盡之矣！兩漢之士，其有歉于是乎？此所以千載之下不能無遺憾也。雖然，天地之正氣，賦于人而為節義。孟軻氏曰：「其為氣也，至大至剛，以直養而無害，則塞于天地之間。」東都諸君子奮迅感慨，視死如歸，激素行以耻威權，立廉隅以震貴勢。雖於中庸之道有未盡，然能維持漢祚而賴以不墜
translation_en: …[?] Before long, calamity reached his friends and associates. These men certainly revered moral integrity and righteousness. Yet, conspicuously displaying their sharp edges, they failed to understand how to conduct themselves in adversity; charging courageously forward, they also missed the way to bring success out of difficulty. Thus they stirred up snakes and trod upon tigers, spreading venom among the official elite; their breath withered or revived others, leaving disaster to the common people. How could this be the fault of integrity and righteousness? Classical learning is the achievement of study; integrity and righteousness are the excellence of natural endowment. When natural endowment is supplemented by learning, conduct is thorough in every respect, and its application invariably beneficial. In office, one practices the Way to aid one's age; in retirement, one lives in seclusion to fulfill one's aspirations. If, unfortunately, one encounters an age unsuited to one's purposes, one sacrifices one's life to fulfill benevolence. Then one is worthy of being called a scholar. Well did Master Zhang say: “The scholars of old had long cultivated abundant learning. When they put it into practice, it manifested itself according to the circumstances. They did not seek to establish a reputation for integrity, yet their integrity could not be wrested from them; they did not seek to pursue fame, yet fame followed them.” Ah, this says it all! Did the scholars of the two Han dynasties fall somewhat short of this? This is why, a thousand years later, regret cannot be wholly absent. Nevertheless, the upright vital force of Heaven and Earth, bestowed upon human beings, becomes integrity and righteousness. Meng Ke said: “As vital force, it is supremely great and supremely firm. Nourish it with uprightness and do it no harm, and it will fill the space between Heaven and Earth.” The gentlemen of the Eastern Capital rose vigorously, stirred by indignation, and regarded death as a homecoming. They intensified their accustomed virtuous conduct to shame those wielding coercive authority, and established firm moral boundaries to overawe the powerful and exalted. Although they did not fully realize the Way of the Mean, they were able to sustain the Han dynasty, which relied upon them to keep from falling …

…How could their achievement have been small? Ah! Let gentlemen of later generations never say that merely having a reputation for integrity and righteousness is enough. Such is my limited view; may you instruct me further.
Fifth Question
Li Shifang
Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: From his writing on the classics, I already knew that he was extraordinary. When I examined his work for the middle and final sessions, his talent and spirit proved commanding and outstanding. It was like entering an arsenal, with spears and halberds arrayed in imposing ranks, dazzling the beholder. Ah! Who says that the examination system cannot discover worthy men?
Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: All five policy essays in this script merit inclusion, but I have included only the one on learning, to assess his final performance. By assessing the final performance, one can see all the rest. The Book of Changes section certainly has many able candidates; surely you are among its exceptional ones! To have found such a man gives the presiding examiner real satisfaction.
Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor: His talent and spirit are compelling, and his keen edge repeatedly shows itself; yet his aspirations are thoroughly upright, as this policy essay reveals. I shall watch eagerly to see what he achieves.
There is a correct path in learning: those who dislike complexity and delight in simplification will inevitably drift into heterodox teachings. There are fundamental principles in government: those who see only small gains and desire quick results often content themselves with minor accomplishments. Scholars without aspirations are not worth discussing. But to aspire to learning yet enter into heterodoxy, or to aspire to government yet settle for minor accomplishments, is a fault arising from failure to examine these matters thoroughly. In setting this policy question, you seek to clarify the principles of learning and advance the candidates, so that they do not lose their sense of direction…

text:
惠甚渥也愚也敢不悉心以對夫學必師
孔孟治必法三代自宋儒著爲定論學者
守爲家法而
國朝養士於學校取士於科目尊崇六經罷
黜百家一以程朱之說爲主其道德固已
一而風俗固已同矣執事過慮恐爲學者
有近於佛老而爲政者或流於申韓愚也
亦不敢謂無其人也夫自王者之迹熄而
聖人之道不明於是申韓于秦黃老于漢
===
===
而大壞于晉宋齊梁之間彼秦用法令以
收富彊之效而遂并天下申商若可用矣
然徒文具而無惻隱之實二世之敗天下
土崩以爲可用者見其利未見其害也漢
用清淨以脩玄默之化而致黎民醇厚黃
老若可用矣然禁網疎闊豪強莫制七國
之變漢事幾殆以爲可用者見其得未見
其失也儒者必深斥之不少假借者非以
此歟韓非論法術謂人主之大物非法則

punctuated: 惠甚渥也。愚也敢不悉心以對？夫學必師孔孟，治必法三代，自宋儒著爲定論，學者守爲家法。而國朝養士於學校，取士於科目，尊崇六經，罷黜百家，一以程朱之說爲主，其道德固已一，而風俗固已同矣。執事過慮，恐爲學者有近於佛老，而爲政者或流於申韓，愚也亦不敢謂無其人也。夫自王者之迹熄，而聖人之道不明，於是申韓于秦，黃老于漢，而大壞于晉宋齊梁之間。彼秦用法令以收富彊之效，而遂并天下，申商若可用矣。然徒文具而無惻隱之實，二世之敗，天下土崩，以爲可用者，見其利，未見其害也。漢用清淨以脩玄默之化，而致黎民醇厚，黃老若可用矣。然禁網疎闊，豪強莫制，七國之變，漢事幾殆，以爲可用者，見其得，未見其失也。儒者必深斥之，不少假借者，非以此歟？韓非論法術，謂人主之大物，非法則
translation_en:
…Your kindness is most generous. How could I, unworthy though I am, dare not devote my whole mind to answering? In learning, one must take Kongzi and Mengzi as teachers; in government, one must take the Three Dynasties as models. Since the Song Confucians established this as a settled judgment, scholars have upheld it as their inherited rule. Our dynasty nurtures scholars in its schools and selects them through the examinations. It honors the Six Classics and rejects the Hundred Schools, taking the teachings of Cheng and Zhu alone as its guide. Its moral principles have thus already been unified, and its customs brought into accord. You, sir, in your solicitude, fear that those pursuing learning may approach Buddhism and Daoism, while those conducting government may drift toward the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei. I would not venture to claim that no such people exist.

Once the traces of true kingship had vanished and the Way of the sages was no longer clear, the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei prevailed under the Qin, and those of Huangdi and Laozi under the Han; the Way then fell into profound ruin during the Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang dynasties. The Qin employed laws and commands to attain wealth and strength, eventually unifying all under Heaven. Thus the teachings of Shen Buhai and Shang Yang might seem serviceable. Yet they furnished only formal provisions, without the substance of compassion. With the defeat of the Second Emperor, the realm crumbled. Those who deemed these teachings serviceable saw their benefits but not their harm.

The Han employed purity and tranquillity to cultivate transformation through profound stillness, making the common people simple and sincere. Thus the teachings of Huangdi and Laozi might seem serviceable. Yet the net of prohibitions was so loose that powerful local magnates went unchecked. During the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms, the Han state nearly fell into ruin. Those who deemed these teachings serviceable saw their gains but not their losses. Is this not why Confucians must condemn them severely, granting them not the slightest indulgence? In discussing laws and administrative techniques, Han Fei said that the great instruments of the ruler were either laws or…

潜御羣臣者也法莫如顯而術不欲見又
曰申不害言術公孫鞅爲法則其爲用有
異矣儒者雖或有所不廢而所謂以不忍
人之心行不忍人之政者彼盖未之聞也

因應爲用其言似亦幾矣然大易不言有
無言有無者皆諸子之陋也今之學者溺

而脫去凡近以求高明者又多流於異學

punctuated:
□□者，編著之圖籍，設之於官府而布之於百姓者也。術者，藏之胷中，以偶衆端而潜御羣臣者也。法莫如顯，而術不欲見。又曰：「申不害言術，公孫鞅爲法。」則其爲用有異矣。儒者雖或有所不廢，而所謂以不忍人之心行不忍人之政者，彼盖未之聞也。
道家稱無爲，又曰無不爲，以虛無爲本，以因應爲用，其言似亦幾矣。然大易不言有無，言有無者皆諸子之陋也。
今之學者溺於訓詁詞章之習，既不足以知大道之要，而脫去凡近以求高明者，又多流於異學而不自知。爲政者玩於苟且偷惰之風，既不足以宣至治之澤，而專事操切以急近功者，又多傷於刻核而不之反。執事之憂，非過也。愚也不敏，請熟誦伊洛關閩之書而敬守之，則庶乎其不悖矣。
translation_en:
…[Two illegible characters] [?] are compiled and written into books, established in government offices, and promulgated among the common people. Techniques of rule are concealed within the ruler’s breast, to meet the many contingencies of affairs and covertly control his ministers. Laws are best made manifest, whereas techniques of rule should not be revealed. He further says: “Shen Buhai spoke of techniques of rule; Gongsun Yang instituted laws.” Thus their applications differ. Although Confucians may retain some elements of these, those men presumably never heard of what is called exercising government that cannot bear others’ suffering through a heart that cannot bear others’ suffering.
The Daoists advocate nonaction, yet also say that nothing is left undone. They take emptiness and nothingness as their foundation and responsive adaptation as their practical application. Their words seem, indeed, to come close to the Way. Yet the great Book of Changes does not speak of being and nonbeing; discourse on being and nonbeing is a limitation shared by the various philosophical masters.
Scholars today are immersed in the practice of textual exegesis and literary composition, which is insufficient to enable them to understand the essentials of the Great Way. Yet those who cast off the ordinary and familiar in pursuit of lofty understanding often drift into heterodox learning without realizing it. Those who govern have grown complacent amid habits of expediency and indolence, which leave them unable to extend the blessings of consummate government. Yet those who devote themselves exclusively to coercive measures, hastening after immediate results, often go wrong through harsh and exacting scrutiny and fail to turn back. Your concern, sir, is not excessive. Dull-witted though I am, I would ask to recite thoroughly the writings of the masters of Yi, Luo, Guan, and Min and reverently abide by them. Then I might hope not to depart from the Way.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In autumn, in the eighth month of the jimao year of the Zhengde reign (1519; transcribed 已卯 [?]), the time had come for Provincial Examinations throughout the realm. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture requested that the examination be held according to established precedent. His Majesty commanded his servants Jun, Academician Reader-in-waiting, and Shi, Right Admonisher, to go and preside over the examination. The following day we took leave of His Majesty; twenty-five days later we arrived. Scholars carrying books and writings had gathered like clouds in the capital to sit the examination.

In accordance with imperial regulations, we examined them in three sessions; 135 men passed. Their names, together with a selection of outstanding essays, were engraved and printed as a record for presentation to His Majesty. It fell to your servant Shi to write its postface. I, Shi, reflect that our sagely founder, the Gao Emperor, received Heaven’s great mandate and came to possess all the central realm…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
金陵寔肇迹之地一時佐命
武臣瑰奇偉雋又皆東南之
英得人之盛靡可及矣
聖子神孫飾治弘化保有丕基則
唯文儒是賴而東南之才亦
往往過於他省顧創業之時
其用也出于招延守成之際
===
非科舉則有莫能得者科舉
之設其来尚矣成周以三物
賓興賢能後之選舉實昉焉
然其為法或廣而靡精或狹
而近陋或繁而過猥或泥而
難通是以得才之效代有不
同而政治因之

punctuated: 金陵寔肇迹之地，一時佐命武臣，瑰奇偉雋，又皆東南之英，得人之盛，靡可及矣。聖子神孫飾治弘化，保有丕基，則唯文儒是賴，而東南之才亦往往過於他省。顧創業之時，其用也出于招延；守成之際，非科舉則有莫能得者。科舉之設，其来尚矣。成周以三物賓興賢能，後之選舉實昉焉。然其為法，或廣而靡精，或狹而近陋，或繁而過猥，或泥而難通，是以得才之效，代有不同，而政治因之
translation_en:
…Jinling was indeed the place where his enterprise began. The military officials who assisted in founding the dynasty were extraordinary and outstanding men, all of them also the finest talents of the southeast. Such abundance in obtaining worthy men could not be surpassed. His sage sons and divine grandsons have perfected government, extended moral transformation, and preserved the great dynastic foundation, relying solely upon men of Confucian learning. The talents of the southeast, too, have often surpassed those of other provinces. Yet at the founding of the dynasty, men were brought into service through invitations to serve; in preserving the established realm, some can be obtained only through the civil-service examinations.

The institution of civil-service examinations has a long history. The Zhou dynasty honored and recommended the worthy and capable on the basis of the three categories of instruction; later systems of selection originated in this practice. Yet their methods were sometimes broad without being discerning, sometimes narrow to the point of inadequacy, sometimes elaborate to the point of excessive complication, and sometimes rigid and difficult to apply. Thus their effectiveness in obtaining talent differed from dynasty to dynasty, and the conduct of government varied accordingly…

translation_en:
… [Two illegible characters; the opening syntax is uncertain.] In establishing laws and instituting regulations, he adapted the institutions of the kings of successive ages. Even amid the turmoil of warfare, his plans to secure the welfare of his descendants were especially earnest and thorough. He once said: “Promoting the worthy and employing the talented are the foundation of establishing a state.” He also said: “Since antiquity, no ruler of a state has ever been able to govern alone without relying on worthy and talented men.” Ah, how far-reaching! Thus the system for seeking scholars was excellent in every respect and exceptionally comprehensive.

Schools were established and teachers appointed to clarify human relationships and foster moral transformation. Scholars studied only the Five Classics, the Four Books, and the histories. The writings formerly associated with diplomatic strategists, emptiness and nonbeing, penal methods and administrative accountability, and achievement and profit were all excluded. The way of nurturing scholars was thus upright. Once every three years, a great examination was held. Candidates’ names were concealed and their scripts recopied; their work was assessed separately according to the Classic in which they specialized, and the presiding examiners determined rejection or advancement. So tightly guarded were the procedures that even ghosts and spirits could not fathom them. The method of selecting scholars was thus impartial. Scholars were advanced …

translation_en:
…in the great court, they serve within the ranked official hierarchy. The Three Dukes, Three Junior Preceptors, protectors and preceptors; officials of the central ministries and courts, censors and remonstrance officials; regional commissioners and local governors—all bear responsibilities as the sovereign’s limbs and are entrusted with the people and their altars of soil. Such responsibilities are entrusted only to scholars. Thus the established practice of employing scholars accords them great weight. For more than a hundred and fifty years, government has flourished, moral transformation has spread everywhere, and all within the seas has enjoyed peace and order. Surely this has its reasons! You scholars are now casting off your moorings and setting your wheels in motion. All of you will have duties concerning these responsibilities as the sovereign’s limbs and custodians of the people and their altars. Should you not give this some thought?
His Majesty has nurtured us in uprightness. When you take office and accept your responsibilities, your words must be upright and your conduct correct; do not twist your learning to curry favor with the world. His Majesty places great weight upon employing us. You must attend peacefully and reverently to your posts. text:
國家作養選擧之意庶幾其不
負矣俾我
朝文德與武功並稱守成與創
業同美曰唯東南之才豈不
休哉諸士生長
王化首被之地漸漬涵濡于斯
三者必槩于其中矣時于其
===
始進也故特言之若夫援經
述史形諸較論渢渢乎
昭代之風一洗六朝之舊固諸
士之所優爲而或藉以爲它
日希崇陟峻之階者又諸士
之所不屑爲也時皆得而畧
云

punctuated: 國家作養選擧之意，庶幾其不負矣。俾我朝文德與武功並稱，守成與創業同美，曰：「唯東南之才。」豈不休哉！諸士生長王化首被之地，漸漬涵濡于斯三者，必槩于其中矣。時于其始進也，故特言之。若夫援經述史，形諸較論，渢渢乎昭代之風，一洗六朝之舊，固諸士之所優爲；而或藉以爲它日希崇陟峻之階者，又諸士之所不屑爲也。時皆得而畧云。
translation_en:
…then perhaps they will not fail the state’s purpose in nurturing and selecting talent. They will enable our dynasty’s civil virtue to be acclaimed alongside its military achievements, and its preservation of the inherited realm to rival the glory of its founding, so that people will say: “This is owing to the talent of the southeast.” Would this not be splendid! You gentlemen were born and raised in the region first touched by the transforming influence of royal rule. Steeped and nurtured in these three things, you must surely feel deeply stirred within [?]. Thus I, Shi [?], speak particularly of these matters as you first advance.

As for drawing upon the classics and recounting history, expressing these in argumentation [?], abundantly displaying the spirit of this illustrious age and sweeping away the old habits of the Six Dynasties—these are certainly things you gentlemen can accomplish with distinction. Yet using such accomplishments as steps by which to seek lofty office and high advancement in the future is something you would disdain to do. I, Shi [?], have been able to speak briefly of all these matters.

translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn of the jimao year of the Zhengde reign (1519; transcribed 已卯 [?]), the time had come for the selection of scholars throughout the empire. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture submitted a memorial requesting Examiners. His Majesty accordingly appointed your servant Jun, Expositor-in-Waiting, and your servant Shi, Right Exhorter. When they arrived, the Associate Examiners were your servant Shenfu, Professor; your servant Feng, Instructor; and your servants Ji, Qi, Tingmei, Mingluan, and Rudeng, all Instructors. Supervising the examination were your servants Bijin and Shitong, Investigating Censors. These, together with the personnel serving within and outside the examination compound, were all engaged or selected to fill their posts. The Proctors were your servant Zongdao, Prefect, and your servant Tingguang, Vice Prefect. Altogether, more than two thousand scholars presented themselves for the examination.

Previously, those submitting proposals had requested that the number admitted to the examination compound be reduced to save expenses. His Majesty regarded the matter as important and decreed that the existing practice should continue. The responsible officials, however, differed in their implementation: some selected candidates strictly to facilitate screening, while others broadly…

text:
壯益甚則又見夫黄河之會
渡淮陰入邗溝以臨真揚則
又見夫長江之險江河之經
流于中國殆不下萬里而其
委皆在於南服俊於是得巨
觀焉南望羣山扶輿磅礴廻
翔飛翥若自天而降者蟠而
爲龍踞而爲虎以開
帝王之真宅而我
高皇帝之基命實肇於此夫豈偶
然之故哉東南之人物與其
財賦並稱甲於天下其地産
有固然歟俊未及供事而知
其文章之鉅麗必將大有發

punctuated: 壯益甚，則又見夫黄河之會。渡淮陰，入邗溝，以臨真揚，則又見夫長江之險。江河之經流于中國，殆不下萬里，而其委皆在於南服。俊於是得巨觀焉。南望羣山，扶輿磅礴，廻翔飛翥，若自天而降者，蟠而爲龍，踞而爲虎，以開帝王之真宅。而我高皇帝之基命，實肇於此，夫豈偶然之故哉！東南之人物與其財賦，並稱甲於天下，其地産有固然歟？俊未及供事，而知其文章之鉅麗，必將大有發
translation_en: …its grandeur grew still greater, and then I saw the confluence of the Yellow River. Crossing Huaiyin and entering the Han Canal to approach Zhenzhou and Yangzhou, I then saw the formidable natural defenses of the Yangzi River. The Yangzi and Yellow Rivers flow through the Central Lands for no fewer than ten thousand li, yet both empty into the sea in the southern region. Here I, Jun, beheld a magnificent spectacle. Looking south toward the clustered mountains, vast and imposing, wheeling and soaring as though descending from Heaven, I saw them coiled like dragons and crouching like tigers, opening up a true abode for emperors and kings. It was indeed here that our Emperor Gao first laid the foundations of his receipt of Heaven’s mandate. How could this have been mere chance? The people of talent in the southeast and its wealth and tax revenues alike are acclaimed as foremost in the realm. Is there something inherent in what this land produces? Before I, Jun, had even begun my duties, I knew that the grandeur and beauty of its literary compositions would surely provide great inspiration…

化之全也殆未可乎抑建康
之勝舊矣吳及六朝下逮南

translation_en:
…from their hearts. Then I questioned them repeatedly to observe their responses: some rang out resonantly, some shone with a quiet radiance, and some flowed abundantly, like what I had earlier witnessed on the Yellow River and the Yangzi. Surely one could hardly deny that they had received the fullness of the transforming vital force?
Yet Jiankang’s preeminence is longstanding. Wu and the Six Dynasties, down to the Southern Tang, all made use of it, but ultimately remained confined to one corner of the realm. The splendor of complete unification first emerged in our own day. Certainly, our Emperor Gao employed the forces of Xia to expel the Hu, achieving merit surpassing all antiquity and fully matching the flourishing of cosmic fortune. Yet this was also because our Emperor Wen moved his seat northward, securing all the strategic passes of the Central Realm and facing south to attend to government. Thus the two mighty capitals stand loftily facing one another at the convergence of those coming to pay court …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
會海内帖然以就撫馭籍其
財賦以制用收其譽髦以佐
理所以爲
詒燕之圖者可謂宏且遠矣丙
子之秋俊執事于北見才焉
雄深博大往往有竒氣今茲
之南也見才焉如前所云率
===
皆稱其山川至其尊王而賤
伯崇經而黜子則又未嘗有
二說也盖道德之一而風俗
之同也乆矣俊既以得士爲
朝廷賀而於其始進也張之以
昌其志俾其知所生之地所
際之時如是之不偶也他日

雄深博大往往有奇氣今兹
之南也見才焉如前所云幸
===
皆稱其山川至其尊王而賤
伯崇經而黜子則又未嘗有
二說也蓋道德之一而風俗
之同也久矣〔俊〕既以得士爲
