translation_en:
…where tribute converges. All within the seas have peacefully submitted to governance. Drawing upon their revenues to meet expenditures and recruiting their distinguished talents to assist in government, the plan thus laid for the well-being of posterity may indeed be called grand and far-reaching. In the autumn of the bingzi year, I, Jun 俊, served in the north and encountered men of talent: vigorous, profound, broadly learned, and capacious in understanding, often possessing an extraordinary spirit. Now, coming south, I have encountered men of talent such as those described above, all generally worthy of their mountains and rivers. As for honoring the true kings and esteeming the hegemons less, exalting the Classics and subordinating the philosophical masters, there have never been two opinions. Indeed, moral principles have been unified and customs shared for a long time.

Having congratulated the court on obtaining worthy men, I now, at the outset of their advancement, elaborate upon this to strengthen their aspirations, so that they may understand how exceptional are the place of their birth and the age in which they find themselves. In days to come…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
效用無違其所言無棄其所
學平時則名檢自飭臨事則
忠義奮發曰
上之人於我乎求佐理焉非苟以
榮其身家而已則於
國家化成之厚山川孕毓之勤
為不負矣是舉之興也適南
===
方有兵事倥傯不給卒獲如
期而集者諸司有貞固之幹
焉苟後之議者曰是科盖得
人為多則俊等皆可以忘其
勞矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
汪俊謹序

===
方有兵事倥偬不給卒獲如
期而集者諸司有貞固之幹
焉苟後之議者曰是科蓋得
人為多則俊等皆可以忘其
勞矣
翰林院侍讀學士奉直大夫
汪俊謹序
punctuated:
效用，無違其所言，無棄其所學。平時則名檢自飭，臨事則忠義奮發，曰：「上之人於我乎求佐理焉，非苟以榮其身家而已。」則於國家化成之厚、山川孕毓之勤，為不負矣。
是舉之興也，適南方有兵事，倥傯不給。卒獲如期而集者，諸司有貞固之幹焉。苟後之議者曰：「是科盖得人為多。」則俊等皆可以忘其勞矣。
翰林院侍讀學士、奉直大夫汪俊謹序。
translation_en:
…when they enter service, may they neither act contrary to their words nor abandon what they have learned. In ordinary times, may they discipline themselves by attending to their reputation and conduct; when affairs demand action, may they rise to the occasion with loyalty and righteousness, saying: “Those above seek our assistance in governing, not merely to confer glory upon ourselves and our families.” Then they will not have failed to repay the state’s generous work of moral transformation or the mountains and rivers’ tireless nurturing.
When this examination was undertaken, military affairs were occurring in the south, leaving us hard-pressed and unable to attend to everything. That the examination was nevertheless completed on schedule was due to the steadfast competence of the various offices. If those who assess it afterward should say, “This examination indeed selected many worthy men,” then I, Jun, and my colleagues may all forget our toil.
Respectfully prefaced by Wang Jun, Academician Reader-in-Waiting of the Hanlin Academy and Grand Master for Upright Service.

First Session

Four Books

To fail to speak with someone worth speaking with is to lose that person; to speak with someone not worth speaking with is to waste one's words. The wise lose neither people nor words.

Occupy their positions, perform their rites, play their music, revere those whom they honored, and love those whom they held dear.

Everyone has things they cannot bear to do; extending this feeling to what they can bear to do is benevolence. Everyone has things they will not do; extending this restraint to what they will do is righteousness.

Book of Changes

A great example stands above. Compliant and gentle, central and correct, he presents himself for contemplation by all under Heaven.

Against leakage, there are cloth rags [?]; remain vigilant throughout the day.

In dealings with those above him, the gentleman does not flatter; in dealings with those below him, he is not disrespectful. Does he not understand the first signs of things?

Kun is earth: all things receive nourishment from it. Thus it is said, “He brings service to completion in Kun.” Dui is mid-autumn, in which all things rejoice. Thus it is said, “He brings joy in Dui.”

Book of Documents

Yu said, “Ah! Emperor, be mindful of your position.” The emperor said, “Yes.”

Alas! The former king began by establishing the guiding principles of human relationships. He followed remonstrance without resisting it and took the worthy men of old as his models.

…In a superior position, he could exercise discernment; in a subordinate position, he could be loyal. He did not demand perfection from others, and examined himself as though he had not done enough. The awe inspired by virtue alone was to be feared; the illumination of virtue alone was true illumination.

Book of Odes
Before the sky grows dark with rain, I strip the bark from those mulberry roots and bind tight the windows and door. Now, you people below, would any dare to insult me? Reverent and vigilant, they undertake martial service; they undertake martial service to bring stability to the royal realm. They give support and assistance; they possess filial devotion and virtue. They lead and sustain. The amiable and gracious lord is a model for the four quarters. Heaven's mandate descended with watchful scrutiny; the people held it in awe. Neither erring nor exceeding proper bounds, he dared not be idle or seek ease. Heaven bestowed its command upon the realm below, firmly establishing its blessings.

translation_en:
…all been put into effect; moreover, [the Han ruler] remained content with the habits of horseback and did not apply himself to the Odes and Documents. After our Taizu had pacified the realm, he personally brought about an age of peace. Regulations and institutional forms were fully provided, and the responsible officials maintained them generation after generation. As for the pronouncements through which he bequeathed his instructions, every word and principle shone as brightly as the Six Classics. There are also many scattered among the sayings transmitted and recited by village elders and the compilations of Confucian court officials. You candidates have been among the earliest, and have long continued, to receive the nurturing influence of the sage ruler’s transforming instruction. Give a full answer based on what you have studied; you must not draw on the Han as an analogy.
Question: The Odes says, “Diligent is our king, ordering the four quarters.” The Record of Rites says, “Once the guiding principles of government are correctly established, all under Heaven is firmly settled.” Thus these principles are certainly something that those who rule a state cannot lack for even a single day. Examining antiquity, we find such examples as Emperor Xuan of Han, who comprehensively checked actual performance against nominal responsibilities, reliably bestowed rewards, and invariably imposed punishments; Emperor Taizong of Tang, who exerted himself rigorously to correct and reform, putting every detail of administration into effect; and Emperor Taizong of Song, who planned profoundly, decided boldly, assessed merit, and exercised care in punishment. It cannot be said that the guiding principles of government were not established under them. Yet among their successors, some declined because they failed to reinvigorate these principles, while others tried to reinvigorate them but instead brought about decline. Why was this?
Our Taizu, the Exalted Emperor, expelled the non-Chinese Yuan, pacified and unified all within the seas, corrected abuses, and established laws, comprehensively drawing together the traditions of the kings of old. For a hundred and fifty years, people have known to abide by the laws; those above have been secure and those below obedient, enjoying a radiant age of Great Unity. This may indeed be called flourishing government. Recently, however, judging by prevailing customs, the application of these guiding principles seems in some respects no longer what it once was. 飭治振起，以復祖宗之盛，其道何居？昔荀悅作《申鑒》，謂人主致治之術，先屏四患，乃崇五政，固紀綱之說也。其論然歟？抑可行于今歟？五政之中，何者為最要歟？朱子又謂綱紀在于辨賢否以定上下之分，核功罪以公賞罰之施，於悅之言亦有同歟？請詳著于篇，以為皇上勵精之助。

問：經以載道，史以載事，固也。然則道與事果有二乎？孔子因魯史作《春秋》，與《易》《詩》《書》《禮》《樂》並為六經。論者謂聖人述史三焉：《書》也，《詩》也，《春秋》也。三者同出於史而不可雜，是蓋有說矣，可得聞歟？劉歆叙《七畧》，王儉撰《七志》，《史記》以下皆附《春秋》，其亦有見歟？經史之分始於何人？至於為學，遂有以經稱者，有以史稱者，若宋司馬氏、王氏，其最著也。得失之故亦有
translation_en:
…to put government in order and reinvigorate it, thereby restoring the flourishing rule of the imperial ancestors: what course should be followed? In former times, Xun Yue wrote the Extended Reflections (Shen jian), declaring that a ruler’s method for achieving good government was first to eliminate the four afflictions and then to promote the five measures of government. This is certainly an argument concerning the guiding principles and disciplinary order of government. Is his argument sound? Can it be put into practice today? Of the five measures, which is most essential? Master Zhu also said that this order rests on distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to establish the proper distinctions between superiors and inferiors, and on examining achievements and offenses to ensure fairness in administering rewards and punishments. Does this also have something in common with Yue’s words? Please set out your views in detail in your essay, to assist His Majesty in his earnest efforts toward good government.

Question: The Classics convey the Way, and histories record events: this is certainly so. But are the Way and events really two distinct things? Confucius drew upon the history of Lu to compose the Spring and Autumn Annals, which, together with the Changes, Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music, constitute the Six Classics. Commentators say that the Sage transmitted history in three works: the Documents, the Odes, and the Spring and Autumn Annals. These three all derive from historical records, yet cannot be conflated. There must be an explanation for this; may we hear it? When Liu Xin compiled the Seven Epitomes and Wang Jian composed the Seven Classifications, they placed the Records of the Historian and subsequent histories under the Spring and Autumn Annals. Did they, too, have some insight in doing so? With whom did the separation of Classics and histories begin? title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
可言者歟諸士子學於斯二者乆矣其
所得何者爲多請遂言之毋讓
問西漢之士尚經術東漢之士崇節義儒
先有是言矣自今觀之有不盡然者如
直諫守節而淮南寢謀持節虜庭而名
標麟閣借劍尚方折檻大呼職在師傅
不肯就吏或印綬加身輒推不受或安
車再迎堅卧不起却牛衣之言甘心于
繫獄拒蘧氏之譬負直以自斃解𦈡細
===
故也不從以請退免冠随俗也堅執以
去官此皆士之著名西漢者也不崇節
義歟篤信好古經爲人師徧習經書剖
析疑異或刪定春秋而號樊侯學或考
論圖緯而嘆吾道東兄弟習魯詩爲學
士所歸父子明左氏爲諸儒所法隱居
教授而名重關西正定五經而學宗當
代此皆士之著名東漢者也不尚經術
歟乃偏言之何也西漢之經術尚矣何

可言者歟？諸士子學於斯二者乆矣，其所得何者爲多？請遂言之，毋讓。
問：西漢之士尚經術，東漢之士崇節義，儒先有是言矣。自今觀之，有不盡然者。如直諫守節而淮南寢謀，持節虜庭而名標麟閣，借劍尚方、折檻大呼，職在師傅、不肯就吏；或印綬加身，輒推不受；或安車再迎，堅卧不起；却牛衣之言，甘心于繫獄；拒蘧氏之譬，負直以自斃。解𦈡，細故也，不從以請退；免冠，随俗也，堅執以去官。此皆士之著名西漢者也，不崇節義歟？篤信好古，經爲人師；徧習經書，剖析疑異；或刪定春秋，而號樊侯學；或考論圖緯，而嘆吾道東；兄弟習魯詩，爲學士所歸；父子明左氏，爲諸儒所法；隱居教授，而名重關西；正定五經，而學宗當代。此皆士之著名東漢者也，不尚經術歟？乃偏言之，何也？西漢之經術尚矣，何
translation_en:
…might also be discussed? You candidates have long studied these two fields. From which have you gained more? Please set forth your views without reserve.
Question: Earlier Confucian scholars have said that the scholars of the Western Han esteemed classical learning, whereas those of the Eastern Han revered moral integrity and righteousness. Viewed from the present, this does not seem entirely true. There was one whose forthright remonstrance and steadfast integrity caused the king of Huainan to abandon his plot; another who upheld his mission in a foreign court and whose name was honored in the Qilin Pavilion; one who requested a sword from the Imperial Manufactories Office and, breaking the balustrade, cried out loudly; and one who, holding office as an imperial tutor, refused to submit to the judicial officials. Some, when presented with seals and ribbons of office, immediately declined them; others, twice summoned with carriages in which they could ride seated comfortably, steadfastly remained in bed. One rejected the counsel given beneath an ox-covering and willingly endured imprisonment; another rejected an analogy drawn from Master Qu and, relying on the righteousness of his position, brought about his own death. Undoing a garment [?] was a small matter, yet one refused and requested retirement; removing one’s cap was customary, yet another held firm and left office over it. These were all celebrated scholars of the Western Han. Did they not revere moral integrity and righteousness?
There were those who were steadfast in faith and loved antiquity, teaching others the Classics; those who studied the classical writings comprehensively and analyzed doubtful passages and divergent interpretations. One edited and established the text of the Spring and Autumn Annals, and his teaching was called the learning of the Marquis of Fan; another examined and discussed the prophetic charts and apocryphal texts, prompting the exclamation, “My Way has gone east!” Brothers studied the Lu tradition of the Book of Odes, and scholars flocked to them; father and son elucidated the Zuo Commentary, and other Confucian scholars took them as models. One lived in retirement and taught, earning great renown west of the passes; another corrected and established the texts of the Five Classics, and his scholarship became authoritative in his age. These were all celebrated scholars of the Eastern Han. Did they not esteem classical learning? Why, then, make such one-sided statements? The classical learning of the Western Han was indeed exalted; why…

正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
楊春芳
同考試官教諭魏批題本正大作者往往掇
拾陳言令人厭觀晚得此卷能道人所不能道且詞
旨暢達讀之鏘然有餘韻噫子之所養其殆與人殊
乎
考試官右諭德李批語有所見塲中似此者絶少
考試官侍讀學士汪批其指先王也詞不費而義足
其詳見廟議可考是作盖得其説故録
承先王之所貽者而仁先王之所厚者此聖人
===
之孝也盖先王之所以貽後人者甚備也既承
其所貽矣而於其所厚者豈容有所薄哉中庸
論武王周公之孝既詳其所制之禮而又結之
如此謂夫聖人之孝繼述爲大繼述之善愛敬
爲先彼負扆而朝卓乎大觀之在上嚮明而治
巍乎飛龍之在天人見聖人踐天子之位矣不
知垂創本于先王而我則纉其緒者也所踐者
非先王之位而何郊社禘嘗而禮無不具與天
地同其節雲咸韶濩而樂無不備與天地同其

楊春芳

同考試官教諭魏批：「題本正大，作者往往掇拾陳言，令人厭觀。晚得此卷，能道人所不能道，且詞旨暢達，讀之鏘然有餘韻。噫！子之所養，其殆與人殊乎！」

考試官右諭德李批：「語有所見，塲中似此者絶少。」

考試官侍讀學士汪批：「其指先王也，詞不費而義足。其詳見廟議可考。是作盖得其説，故録。」

承先王之所貽者，而仁先王之所厚者，此聖人之孝也。盖先王之所以貽後人者甚備也，既承其所貽矣，而於其所厚者，豈容有所薄哉？《中庸》論武王、周公之孝，既詳其所制之禮，而又結之如此。謂夫聖人之孝，繼述爲大；繼述之善，愛敬爲先。彼負扆而朝，卓乎大觀之在上；嚮明而治，巍乎飛龍之在天。人見聖人踐天子之位矣，不知垂創本于先王，而我則纉其緒者也。所踐者，非先王之位而何？郊社禘嘗，而禮無不具，與天地同其節；雲咸韶濩，而樂無不備，與天地同其
translation_en:
Yang Chunfang

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor: “The topic is inherently upright and grand, yet writers repeatedly gather up stale expressions, making their work tiresome to read. Late in the proceedings I obtained this paper. It expresses what others cannot express, and its language and meaning flow freely. Read aloud, it rings out with a lingering resonance. Ah! Surely what you have cultivated within yourself is different from that of others!”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: “These words show insight. Papers like this are exceedingly rare in the examination hall.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “Its reference is to the former kings. The language is economical, yet the meaning complete. The details may be checked in the deliberations on ancestral temples [?]. This composition has, I think, grasped the explanation, and so I have selected it for inclusion.”

To inherit what the former kings bequeathed, and to treat benevolently those whom the former kings cherished: this is the filial piety of the sage. What the former kings provided as a legacy for later generations was indeed comprehensive. Having inherited their bequest, how could one possibly slight those whom they cherished? In discussing the filial piety of King Wu and the Duke of Zhou, the Doctrine of the Mean has already described in detail the rites they instituted, and then concludes in this manner. Its meaning is that, in the sage’s filial piety, carrying on his predecessors’ purposes and undertakings is paramount; and in doing this well, love and reverence come first.

With his back to the ceremonial screen, he holds court, standing forth as a lofty example above; facing the light, he governs, majestic as a flying dragon in heaven. People see that the sage occupies the position of the Son of Heaven. They do not understand that the founding work and the legacy originated with the former kings, while ‘I’ merely carry forward their succession. What position does he occupy, if not that of the former kings? With the suburban sacrifices to Heaven, the sacrifices to the soil, the di ancestral sacrifices, and the autumn offerings, no rite is lacking: their rhythms accord with those of Heaven and Earth. With the Yun, Xian, Shao, and Huo ceremonial music, no music is lacking: it shares with Heaven and Earth their…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
初人見聖人用天子之禮樂矣不知制作出於
先王而我則紹其傳者也其所行者非先王之
禮所奏者非先王之樂而何若夫先王之所尊
者祖考也吾獨弛其所尊可乎於是致孝享於
假廟之時嚴對越於昭格之頃修廟陳器而報
本追遠之意不少衰焉設衣薦食而尊祖敬宗
之禮不少替焉是則先王雖往而其尊尊之義
不與之而俱往矣先王之所親者子孫臣庶也
吾獨遺其所親可乎於是惇親睦之情於九族
===
隆手足之愛於羣工序爵序事而禮敬之施無
不備焉逮賤序齒而恩意之推無不周焉是則
先王雖遠而其親親之惠不與之而俱遠矣位
也禮也樂也先王之所貽者自我承之至於尊
也親也先王之所厚者我則篤之而不敢薄焉
則其繼述之善也為何如哉此武王周公所以
為孝之至歟嗟夫人之情所賴乎其後者無貴
賤無大小欲其有所繼述而已故繼志述事謂
之達孝然而克盡其道者其惟聖人乎故特舉

translation_en: …beginnings [?]. People see the sage employing the rites and music of the Son of Heaven, but do not understand that their creation originated with the former kings, and that he carries on what they transmitted. What could the rites he performs be but those of the former kings, and the music he plays but theirs? As for those whom the former kings honored, these were their ancestors. Could I alone neglect those they honored? Thus, upon entering the ancestral temple, he offers sacrifices with filial devotion; when the spirits manifest their presence, he stands reverently before them. He maintains the temples and sets out the vessels, never diminishing his resolve to repay his origins and remember his distant forebears. He lays out their robes and presents food, never allowing the rites of honoring ancestors and revering the ancestral line to lapse. Thus, although the former kings have passed away, their commitment to honoring the honored has not passed away with them. Those whom the former kings cherished were their descendants, ministers, and common people. Could I alone abandon those they cherished? Thus he strengthens affection and harmony among the nine degrees of kinship and deepens brotherly love toward the assembled officials. By arranging participants according to rank and assigning their ritual duties, he makes every provision for reverent treatment; by extending consideration to the lowly and arranging participants according to age, he ensures that kindness reaches everyone. Thus, although the former kings have become distant, the benevolence with which they cherished their kin has not grown distant with them. The throne, the rites, and the music are the legacy of the former kings, which I myself inherit. As for honoring and cherishing, I deepen my devotion to those whom the former kings treated generously, never daring to slight them. How excellent, then, is his continuation of their purposes and undertakings! Is this not why King Wu and the Duke of Zhou exemplify filial piety at its utmost? Alas! What people hope for from their descendants, whether noble or lowly, great or small, is simply that they carry on their purposes and undertakings. Hence, carrying on one’s forebears’ intentions and continuing their work is called universally acknowledged filial piety. Yet is it not only the sage who can fully realize this way? …and applied it to King Wu and the Duke of Zhou. Only a benevolent person can offer sacrifice to the Supreme Lord; only a filial son can offer sacrifice to his parents. Once one understands this teaching, the way of serving Heaven likewise lies within it.

“All people have things they cannot bear to do; extending this to what they do bear to do is benevolence. All people have things they will not do; extending this to what they do is righteousness.”
Wu Huai 吳淮

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: In explaining “extending,” many papers interpret it through the word “filling out,” which seriously contradicts the original purport. This essay builds its argument on “extending outward,” fully grasping the intention behind Mencius’s words. Its phrasing is concise and apt, and its literary elegance is abundant. The author evidently has devoted thought to seeking benevolence and righteousness. This paper deserves selection.

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: An exposition on the Mencius is not difficult to write, but even in the examination hall, papers as clear and incisive as this are seldom found.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: When Mencius speaks of benevolence and righteousness, his words are as plain and grounded as this. Yet those writing expositions generally err through excessive elaboration and diffuseness. This essay is precise and orderly, and merits attention.

The great worthy says that if people can extend what they already possess, benevolence and righteousness are to be found therein. For what one cannot bear to do and what one will not do are the beginnings of benevolence and righteousness, which everyone necessarily possesses. If one can extend outward from these, how could benevolence and righteousness lie elsewhere? Mencius’s meaning was that people know how difficult it is to attain benevolence and righteousness in their fullness, but do not know how very easy it is to seek them: it lies in recognizing their beginnings and extending…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
廣之耳是故惻隱形於見聞所及孰無不忍之
心乎不忍者仁之端宜念念之皆仁矣然或拘
於氣稟之偏奪於物欲之蔽而於他事有忍之
者心雖暫忍而其本然之天猶夫故也于焉驗
所感之不殊思所發之頓異推不忍而達之於
所忍使所忍者亦不忍焉則一心之內渾然天
理之周流情得其正而慈惠無窮何往而非仁
邪羞惡著於行己之際孰無不為之心乎不為
者義之端宜事事之皆義矣然或局於稟賦之
===
凡移於私邪之誘而於他事有為之者事雖暫
為而其全體之正未嘗息也于焉審事理之無
二思從違之罔同推不為而達之於所為俾所
為者亦不為焉則萬感之間粹然天德之呈露
心得其職而愧耻常存何往而非義邪是則仁
義之用甚廣而其端之推也其易如此人亦何
憚而不為哉嗟夫戰國之時上下馳騖於功利
知所謂仁義者鮮矣矧能擴而充之邪孟子七
篇之作拳拳於四端之論而此章指言仁義之

punctuated: 廣之耳。是故惻隱形於見聞所及，孰無不忍之心乎？不忍者，仁之端，宜念念之皆仁矣。然或拘於氣稟之偏，奪於物欲之蔽，而於他事有忍之者。心雖暫忍，而其本然之天猶夫故也。于焉驗所感之不殊，思所發之頓異，推不忍而達之於所忍，使所忍者亦不忍焉，則一心之內，渾然天理之周流，情得其正而慈惠無窮，何往而非仁邪？羞惡著於行己之際，孰無不為之心乎？不為者，義之端，宜事事之皆義矣。然或局於稟賦之凡，移於私邪之誘，而於他事有為之者。事雖暫為，而其全體之正未嘗息也。于焉審事理之無二，思從違之罔同，推不為而達之於所為，俾所為者亦不為焉，則萬感之間，粹然天德之呈露，心得其職而愧耻常存，何往而非義邪？是則仁義之用甚廣，而其端之推也，其易如此，人亦何憚而不為哉？嗟夫！戰國之時，上下馳騖於功利，知所謂仁義者鮮矣，矧能擴而充之邪？孟子七篇之作，拳拳於四端之論，而此章指言仁義之
translation_en:
…and broaden them, that is all. Thus, when compassion manifests itself in response to what one sees and hears, who lacks a heart that cannot bear the suffering of others? This inability to bear suffering is the beginning of benevolence; every thought should therefore be benevolent. Yet some are constrained by the partiality of their psychophysical endowment and overpowered by the obscuring effects of material desires, so that in other matters they can bear such suffering. Although the heart may momentarily bear it, its original, Heaven-given nature remains as before. One should then examine how the things that move the heart do not differ, and reflect on how sharply its responses diverge. Extend this inability to bear suffering to those instances in which one does bear it, so that there too one can no longer bear it. Then, within the single heart, Heaven’s principle will circulate as an undivided whole; the feelings will attain their proper balance, and kindness and beneficence will be inexhaustible. Wherever one turns, how could there be anything other than benevolence?

When shame and aversion manifest themselves in one’s conduct, who lacks a heart that refuses to do certain things? This refusal is the beginning of righteousness; every action should therefore be righteous. Yet some are limited by the mediocrity of their endowment [?] and swayed by selfish and perverse temptations, so that in other matters they do what they ought not to do. Although they may momentarily act thus, the rectitude of their whole nature has never ceased to exist. One should then scrutinize how the principles governing affairs are consistent, and reflect on how differently one follows or violates them. Extend this refusal to act to those instances in which one does act, so that there too one refrains. Then, amid the myriad things that move the heart, Heaven’s virtue will reveal itself in its purity; the heart will fulfill its proper office, and shame will always remain. Wherever one turns, how could there be anything other than righteousness?

Thus the workings of benevolence and righteousness are exceedingly extensive, yet extending their beginnings is as easy as this. What should people fear that would keep them from doing so? Alas! During the Warring States period, those above and below alike rushed in pursuit of achievement and profit. Few understood what benevolence and righteousness meant; how much less could they broaden them and bring them to fulfillment? 辭又有所謂盥而不薦有孚顒若者何邪蓋君
者民之表一身之小而四方刑焉使輕於自用
則於觀之道有歉臣下將何所儀法哉此所以
必貴乎有始盥之誠而後觀之道可庶幾也噫
小心翼翼萬邦作孚文王其殆以心易而明易
punctuated:
居於大寶，羣黎百姓賴之以安養，以一人而撫萬邦也；握乾闡坤，端拱於南面，九州八荒藉之以統治，以四海而仰一人也。其位固足以為觀矣，然使德有未備，何以副海內之望邪？卦德內坤外巽，為順而巽，是乃積於中者有從容和順之美，施於外者無驕矜凌厲之失，溫柔寬裕，粹乎可親。其所以為人之利見者，盖不獨其位之尊矣。五居上之中，得陽之正，是乃無過不及而建中于民，不偏不倚而表正于下，齊莊中正，儼然可像。其所以為人之瞻仰者，盖不但其勢之崇矣。是則位足觀也，而必本於德；德能觀也，而實資於位。卦之德位兼隆如此，名之為觀，良有以哉！
抑伏羲名卦之義，可謂精且盡矣。文王繫辭，又有所謂「盥而不薦，有孚顒若」者，何邪？盖君者民之表，一身之小而四方刑焉。使輕於自用，則於觀之道有歉，臣下將何所儀法哉？此所以必貴乎有始盥之誠，而後觀之道可庶幾也。噫！「小心翼翼，萬邦作孚。」文王其殆以心易而明易
translation_en:
…occupies the great throne, and the common people depend upon him for security and sustenance: one man thus nurtures the myriad states. Holding sway over Heaven and unfolding the workings of Earth, he sits facing south with hands folded; the Nine Provinces and the Eight Wastes depend upon him for orderly government: all within the Four Seas thus look up to one man. His position certainly suffices to make him an object of contemplation. Yet if his virtue were incomplete, how could he meet the expectations of all under Heaven? In the hexagram’s attributes, Kun is within and Xun without, signifying compliance and humility. Thus what accumulates within possesses the beauty of composure, harmony, and compliance, while what manifests outwardly is free from the faults of arrogance and harshness. Gentle, generous, and magnanimous, he is wholly approachable. What makes it beneficial for people to behold him is therefore not merely the exalted nature of his position. The fifth line occupies the central place in the upper trigram and possesses the correctness proper to yang. This means neither going too far nor falling short, thereby establishing the mean among the people; neither inclining to one side nor leaning to the other, thereby setting an upright example for those below. Reverent, dignified, central, and correct, he is solemnly worthy of emulation. What makes people look up to him is therefore not merely the eminence of his power. Thus his position makes him worthy of contemplation, but must be rooted in virtue; his virtue makes him worthy to be contemplated, but indeed draws support from his position. With virtue and position both so exalted in this hexagram, there is good reason to name it Contemplation (Guan)!
Now the meaning conveyed by Fuxi’s naming of the hexagram may be called both subtle and exhaustive. Why, then, did King Wen, in appending its judgment, also speak of “having washed the hands but not yet presented the offering; possessing sincerity, with a reverent bearing”? The ruler is the people’s exemplar: small as his single person is, all in the four quarters take him as their model. If he rashly relied upon his own judgment, he would fall short in the Way of Contemplation. What, then, would his subjects have to imitate? This is why it is essential to possess the sincerity present at the initial washing of the hands; only then can the Way of Contemplation come close to being realized. Ah! “Careful and reverent, he became the trusted model of the myriad states.” King Wen perhaps used the Changes within his heart to illuminate the Changes…

“The gentleman, in associating with those above him, does not flatter; in associating with those below him, he is not disrespectfully familiar. Does he not understand the incipient signs?”

Wang Shou

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Instructor: “Anyone can speak of avoiding flattery and disrespectful familiarity. But when they reach the matter of understanding incipient signs, they offer only a few sparse words. Is this because such subtle beginnings are difficult to describe? This essay alone can develop the point fully; from it one can discern the depth of your understanding.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Mentor: “His explanation of understanding incipient signs differs from that of others.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting: “Grasps the essential meaning.”

The Great Commentary demonstrates the gentleman’s clarity in perceiving incipient signs through his discernment in social intercourse. For it is within social intercourse that these signs reside. Without the gentleman’s clear perception, how could he discern the appropriate conduct for each situation? Such is the Great Commentary’s explanation of the meaning of the second, yin line of the hexagram Yu (Enthusiasm). Indeed, nothing in the affairs of the world is ever without incipient signs, yet only the gentleman perceives them clearly. Why not observe this in social intercourse?

Among those with whom a person associates, there must be some who stand above him. Few associate with their superiors without flattery. In attending upon them, the gentleman upholds only the ritual proprieties that ought to be observed. Although he fully displays reverence and awe, he never compromises his fundamental integrity. He never goes so far as flattery.

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
存禮遇之心雖曰詞色之是假而禮貌之不衰
敬之如賓而簡傲不事也待如長者而惰慢不
施也未甞至於瀆焉若是者不其知幾乎盖上
交貴恭遜恭遜一形而不加察焉諂斯至矣事
在毫忽之間而得失所由分也今於易流之地
乃有特立不移之節非其明炳幾先而燭理之
微者安能不諂邪下交貴和易和易一生而不
知省焉瀆斯蹈矣心在擬議之頃而當否所由
判也今於可忽之時不失當然不易之則非其
===
聰明先物而見事幾之審者安能不瀆邪是則
一交際之間而能知幾若此所貴於君子者有
如是夫抑幾之為說其義廣矣周子曰幾善惡
又曰誠神幾夫子乃獨以交際言之何邪盖事
之最近而幾之易忽者莫如交際苟于斯審焉
則餘可以類推矣然非有安靜之德則亦莫之
能也故曰介于石不終日貞吉有事于知幾者
當自謹德始

punctuated:
存禮遇之心，雖曰詞色之是假，而禮貌之不衰。敬之如賓，而簡傲不事也；待如長者，而惰慢不施也。未甞至於瀆焉。若是者，不其知幾乎？盖上交貴恭遜，恭遜一形而不加察焉，諂斯至矣。事在毫忽之間，而得失所由分也。今於易流之地，乃有特立不移之節，非其明炳幾先而燭理之微者，安能不諂邪？下交貴和易，和易一生而不知省焉，瀆斯蹈矣。心在擬議之頃，而當否所由判也。今於可忽之時，不失當然不易之則，非其聰明先物而見事幾之審者，安能不瀆邪？是則一交際之間，而能知幾若此，所貴於君子者有如是夫！抑幾之為說，其義廣矣。周子曰：「幾，善惡。」又曰：「誠、神、幾。」夫子乃獨以交際言之，何邪？盖事之最近而幾之易忽者，莫如交際。苟于斯審焉，則餘可以類推矣。然非有安靜之德，則亦莫之能也。故曰：「介于石，不終日，貞吉。」有事于知幾者，當自謹德始。

translation_en:
…maintains an intention to treat them with ritual courtesy. Though he shows them a kindly countenance and gracious words, his respectful bearing does not diminish. He respects them as guests and does not act disdainfully; he treats them as elders and shows no negligence or arrogance. He never lapses into undue familiarity. Does someone like this not understand the incipient signs of change?

In associating with those above oneself, respect and deference are prized. Yet once respect and deference take outward form, flattery will follow if one fails to examine them. The matter turns on the slightest distinction, but it is here that right conduct and error diverge. Now, where one might easily be swept along, he maintains an integrity that stands firm and unmoved. Unless his insight shines ahead of the incipient signs and illuminates the subtleties of principle, how could he avoid flattery? In associating with those below oneself, affability and ease are prized. Yet once affability and ease arise, one will lapse into undue familiarity if one fails to reflect. The mind is poised at the moment of deliberation, and it is here that propriety and impropriety are distinguished. Now, at a moment when one might be heedless, he does not lose sight of the unchanging standard of what is right. Unless his perceptiveness anticipates events and discerns their incipient signs precisely, how could he avoid undue familiarity? Thus, even within social intercourse alone, he can understand incipient signs to this degree. Such is what we value in the gentleman!

Yet the meaning of incipient signs is broad. Master Zhou said, “Incipience: good and evil.” He also spoke of “sincerity, spiritual efficacy, and incipience.” Why, then, did the Master speak of it solely in terms of social intercourse? Because nothing is closer to our daily affairs, or more liable to have its incipient signs overlooked, than social intercourse. If one examines these signs carefully here, the rest can be inferred by analogy. Nevertheless, without the virtue of calm and stillness, no one can accomplish this. Hence it is said: “Firm as a rock; not waiting out the day. Perseverance brings good fortune.” Those who devote themselves to understanding incipient signs should begin by attending carefully to their virtue.

“Yu said: ‘Ah! Emperor, be heedful of the position you occupy.’ The Emperor said: ‘Yes!’”

Comment by Associate Examiner Yin, Instructor: Throughout the examination, most candidates have already introduced such phrases from Cai’s commentary as “a single day or a single thought without due care” into their treatment of the opening sentence, leaving little savor in their exposition of the word “Yes.” This paper has considerable stature and force. Free of ornate embellishment, it portrays almost fully the atmosphere of an enlightened ruler and worthy ministers at the court of Yu. Ah! Among the scholars of the Southern Metropolitan Region, I know that men like you can be counted on very few fingers. Placing this paper high in the rankings truly accords with general opinion.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Professor: The ruler and ministers of Yu were equally earnest in their desire to preserve good government. Here Yu says “Ah!” and Shun immediately assents, as swiftly as a shadow follows a form or an echo follows a sound. This essay succeeds in portraying this, and its language and tone have a springlike grace through which one can envision the atmosphere at the court of Yu. Reading it makes one stir with reverence.

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Mentor: Concise in expression and comprehensive in meaning.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Hanlin Academician Reader-in-Waiting: It offers illuminating insights.

A great minister makes a submission and brings out its essential point; a sage ruler is moved and accords deeply with it. 其我之龜鑑乎無疆之休亦有無疆之恤而我

…above high Heaven, one might seem entitled to ease. Yet whether Heaven’s mandate stays or departs is uncertain: this is a position in which that mandate is difficult to trust. How could one fail to exercise care? Sitting with folded hands in solemn serenity, presiding over the myriad people, one might seem entitled to act at will. Yet their allegiance or disobedience is unsettled: this is a position in which the people’s hearts are difficult to retain. How could one fail to be vigilant? The earth has been brought to order and Heaven’s work accomplished; good government has already been achieved. Yet in securing order before disorder arises, one must not allow oneself leisure for even a single thought. The people have enough and the realm is well governed; peace has already been achieved. Yet in safeguarding the realm before danger arises, one cannot permit even the slightest lapse for a single day.

Thus, as soon as Emperor Shun heard these words, they struck home in his heart, and he responded: “Yes! An extraordinary position carries extraordinary responsibilities, and I indeed bear them. Are your words not my divining tortoise and mirror? Boundless blessings also entail boundless cares, and I have no means to bear them. Is your counsel not my medicine and healing stone? A single careless thought bequeaths sorrow to all within the Four Seas. The admonition to be vigilant in one’s position is an excellent plan for securing order. A single day’s carelessness brings calamities lasting hundreds or thousands of years. The instruction to be vigilant in one’s position is the essential way to safeguard the realm.”

Ah! In the court of Yu, sovereign and ministers exchanged words of praise and assent together in one hall, and what they spoke of never went beyond this. This, too, may serve as a mirror. Alas! All under Heaven is a weighty vessel. The sage exercises vigilance in everything; how much more so when ruling all under Heaven! title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
少也凡發於其政見於其事者惟恐不當乎人
心非仁無居非義無行形於一身皆天下之度
也無賢不親有罪必斥垂於後世皆永久之圖
也其爲善也如此豈容有自足之心哉是故夙
而興夜而寐凡分之所當爲者靡不盡也而心
猶不敢以自慰晝有爲宵有得凡力之所能及
者無不周也而意猶不敢以自慊仁未能存歟
義未能徙歟而日月之逾邁若弗云來也賢未
及舉歟邪未及遠歟而歲月之遷逝若不我與
===
也夫爲善而惟日不足則其善也寧有既哉非
吉人其孰能與於此大抵陰陽晝夜每每相反
吉人之於善猶凶人之於惡也吉凶其所致者
而遂以目其人古人垂訓之意不其至哉彼凶
人者移其惟日不足之心轉而之善則亦孰能
禦之故曰惟狂克念作聖惜乎紂不足以語此
而孟津之師有不容已者可慨也夫

有馮有翼有孝有德以引以翼豈弟君子
punctuated:
少也。凡發於其政、見於其事者，惟恐不當乎人心。非仁無居，非義無行，形於一身，皆天下之度也；無賢不親，有罪必斥，垂於後世，皆永久之圖也。其爲善也如此，豈容有自足之心哉？是故夙而興，夜而寐，凡分之所當爲者靡不盡也，而心猶不敢以自慰；晝有爲，宵有得，凡力之所能及者無不周也，而意猶不敢以自慊。仁未能存歟？義未能徙歟？而日月之逾邁，若弗云來也。賢未及舉歟？邪未及遠歟？而歲月之遷逝，若不我與也。夫爲善而惟日不足，則其善也寧有既哉？非吉人，其孰能與於此？大抵陰陽晝夜，每每相反。吉人之於善，猶凶人之於惡也。吉凶，其所致者，而遂以目其人，古人垂訓之意，不其至哉？彼凶人者，移其惟日不足之心，轉而之善，則亦孰能禦之？故曰：「惟狂克念作聖。」惜乎紂不足以語此，而孟津之師有不容已者，可慨也夫！

有馮有翼，有孝有德，以引以翼，豈弟君子
translation_en:
…may be lacking. In everything expressed through his government and manifested in his affairs, his sole fear is that it may fail to accord with the hearts of the people. He abides in nothing that is not benevolent and undertakes nothing that is not right. All that he manifests in his own person serves as a standard for the world. He draws close to every worthy person and invariably dismisses those who are guilty. All that he bequeaths to later generations constitutes a plan for enduring rule. Such is his practice of goodness: how could he allow himself any feeling of self-satisfaction?

Thus he rises early and retires late. He leaves nothing undone that his duty requires, yet still dares not comfort himself with what he has achieved. By day he acts; by night he gains understanding. He attends fully to everything within his power, yet still dares not feel content. Has he not yet been able to preserve benevolence? Has he not yet been able to move toward righteousness? The days and months pass swiftly, as though never to return. Has he not yet promoted the worthy? Has he not yet distanced himself from the wicked? The years and months slip away, as though unwilling to wait for him.

If, in doing good, he fears only that the days are insufficient, how could his goodness ever reach an end? Who but an auspicious man could attain this? Generally, yin and yang, day and night, stand opposed to one another. The auspicious man’s devotion to goodness resembles the inauspicious man’s devotion to evil. Good and ill fortune are what they bring upon themselves, and these terms consequently become designations for the men themselves. Was not the intention of the ancients in transmitting this admonition most profound? If that inauspicious man redirected his feeling that the days were insufficient and turned toward goodness, who could restrain him? Hence it is said: “If even a madman can turn his thoughts aright, he becomes a sage.” Alas, Zhou was unfit to be addressed in these terms, and the military expedition at Mengjin could not be called off. How lamentable!

text:
國之拂士而爲王之可輔者豈無其人乎能事
與親之謂孝天倫克盡而爲宗族所稱又有所
謂能孝者矣得於已者之謂德善體諸身而爲
國人所賢又有所謂有德者矣以斯人也使之
立于王朝導之於前不惟能陳善閑邪而醇德
懿行自有薰陶漸染之益俾之居于王所相厥
左右不惟能忠告善道而容色聞望自有潜移
默化之功由是王之性日進於高明而厥德爲
之允脩王之心日歸於廣遠而其身以之克正

凡我黎民瞻王之度者自然取法之不遑羣黎
百姓仰王之儀者翕然是効之恐後遠之有望
近之不厭慕豈弟之風者合遠近而一轍何也
王之善集衆人之善也在彼無惡在此無射企
樂易之休者齊彼此於一揆何也衆人之賢爲
王之賢也夫然則天位可以居之而無忝天祿
可以受之於無窮而王之游日益休矣得賢之
助如此奭敢不以爲吾王陳哉嗟夫太和極治
之時正上下交警之地以虞廷之盛而有皐陶

立于王朝導之於前不惟能陳善閉邪而醇德
懿行自有薰陶漸染之益俾之居于王所相厥
左右不惟能忠告善道而容色閒望自有潛移
默化之功由是王之性日進於高明而厥德爲
之允脩王之心日歸於廣遠而其身以之克正
===
凡我黎民瞻王之度者自然取法之不違羣黎
百姓仰王之儀者翕然是効之恐後遠之有望
近之不厭慕豈弟之風者合遠近而一轍何也
王之善集衆人之善也在彼無惡在此無射企
樂易之休者齊彼此於一揆何也衆人之賢爲
王之賢也夫然則天位可以居之而無忝天祿
可以受之於無窮而王之游日益休矣得賢之
助如此𢿋敢不以爲吾王陳哉嗟夫太和極治
之時正上下交警之地以虞廷之盛而有皐陶
punctuated:
國之拂士，而爲王之可輔者，豈無其人乎？能事與親之謂孝，天倫克盡而爲宗族所稱，又有所謂能孝者矣。得於已者之謂德，善體諸身而爲國人所賢，又有所謂有德者矣。以斯人也，使之立于王朝，導之於前，不惟能陳善閑邪，而醇德懿行，自有薰陶漸染之益；俾之居于王所，相厥左右，不惟能忠告善道，而容色聞望，自有潜移默化之功。由是，王之性日進於高明，而厥德爲之允脩；王之心日歸於廣遠，而其身以之克正。凡我黎民瞻王之度者，自然取法之不遑；羣黎百姓仰王之儀者，翕然是効之恐後。遠之有望，近之不厭，慕豈弟之風者，合遠近而一轍，何也？王之善，集衆人之善也。在彼無惡，在此無射，企樂易之休者，齊彼此於一揆，何也？衆人之賢，爲王之賢也。夫然，則天位可以居之而無忝，天祿可以受之於無窮，而王之游日益休矣。得賢之助如此，奭敢不以爲吾王陳哉？

嗟夫！太和極治之時，正上下交警之地。以虞廷之盛，而有皐陶
translation_en:
…as upright counselors of the state, capable of assisting the king—can there be none? The ability to serve one’s parents [?] is called filial piety. Those who fully discharge the obligations of family relationships and earn the praise of their clans are what we call men capable of filial devotion. What one has attained within oneself is called virtue. Those who embody goodness in their own persons and are esteemed as worthy by the people of the state are what we call men of virtue.

Have such men take their places at the royal court and lead the king forward: they can not only set forth what is good and ward off what is perverse; their pure virtue and admirable conduct will also exert a gradually nurturing influence. Have them dwell beside the king and assist him on his right and left: they can not only offer loyal admonition and guide him well; their bearing and reputation will also transform him quietly and imperceptibly. Thus the king’s nature will advance daily toward loftiness and clarity, and his virtue will become truly cultivated. His mind will daily grow broader and more far-reaching, and his person will thereby be set aright.

All our common people who behold the king’s conduct will naturally hasten to take it as their model. The multitudes who look up to his deportment will emulate it with one accord, fearing to lag behind. Those far away look toward him with hope; those nearby never tire of him. Why do those who admire his kindly and gracious manner follow the same course, whether near or far? Because the king’s goodness gathers together the goodness of all. There is no hatred of him there, and no weariness of him here. Why do those who aspire to the excellence of his affability and ease share the same standard, wherever they are? Because the worthiness of all becomes the king’s own worthiness. Then he may occupy Heaven’s throne without dishonoring it, receive Heaven’s bounty without end, and find his excursions increasingly blessed. Such is the assistance afforded by worthy men. Dare I, Shi, fail to set this before my king?

Ah! A time of supreme harmony and consummate order is precisely when those above and below should admonish one another. Even amid the flourishing court of Shun, there was Gao Yao…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之賡歌古之人所以慎乎其微者盖未嘗少忽
也成王以幼冲之年承文武之緒當卷阿之游
召公不乘間以規何取於師保之任邪故上章
既以福祿歆動於前而此後又以人才之盛告
之其開導誘掖之者至矣厥後成王任賢使能
卒為有周之令主謂非有得於召公之戒可乎
天命降監下民有嚴不僭不濫不敢怠遑
命于下國封建厥福
張鳳来
===
同考試官教諭緒批商人頌高宗中興之由
總在不僭不濫一句作者不知歸宿冗迂可厭有典
有則若此篇者可多得邪
同考試官教諭劉批題本冠冕作者類能成
篇至於高宗所以合天人而一之處殊欠提掇觀此
篇可以見大方家矣
考試官右諭德李批頌義典則難體此篇獨得其肯
綮盖善於說詩者
考試官侍讀學士汪批亦善言天人之際者

punctuated:
之賡歌。古之人所以慎乎其微者，盖未嘗少忽也。成王以幼冲之年承文武之緒，當卷阿之游，召公不乘間以規，何取於師保之任邪？故上章既以福祿歆動於前，而此後又以人才之盛告之，其開導誘掖之者至矣。厥後成王任賢使能，卒為有周之令主，謂非有得於召公之戒可乎？

天命降監，下民有嚴。不僭不濫，不敢怠遑。命于下國，封建厥福。

張鳳来

同考試官教諭緒批：商人頌高宗中興之由，總在不僭不濫一句。作者不知歸宿，冗迂可厭。有典有則若此篇者，可多得邪？

同考試官教諭劉批：題本冠冕，作者類能成篇，至於高宗所以合天人而一之處，殊欠提掇。觀此篇，可以見大方家矣。

考試官右諭德李批：頌義典則難體，此篇獨得其肯綮，盖善於說詩者。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：亦善言天人之際者。
translation_en:
…Gao Yao’s answering song. The men of antiquity, in attending carefully to the slightest beginnings, surely never allowed themselves the least negligence. King Cheng inherited the legacy of Wen and Wu while still a young child. During the excursion to Juan’e, had the Duke of Shao failed to seize an opportunity to remonstrate, what purpose would his appointment as tutor and protector have served? Thus, having first stirred the king’s aspirations with blessings and emoluments in the preceding stanza, he went on to tell him of the abundance of talented men. His guidance, encouragement, and support were consummate. Thereafter King Cheng employed the worthy and entrusted responsibilities to the capable, ultimately becoming an excellent ruler of the Zhou. Can one say that he gained nothing from the Duke of Shao’s admonition?

“Heaven sent down its mandate and oversight; the people below held him in awe. He neither bestowed rewards improperly nor imposed punishments excessively, and dared not indulge in idleness or leisure. Heaven appointed him over the states below and firmly established his blessings.”

Zhang Fenglai

Associate Examiner Xu, Instructor, comments: The reason for Gaozong’s restoration of Shang, celebrated by the people of Shang, lies entirely in the phrase ‘neither bestowed rewards improperly nor imposed punishments excessively.’ Writers who do not understand where their argument should lead are tiresomely verbose and circuitous. Can one often find a piece as classically grounded and well ordered as this?

Associate Examiner Liu, Instructor, comments: The topic itself is grand and dignified, and writers can generally produce an essay on it. But they fall conspicuously short in bringing out how Gaozong united Heaven and humanity as one. In this essay one can recognize an accomplished master.

Examiner Li, Right Adviser to the Heir Apparent, comments: The meaning of this hymn is classically grounded and well ordered, and difficult to embody in writing. This essay alone grasps its essential point. Its author is surely skilled at interpreting the Book of Odes.

Examiner Wang, Hanlin Reader-in-Waiting, comments: This author, too, speaks well of the relationship between Heaven and humanity.

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
知天之不能外乎民則知聖人之所以得乎天
蓋天因於民得民斯得天矣然則高宗受天命
之隆者豈無自而然哉此商人祀高宗之樂蓋
謂我高宗之中興也外服遠夷內懷諸夏天實
命之而致此者豈無其道乎誠以仰瞻彼天蒼
蒼之表有予有奪而每鑒觀乎萬方者非自用
其聰明也惟民是託焉耳冥冥之中有禍有福
而每照臨乎下土者非自役其視聽也惟民是
寄焉耳是則俯視斯民其微若可忽矣而天實
===
在焉可忽之而不敬乎其近若可狎矣而天實
寓焉可狎之而不畏乎我高宗知其然賞一人
也必民心之所共好奉天之命何有於僭差然
尤不敢以自怠焉罰一人也必民心之所共惡
致天之討何有於濫及然尤不敢以自遑焉由
是克享天心集此大命合人心於已離而天下
為之大定保佑之命方申而無窮也振王綱於
既墜而商業為之再興隆昌之運自是其有永
也謂之大建厥福信乎其福之無以加矣吁上

也謂之大建厥福信乎其福之無以加矣吁上
punctuated:
知天之不能外乎民，則知聖人之所以得乎天。

蓋天因於民，得民斯得天矣。然則高宗受天命之隆者，豈無自而然哉？此商人祀高宗之樂，蓋謂我高宗之中興也，外服遠夷，內懷諸夏，天實命之。而致此者，豈無其道乎？誠以仰瞻彼天，蒼蒼之表，有予有奪，而每鑒觀乎萬方者，非自用其聰明也，惟民是託焉耳；冥冥之中，有禍有福，而每照臨乎下土者，非自役其視聽也，惟民是寄焉耳。是則俯視斯民，其微若可忽矣，而天實在焉，可忽之而不敬乎？其近若可狎矣，而天實寓焉，可狎之而不畏乎？我高宗知其然，賞一人也，必民心之所共好，奉天之命，何有於僭差？然尤不敢以自怠焉。罰一人也，必民心之所共惡，致天之討，何有於濫及？然尤不敢以自遑焉。由是克享天心，集此大命，合人心於已離，而天下為之大定，保佑之命方申而無窮也；振王綱於既墜，而商業為之再興，隆昌之運自是其有永也。謂之大建厥福，信乎其福之無以加矣！吁！上
translation_en:
To understand that Heaven cannot stand apart from the people is to understand how the sage wins Heaven’s favor.

Heaven acts through the people: winning the people thus means winning Heaven. Could the abundant mandate that Gaozong received from Heaven, then, have come about without a cause? This music performed by the people of Shang in sacrifices to Gaozong declares that, when our Gaozong restored the dynasty, he brought distant foreign peoples into submission abroad and won the allegiance of the Xia states within. Heaven indeed commanded this. Yet could there have been no way by which he achieved it? Looking upward to Heaven, beyond the azure expanse, we find that it grants and withdraws its gifts and constantly surveys the myriad regions. It does not exercise its intelligence independently, but entrusts itself solely to the people. Within its unseen workings, it brings calamity and blessing and constantly watches over the earth below. It does not employ its sight and hearing independently, but relies solely upon the people. Thus, looking down upon these people, their lowliness might seem to make them negligible; yet Heaven is truly present among them. Can they be disregarded and treated without reverence? Their nearness might seem to invite overfamiliarity; yet Heaven truly dwells among them. Can they be treated casually and without awe?

Our Gaozong understood this. Whenever he rewarded someone, that person was necessarily one whom the people’s hearts all approved. In carrying out Heaven’s command, how could he err by bestowing an undeserved reward? Yet he still dared not grow lax. Whenever he punished someone, that person was necessarily one whom the people’s hearts all condemned. In executing Heaven’s chastisement, how could he extend punishment indiscriminately? Yet he still dared not allow himself ease. Thus he could enjoy Heaven’s favor and secure this great mandate. He reunited the people’s hearts after they had become estranged, and thereby brought profound stability to all under Heaven; Heaven’s charge to protect and sustain him was renewed without end. He restored the bonds of royal governance after they had fallen into ruin, and thereby revived the dynastic enterprise of Shang; from this point its flourishing fortunes would endure. It is said that he ‘greatly established his blessings’: truly, nothing could have added to those blessings! Ah, Heaven above…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
天因民以為命而高宗因民以得天天人之際
其微矣哉抑考周公作立政以戒成王曰其克
詰爾戎兵以覲耿光而揚大烈武之不可以已
也如是况中興之君繼衰亂之後未有不以武
德勝者若殷之高宗周之宣王是已然詩頌高
宗之功而卒歸之於不僭不濫之一言則其所
以用武者亦必有道矣後世徒以窮黷為事者
其未可輕以藉口哉
春秋
===
公會齊人宋人陳人蔡人伐衛莊公五年
王人子突救衛莊公六年

天因民以為命，而高宗因民以得天，天人之際，其微矣哉！抑考周公作《立政》以戒成王，曰：「其克詰爾戎兵，以覲耿光，而揚大烈。」武之不可以已也如是，况中興之君，繼衰亂之後，未有不以武德勝者，若殷之高宗、周之宣王是已。然詩頌高宗之功，而卒歸之於不僭不濫之一言，則其所以用武者亦必有道矣。後世徒以窮黷為事者，其未可輕以藉口哉！

諸侯黨惡，春秋削爵以致貶；王臣恤患，春秋稱
translation_en:
…Heaven determines its mandate through the people, while Gaozong gained Heaven’s favor through the people. How subtle is the relationship between Heaven and humanity! Consider, moreover, how the Duke of Zhou composed “Establishing Government” to admonish King Cheng, saying: “Be able to put your military forces in order, so as to display your brilliant light and magnify your great achievements.” Such is the indispensability of military force. How much more so for rulers who restore a dynasty after decline and disorder: none has succeeded without martial virtue. Gaozong of Yin and King Xuan of Zhou are examples. Yet the Classic of Poetry praises Gaozong’s achievements and ultimately sums them up in the single phrase “neither erring in rewards nor excessive in punishments.” Thus there must also have been a proper Way governing his use of military force. Those in later ages who merely pursue militarism to excess surely cannot lightly invoke him as their excuse!

Spring and Autumn Annals

“The duke joined men of Qi, Song, Chen, and Cai in attacking Wei.” Fifth year of Duke Zhuang.
“The king’s man, Zitu, came to Wei’s aid.” Sixth year of Duke Zhuang.

Xie Yinglong

Comment by Associate Examiner Wei, an Instructor: “Expositions on the Spring and Autumn Annals prize precision and rigor. This essay clearly distinguishes approval from condemnation, and its arguments bristle with sharp points. The other scripts are left staring from far behind [?].”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: “Only the Sage could adjudicate departures from the established conventions of the Spring and Autumn Annals. This composition makes that clear.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting: “It achieves a precise and rigorous style.”

When the feudal lords sided with wrongdoing, the Spring and Autumn Annals stripped away their ranks to express condemnation; when the king’s minister showed concern for those in distress, the Spring and Autumn Annals designated him …

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
字以致褒此可見聖人予奪之公不以諸侯之
貴而少狗不以王人之卑而有遺也且春秋何
爲而作也爲正名分而作也爲正名分而作則
尊卑之叙宜無所苟矣魯莊公即位之五年嘗
會齊宋陳蔡之君以伐衛四國諸侯也聖人書
經侯之公之可也乃各以人稱何邪盖衛朔以
麀聚之孽構二兄之禍篡居其位而見逐於國
人出奔於外而獲罪於天子是嘗以王命絕之
矣魯力不能誅遠之可也今乃連四國之師爲
===
納朔之舉興兵動衆肆意於抗王拂義亂常甘
心於黨惡天理絕而人心亡故聖人於四國各
削其爵以稱人人諸侯所以人莊公也其義何
嚴乎明年王人子突救衛子突下士也聖人書
經人之名之可也乃獨以字稱何邪盖黔牟之
立出於天王之命諸侯無故興師而欲墟其國

…by his courtesy name to confer praise. Here one can see the impartiality of the Sage’s praise and blame: he makes no slight concession [?] on account of the feudal lords’ exalted rank, nor does he overlook a royal officer because of his lowly station. Moreover, why was the Spring and Autumn Annals composed? To rectify names and distinctions of status. Since it was composed to rectify names and distinctions of status, the ordering of high and low must admit of no carelessness.

In the fifth year after Duke Zhuang of Lu ascended the throne, he joined the rulers of Qi, Song, Chen, and Cai in attacking Wei. These were the feudal lords of four states. When writing the classic, the Sage might properly have designated them as marquises or dukes. Why, then, did he call each merely a “man”? Shuo of Wei, amid the evil of incestuous relations, had engineered the calamity that befell his two elder brothers and usurped the rulership. He was driven out by the people of his state, fled abroad, and incurred the Son of Heaven’s condemnation. He had thus already been repudiated by royal command. If Lu lacked the strength to punish him, it could properly have kept its distance. Instead, it now combined the armies of the four states in an undertaking to restore Shuo. Raising troops and mobilizing the multitude, they brazenly opposed the king; defying righteousness and disrupting the enduring norms, they willingly sided with evil. Heavenly principle was severed, and humane feeling extinguished. Thus the Sage stripped each of the four rulers of his title and called him a “man.” To call the feudal lords “men” was thereby to reduce Duke Zhuang himself to a “man.” How stern is the judgment!

The following year, the royal officer Zitu came to Wei’s rescue. Zitu was a lower serviceman. When writing the classic, the Sage might properly have designated him simply as a “man” or recorded his personal name. Why, then, did he single him out by using his courtesy name? Qianmou’s installation had proceeded from the command of the Heavenly King. The feudal lords raised armies without cause and sought to lay waste his state; restoring an exile and abetting tyranny, they dared act wantonly against Zhou. Surely this was conduct upon which Heaven’s punishment must fall. Though Zitu’s standing was low, he could uphold the royal command. Accordingly, he led a brigade of troops and made an imposing effort to remedy the disorder, seeking to punish the wickedness of the rebel Shuo and safeguard the ancestral temples and altars of state, to crush the five…

國之兵，而王法是正，功雖不就，而志則可尚。故聖人特變其例以書字，嘉王人所以嘉王命也，其義何精乎！是則黨惡之戒明，則世無背公之臣；恤患之功錄，則人有赴義之志。聖人垂訓立教之意，其深矣哉！抑不特是，朔之復國，書名、書入；莊公歸魯，書至。《春秋》大義在於天下爲公，選賢與能，而不拘大人世及之禮。雖以正取國，猶未之貴，況殺其兄，又逆天王之命者乎？是以前後書法，皆以著朔之惡，凛乎斧鉞之誅，而有不容逭者。儒先謂《春秋》非聖人不能作，信夫！

translation_en:
…the armies of the five states, and thereby uphold royal law. Although his undertaking did not succeed, his resolve deserves esteem. Thus the Sage departed from his usual practice and recorded his courtesy name: to commend the king’s representative was to commend the king’s command. How subtle the principle is! When the warning against siding with evil is made clear, the world will have no ministers who betray the common good; when the merit of relieving distress is recorded, people will aspire to act for righteousness. How profound was the Sage’s intention in bequeathing instruction and establishing moral teaching! Nor is this all. In recording Shuo’s restoration to his state, the text gives his personal name and uses the word “entered”; in recording Duke Zhuang’s return to Lu, it uses “arrived.” The great principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals is that the realm belongs to all, and that the worthy and capable should be selected, without being bound by the ritual convention of hereditary succession among great men. Even acquiring a state by rightful means does not in itself earn esteem; how much less could this be so for someone who killed his elder brother and defied the command of the Son of Heaven? Thus the wording both before and after exposes Shuo’s wickedness, imposing an awe-inspiring judgment like execution by the headsman’s axe, from which there can be no escape. Earlier Confucian scholars said that only a sage could have composed the Spring and Autumn Annals. How true!
The duke met with the Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, the Earl of Zheng, the Earl of Cao, and a representative of Zhu at Cheng. 〔First year of Duke Xi〕 The Marquis of Qi, the Duke of Song, and representatives of Jiang and Huang met at Yanggu. 〔Third year of Duke Xi〕 They then attacked Chu and encamped at Xing. Qu Wan of Chu came to the army to conclude a covenant; they concluded the covenant at Shaoling. 〔Fourth year of Duke Xi〕
Yang Chunfang

Such indeed is your remarkable talent!”

The Spring and Autumn Annals accords approval to the hegemonic state: it employed planning to restrain outside powers and ritual propriety to bring them into submission. How very difficult Chu was to subdue! Had Duke Huan and Guan Zhong not restrained it through planning and brought it into submission through ritual propriety, how could they have accomplished the repulsion of outside powers? Early in Duke Xi’s reign, Chu first began to be recorded under the designation ‘men’: its strength was gradually increasing. Fortunately, Duke Huan of Qi assumed the hegemony, with Guan Zhong assisting him. Ruler and minister planned together and exerted themselves to check Chu. With their hegemonic enterprise newly underway, where could they go without success? Yet Duke Huan and Guan Zhong considered that Chu’s power was then flourishing and that it would be difficult to strike directly at it. Without profound deliberation, they could not qualify as those who ‘delight in planning and bring matters to completion.’ Accordingly, they held a great assembly at Cheng, mobilizing assistance for the people of Zheng to [illegible] the might of the Central States; they met again at Yanggu, winning the allegiance of Jiang and Huang to secure the trust of distant states. Did they not wish to press ahead and fulfill their ambitions? Yet until their might had been made manifest, they could not strip Chu of its determination to keep advancing; without establishing relations with distant states, they could not deprive it of the strength of its supporting allies. Thus they held the great assembly at Cheng and met again at Yanggu: the substantial forces gathered could then be mobilized, and allies positioned to exert pressure from different directions could be relied upon. Such was the depth of their deliberation. Chu would recognize that our Central States were prepared and that it could not recklessly unleash its strength. How, then, would it dare resist? Was not this superior ability and discernment of Duke Huan and Guan Zhong in restraining Chu worthy of approval?

…the feudal lords attacked Chu, yet halted specifically at Xing, intending to perfect the wording of their formal declaration. When Qu Wan arrived, they withdrew their encampment to Shaoling, thereby completing the rites of assembly and covenant. Did Duke Huan not wish to give full rein to his power? Yet unless our declaration was properly composed, it would not suffice to awe Chu into sincerely acknowledging its guilt; unless our rites were completed, they would not suffice to reassure Chu in its earnest submission to righteousness. Thus they halted at Xing and concluded a covenant at Shaoling: our rightful claims were vindicated, while those wavering on the other side were reassured. Such was their scrupulous observance of ritual. Chu would recognize the cultural refinement of our Central States and could not remain content in its own uncouthness [?]. How could it fail to submit? Was not this superior ability and judgment of Duke Huan and Guan Zhong in securing Chu’s submission worthy of approval?
Nevertheless, had they preserved this intention and advanced in goodness, Duke Huan could have become a true king, and Guan Zhong could have become a king’s supporting minister. After Shaoling, however, arrests and punitive expeditions against Chen followed in profusion. Proud and self-satisfied, they could make no further progress. Here the gentleman deeply regrets the inadequacy of their capacity and breadth of mind.

任不強其所不及使人之道有不盡乎吁道盡

豫則廢敎世子爲天下之豫也蚤諭敎敎世子

之豫乎周公相成王抗世子法於伯禽欲令知

長人以役于我，則所求乎人者，又豈遠於我而得之哉？是必隨器而使，不責其所不能；因材而任，不強其所不及。使人之道，有不盡乎？吁！道盡於下，而後可以爲人上。如此，則夫欲善世子者，其敎豈有要於斯哉？大抵天下之事，豫則立，不豫則廢。敎世子，爲天下之豫也；蚤諭敎，敎世子之豫也。然則子其父之豫，臣其君之豫，少其長之豫乎？周公相成王，抗世子法於伯禽，欲令知父子、君臣、長幼之義，而記者有發於此，其知聖人之用豫矣。吁！旨哉！

「臣儀行，不重辭，不援其所不及，不煩其所不知，則君不勞矣。」
盧淮

同考試官學正唐批：「它卷講君不勞處，不泛則鑿。義理精當，而語意明潔者，無如此篇。刻之以式夫讀禮者。」
考試官右諭德李批：「文以足言，可取。」
考試官侍讀學士汪批：「能悉見可而進之義。」
translation_en:
…to preside over others and have them serve me: could what I seek from others be obtained anywhere far removed from myself? One must employ them according to their capacities, without demanding what they cannot do; assign them responsibilities according to their talents, without forcing them beyond their abilities. Would this not fulfill the way of employing others? Ah! Only after fulfilling the Way in a subordinate position can one become a superior to others. If so, for those who wish to make the heir apparent good, could there be anything more essential to his education than this? Generally, the affairs of the world succeed through preparation and fail without it. Educating the heir apparent is preparation for governing the world; instructing him early is preparation for educating him. Thus, is being a son preparation for being a father, being a minister preparation for being a ruler, and being a junior preparation for being a senior? When the Duke of Zhou assisted King Cheng, he established the educational rules for the heir apparent in his treatment of Bo Qin, wishing him to understand the proper relations between father and son, ruler and minister, and senior and junior. The author of the Record elucidated this point: he understood the sage’s use of preparation. Ah, how profound!

“When a minister makes his conduct exemplary, does not set store by words, does not undertake what lies beyond his abilities, and does not trouble his ruler with what he does not understand, then the ruler will not be burdened.”
Lu Huai

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, School Instructor: “In explaining the passage about the ruler not being burdened, other papers are either vague or strained. None equals this essay in the precision and soundness of its principles and the clarity and purity of its expression. Print it as a model for those who study the Book of Rites.”

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Mentor: “The composition adequately conveys its meaning and merits acceptance.”

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: “It fully elucidates the meaning of advancing when one sees that it is appropriate to do so.”

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
人臣知所以事君則君逸於上矣蓋人臣事君
之道在乎忠也忠則易知而君有不逸者哉緇
衣載孔子之言如此謂夫下難知則君長勞固
矣誠使爲人臣者道積厥躬而形於外者公正
不頗偉然德行之可尊善有諸己而見諸事者
純明有執凝然丰範之可則容色足以消其逸
志而所以正乎其君者不規規於諫諍之間聞
望足以弭其邪心而所以匡乎其上者不拘拘
於言詞之末君之力所能及也則因其所及者
===
而輔之不擾其所不及而彊之使從君之智所
能知也則就其所知者而導之不煩其所不知
而勉之使聽夫然則凡有所行者行無僞行觀
之而易知凡有所言者言無虛言聆之而可信
心有感通之誠事無扞格之患謨無不明弼無
不諧展轉反覆所以疑乎其臣者可無矣政有
可託安然其自適也諫焉而行言焉而聽疲神
焦思所以憂乎其治者可免矣臣有可憑處然
其自遂也夫君不勞由於臣之易知如此然則

punctuated: 人臣知所以事君，則君逸於上矣。蓋人臣事君之道在乎忠也，忠則易知，而君有不逸者哉？《緇衣》載孔子之言如此，謂夫下難知，則君長勞，固矣。誠使爲人臣者道積厥躬，而形於外者公正不頗，偉然德行之可尊；善有諸己，而見諸事者純明有執，凝然丰範之可則。容色足以消其逸志，而所以正乎其君者不規規於諫諍之間；聞望足以弭其邪心，而所以匡乎其上者不拘拘於言詞之末。君之力所能及也，則因其所及者而輔之，不擾其所不及而彊之使從；君之智所能知也，則就其所知者而導之，不煩其所不知而勉之使聽。夫然，則凡有所行者，行無僞行，觀之而易知；凡有所言者，言無虛言，聆之而可信。心有感通之誠，事無扞格之患，謨無不明，弼無不諧，展轉反覆所以疑乎其臣者可無矣。政有可託，安然其自適也；諫焉而行，言焉而聽，疲神焦思所以憂乎其治者可免矣。臣有可憑，處然其自遂也。夫君不勞，由於臣之易知如此，然則
translation_en:
When a minister knows how to serve his ruler, the ruler enjoys ease above. For the way a minister serves his ruler rests upon loyalty. If he is loyal, he is readily understood; how, then, could his ruler fail to enjoy ease? The Black Robes chapter records words of Confucius to this effect: when those below are difficult to understand, their ruler must toil. This is certainly so. Suppose that a minister truly embodies the Way, and that what manifests itself outwardly is impartial and upright, without bias: his imposing virtue and conduct command respect. Suppose that he possesses goodness within himself, and that what appears in his actions is pure, enlightened, and steadfast: his dignified bearing provides a model to follow. His countenance suffices to dispel his ruler’s inclination toward indulgence, and his means of correcting his ruler are not narrowly confined to remonstrance. His reputation and prestige suffice to quell his ruler’s wayward thoughts, and his means of setting his sovereign right are not restricted to the trifling details of words.

Where the ruler’s strength can reach, he assists him according to that capacity; he does not trouble him with what lies beyond his powers and force him to comply. Where the ruler’s understanding can reach, he guides him on the basis of what he knows; he does not burden him with what he does not know and press him to listen. Thus, in everything the minister does, no action is false: one need only observe him to understand him readily. In everything he says, no word is empty: one need only listen to find him trustworthy. Their hearts communicate through sincerity, and their affairs suffer no obstruction or discord. No counsel is unclear, and no assistance fails to accord with its purpose. The ruler can be free of the doubts about his minister that would otherwise turn over and over in his mind. With someone to whom he can entrust government, he rests contentedly at ease. Remonstrance is acted upon and advice is heard; he can escape the mental exhaustion and anxious thought that arise from concern over his governance. With a minister upon whom he can rely, he calmly [?] achieves his purposes. Such is the way in which the ruler’s freedom from toil depends upon his minister’s being readily understood. This being so, …

不勞於上者古之人若伊尹之於太甲周公之
於成王可謂能盡是道者後世乃取辦於頰舌

translation_en:
…Can those who wish to ease their ruler’s burdens fail to know where to direct their efforts? In general, the distinction in rank between minister and ruler is as strict as that between the hall and its steps, and feelings between superior and subordinate easily grow distant. Unless ministers are loyal, trustworthy, sincere, and honest, holding fast to integrity, good faith, loyalty, and steadfastness, suspicion and distrust will grow daily, and few rulers will escape toil in their exalted position. Among the ancients, Yi Yin in his service to Tai Jia and the Duke of Zhou in his service to King Cheng may be said to have fulfilled this way completely. In later ages, men sought to discharge their duties merely through glib speech: how shallow! The Book of Changes says, “There is sincerity in the Way.” Ah! Only thus can one be without shame in following the way of a minister!

“The Gentleman Harmonizes with Others but Does Not Merely Conform”

The Southern Metropolitan Region certainly has many talented scholars, but could any dare to rank ahead of you?”

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
之對始有其辨矣曰五味之相濟五聲之相成
和也以水濟水而不可食琴瑟之專一而不可
聽者同也其說幾矣然而未盡也夫天下之情
萬殊理則一而已君子求同於理而不求同於
人之情是故天下有公是焉人之所是君子亦
是之天下有公非焉人之所非君子亦非之吾
何異於人哉可謂和矣而非同也彼人之所同
是者或未當於理歟君子以一人而非天下之
所是者有之矣人之所同非者或未當於理歟
===
君子以一人而是天下之所非者亦有之矣非
求異於人也求同於理而不求同於人之情耳
亦何害其為和哉君子之不求同於人之情者
非獨於人為然也於已亦然是故聖人之喜以
物之當喜聖人之怒以物之當怒不以已為喜
怒也堯老而舜禪不敢用其私愛也鯀殛而禹
興不敢用其私怨也夫惟不以已也而後能用
其情非情也理也聖人以其情而為和常人以
其情而為同此無他公私之辨而已矣彼小人

之對，始有其辨矣。曰：「五味之相濟，五聲之相成，和也；以水濟水而不可食，琴瑟之專一而不可聽者，同也。」其說幾矣，然而未盡也。夫天下之情萬殊，理則一而已。君子求同於理，而不求同於人之情。是故天下有公是焉，人之所是，君子亦是之；天下有公非焉，人之所非，君子亦非之。吾何異於人哉？可謂和矣，而非同也。彼人之所同是者，或未當於理歟？君子以一人而非天下之所是者，有之矣。人之所同非者，或未當於理歟？君子以一人而是天下之所非者，亦有之矣。非求異於人也，求同於理，而不求同於人之情耳，亦何害其為和哉？
君子之不求同於人之情者，非獨於人為然也，於已亦然。是故聖人之喜，以物之當喜；聖人之怒，以物之當怒，不以已為喜怒也。堯老而舜禪，不敢用其私愛也；鯀殛而禹興，不敢用其私怨也。夫惟不以已也，而後能用其情。非情也，理也。聖人以其情而為和，常人以其情而為同。此無他，公私之辨而已矣。彼小人
translation_en:
…only with that reply did the distinction begin to emerge. It says: “The five flavors complementing one another and the five tones completing one another constitute harmony. Adding water to water so that it cannot be eaten, or playing the qin and se zithers on a single unvarying note so that they cannot be listened to, constitutes sameness.” This explanation comes close, yet it is not exhaustive. Human feelings throughout the world differ in countless ways, but principle is one. The gentleman seeks agreement with principle, rather than agreement with people’s feelings. Thus, where there is something universally acknowledged as right, the gentleman too affirms what others affirm; where there is something universally acknowledged as wrong, the gentleman too rejects what others reject. How am I different from others? This may be called harmony, but it is not sameness. Yet might what people unanimously affirm fail to accord with principle? There are cases in which the gentleman, standing alone, rejects what the whole world affirms. Might what people unanimously reject fail to accord with principle? There are also cases in which the gentleman, standing alone, affirms what the whole world rejects. He does not seek to differ from others; he merely seeks agreement with principle rather than with people’s feelings. How could this prevent his conduct from being harmonious?
The gentleman’s refusal to seek agreement with people’s feelings applies not only to others but also to himself. Thus, the sage rejoices because something merits rejoicing, and becomes angry because something merits anger; he does not make himself the basis of joy and anger. When Yao grew old and Shun received the throne through abdication, private affection was not allowed to govern the decision. When Gun was put to death and Yu was raised to office, private resentment was not allowed to govern the decision. Only by refusing to make himself the basis can the sage then give effect to his feelings. These are not mere feelings, but principle. The sage acts through his feelings to achieve harmony; ordinary people act through their feelings to achieve sameness. This is nothing other than the distinction between impartiality and self-interest. As for those petty men…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
烏足以及此所比則為同所惡則為異以一己
之好惡帥天下以一己之同異為是非彼視理
為何物是烏得而和哉君子以其一心之和布
而為天下之和施於其家則父子親兄弟宜而
孝弟之實著焉施於其鄉則長幼序鄰里睦而
任恤之行成焉施于朝廷上大夫則誾誾下大
夫則侃侃同列則濟濟而禮讓之風行焉日月
之所以明江河之所以流者此和也天地之所
以變化草木之所以蕃育者此和也彼徒知以
===
同為和者視此何如哉易曰同人于野亨又曰
同人于宗吝君子之和于野之同也小人之同
于宗之同也雖同為同而其所以為同者不同
公私之間而已矣大抵天理人欲同行異情愛
人一也君子為周小人為比自樂一也君子為
泰小人為驕與人一也君子為和小人為同世
之儒者未嘗從事於克己之學而每竊其近似
以自名而不自知其卒陷于小人之歸也可不

punctuated: 烏足以及此？所比則為同，所惡則為異，以一己之好惡帥天下，以一己之同異為是非。彼視理為何物？是烏得而和哉？君子以其一心之和，布而為天下之和。施於其家，則父子親，兄弟宜，而孝弟之實著焉；施於其鄉，則長幼序，鄰里睦，而任恤之行成焉；施于朝廷，上大夫則誾誾，下大夫則侃侃，同列則濟濟，而禮讓之風行焉。日月之所以明，江河之所以流者，此和也；天地之所以變化，草木之所以蕃育者，此和也。彼徒知以同為和者，視此何如哉？《易》曰：「同人于野，亨。」又曰：「同人于宗，吝。」君子之和，于野之同也；小人之同，于宗之同也。雖同為同，而其所以為同者不同，公私之間而已矣。大抵天理人欲，同行異情。愛人一也，君子為周，小人為比；自樂一也，君子為泰，小人為驕；與人一也，君子為和，小人為同。世之儒者，未嘗從事於克己之學，而每竊其近似以自名，而不自知其卒陷于小人之歸也，可不戒哉？
translation_en:
…how could they attain this? They agree with those with whom they form cliques and oppose those whom they dislike. They seek to lead all under Heaven by their own likes and dislikes, and take their own agreements and disagreements as the standard of right and wrong. What do they take principle to be? How could this amount to harmony?

The gentleman extends the harmony within his own heart to become harmony throughout all under Heaven. Applied within his family, it brings affection between father and son and fitting relations between brothers, making filial devotion and fraternal respect manifest in practice. Applied within his community, it brings proper order between elders and juniors and concord among neighbors, establishing the practice of mutual assistance and relief. Applied at court, it makes him forthright yet respectful with superior grand masters, composed and affable with inferior grand masters, and dignified with his peers, so that a spirit of ritual propriety and deference prevails. It is this harmony that makes the sun and moon shine and the rivers flow; it is this harmony that enables Heaven and Earth to transform and plants and trees to flourish. How do those who know only to take conformity for harmony compare with this?

The Book of Changes says: “Fellowship with others in the open country: success.” It also says: “Fellowship with others within the clan: cause for regret.” The gentleman’s harmony is the fellowship of the open country; the petty man’s conformity is the fellowship confined to the clan. Although both are called fellowship, what makes them fellowship differs: it is simply the distinction between public-mindedness and selfishness.

Generally, heavenly principle and human desire may produce the same conduct but differ in their underlying motives. Loving others is common to both, but the gentleman is impartial while the petty man forms cliques. Being content with oneself is common to both, but the gentleman is at ease while the petty man is arrogant. Associating with others is common to both, but the gentleman achieves harmony while the petty man conforms. The scholars of this age have never devoted themselves to the learning of self-mastery, yet repeatedly appropriate its outward semblances to claim its name for themselves, unaware that they will ultimately fall into the ways of petty men. Can one fail to be on guard?

punctuated:
而變生，變成方，而音著。聖人博采風俗，協比律聲，流動精神，消融邪穢，表萬物之理，動四氣之和。舜制簫韶，斯道大闡，奏極九變，鳳凰來儀；克諧八音，百獸率舞。嗣是以後，代有作興，雖義意之相因，各名稱之不襲，莫不事與時並，名與功偕。慨三代之既還，遭嬴秦之絶學，王風載熄，聲器斯淪。漢魏繼興，亦勤脩制，《芝房》《寶鼎》之什，《昭武》《正世》之歌，雖曰徒事鏗鏘，猶知希踪雅頌。及夫晉季，大雅云亡，陳競後庭，詞流侈靡；齊倡伴侣，人事淫哇。祗以導欲增悲，安能移風易俗？隋常釐正，訖無成功。盖分裂之既深，宜中和之難復，是不能不有待于今日也。
欽惟〇〇〇〇，德性夙成，聰明天授。民安物阜，協氣薰洽于兩間；治盛功隆，化澤涵濡于九有。
translation_en:
…and changes arise; when changes take patterned form, musical tones become manifest. The sages broadly gathered local customs and harmonized the sounds with the pitch standards, setting spiritual energies in motion, dissolving depravity and impurity, manifesting the principles of all things, and stirring the harmonious energies of the four seasons. Shun instituted the Shao music, and this Way was greatly elucidated. When its performance reached the ninth transformation, phoenixes came in stately array; when the eight classes of instruments were brought into harmony, all the beasts danced together. Thereafter, each age saw new musical creations. Although their underlying meanings followed one another, their names were not simply copied: in every case, the undertaking accorded with its time, and its name matched its achievement.
Alas, after the Three Dynasties had passed [?], learning was cut off under the Qin of the Ying clan. The influence of the ancient kings was extinguished, and musical sounds and instruments fell into decline. The Han and Wei arose in succession and likewise worked diligently to restore musical institutions. Their verses, such as “The Fungus Chamber” and “The Precious Tripod,” and their songs, such as “Manifest Martial Prowess” and “Rectify the Age,” may have attended merely to ringing sounds, yet they still aspired to follow the footsteps of the Odes and Hymns. By the closing years of the Jin, however, the great refined tradition had perished. Under the Chen, people vied in songs of the “Rear Courtyard” [?], their lyrics descending into extravagance and dissipation; under the Qi, they promoted “Companions” [?], and people devoted themselves to licentious, vulgar music. These served only to incite desire and deepen sorrow: how could they transform prevailing influences and reform customs? The Sui repeatedly undertook corrections but ultimately achieved no success. Since political division had become so profound, it was understandable that balance and harmony were difficult to restore. Their restoration therefore could not but await the present day.
We reverently consider that [〇〇〇〇] your virtuous nature was perfected early, and your intelligence was bestowed by Heaven. The people are at peace and material resources abundant; harmonious energies pervade the space between Heaven and Earth. Your government flourishes and your achievements are lofty; the beneficence of your transforming influence suffuses all the realm…

punctuated: 聲爲律而身爲度，導斯行而動斯和，七政光華，三靈太定。擴齊宣之好樂，陋漢文之未遑。銳意典章，留心禮樂，上承先皇之志，下簡侍從之臣，寬以歲時，俾其考定。臣孝孫準十二月以爲旋宮之法，臣文收協十二律而調五鐘之聲。因變宮爲清宮，緣變徵爲正徵，取法于歲，定名曰和。曲有四十八，更調凡八十四節，始終相禪，大小咸明。宮重商輕，君臣之分以顯；羽清徵濁，事物之用斯彰。八風從律而不姦，五色成文而不亂。盡善盡美，纍纍然若貫珠；純如皦如，洋洋乎其盈耳。一洗齊梁之習，盡消吳楚之風。薦之郊廟而神鬼歆，施之朝廷而天人應。一朝之典有在，百王之制無逾。昔孔子耳聞
translation_en:
…Your voice serves as the pitch standard and your person as the measure; where you lead, things proceed, and when you move, harmony follows. The seven celestial regulators shine brilliantly, and the three numinous powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity—are fully at peace. You extend King Xuan of Qi’s love of music and deem inadequate Emperor Wen of Han’s failure to find time for it. Intent upon institutions and observances, you devote attention to rites and music. Above, you carry forward the late emperor’s aspirations; below, you select ministers from among your attendants, allowing them ample months and years to examine and settle these matters.

Your servant Xiaosun takes the twelve months as the standard for a method of rotating the musical modes; your servant Wenshou harmonizes the twelve pitch standards and tunes the sounds of the five bells. The altered gong becomes the clear gong, and the altered zhi becomes the regular zhi. Taking the annual cycle as their model, they establish the designation “Harmony.” There are forty-eight pieces, with changes of mode totaling eighty-four sections [?]. Their beginnings and endings succeed one another, and greater and lesser are all clearly distinguished. Gong is weighty and shang light, thereby manifesting the distinction between ruler and minister; yu is clear and zhi deep, thereby revealing the functions of affairs and things. The winds of the eight directions follow the pitch standards without deviation; the five colors form patterns without disorder. Perfect in goodness and beauty, the notes follow one another like threaded pearls; pure and distinct, their abundant sound fills the ears. They sweep away the musical habits of Qi and Liang and wholly dispel the styles of Wu and Chu.

Presented at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples, this music delights the spirits; performed at court, it calls forth a response from Heaven and humanity. The ceremonial institutions of this reign are firmly established; the systems of the hundred kings cannot surpass them. Long ago, Confucius heard…

Immersed in your great transforming influence, we cannot exhaust its wonders in words. We humbly hope that you will examine the tones to understand music, and perfect music to govern the heart. …the response at the imperial court.

Comment by Associate Examiner Zhao, Professor: The achievements and cultural accomplishments of our Sagely Founder rival the splendor of the ages of Tang Yao and Yu Shun and the Three Dynasties. Candidates can generally speak of these, yet inevitably mention one thing while omitting ten thousand. This answer alone is detailed and clear, as though pointing to something in one's palm. Might this reflect how deeply the candidate has been steeped in our sage ruler's transforming influence?

Comment by Examiner Li, Right Admonisher: Our Sagely Founder established the dynasty and handed down its enduring succession, far surpassing all earlier ages. In setting aside the Han as unworthy of discussion, there is indeed something on which to rely [?]. You have not only explained this, but have done so in language of classical elegance, displaying uncommon talent and insight. Having obtained a scholar like this, we can report that we have fulfilled His Majesty's command.

Comment by Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting: All five policy essays answer well, offering historical precedents and reasoned discussion. In particular, the candidate's forceful language and vigorous writing fully expound the greatness of our Sagely Founder's achievements and virtue, leaving nothing out. This especially reveals his learning and insight. This essay has been selected for inclusion as representative of the others.

I have long held that a sage's virtue has no fixed bounds, while its practical operation leaves discernible traces. What has no fixed bounds is difficult to name, whereas what leaves traces is easy to perceive. Those skilled at contemplating a sage use what can be perceived to give a name to what cannot be named; thus they may approach some semblance of him. Confucius said: “How majestic! Heaven alone is great, and Yao alone modeled himself upon it.” He also said: “How majestic were his achievements!
