…fully encompass Heaven; yet those who know how to contemplate Yao and Heaven can discern their greatness through these things. Understanding this, we can speak of our sagely ancestor’s mighty achievements in pacification, his grand plans for founding the dynasty and handing it down, and his great instructions for ordering the realm. Allow me to respond to your discerning question by expounding and praising them. Since the Three Dynasties, commentators have held that Emperor Gao of the Han gained All-under-Heaven in the most legitimate manner. This was because he destroyed the Qin, which lacked the Way, and punished the rebel Yu, while his generosity, benevolence, and magnanimity sufficed to lay the foundations for four hundred years of rule. Yet although his main principles were correct, he could not avoid omissions in their many particulars. His raising the banner of righteousness had a worthy name, but he merely borrowed it as a pretext to justify his actions. In other respects, he never abandoned the habits of ruling from horseback throughout his life; the law against possessing books was abolished only in the next generation; and his descendants willingly accepted the shortcomings of mingling hegemonic methods with kingly government. If, at the very founding of the dynasty, this was the legacy bequeathed by its institutions and plans, what could one still expect of succeeding rulers charged with carrying on the line and preserving its accomplishments?

We reverently reflect that our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed with divine sageliness, arose at the juncture when an old order gave way to renewal. Responding to Heaven and following the people, he transformed barbarian ways and employed those of Chinese civilization. He cleansed away defilement unprecedented since the opening of Heaven and Earth and recovered the land in which emperors and kings had established themselves. In his rise to kingship and his undertaking, he had already surpassed the achievements of Tang and Wu. As for the designs and arrangements manifested in his sagely government, these were sufficient to serve as models for all generations. translation_en:
…the Great Ming Code, to correct excesses in statutory provisions. Before his honorific title had been presented, the ancestral temple and altars of soil and grain were already established; while military affairs were still pressing, schools were immediately founded. His sagely governance, as manifested throughout the realm, embraced both fundamentals and details and attended to matters great and small—far more than could be enumerated in a few examples. All these measures served as foundations for ordering the enduring human relationships and clarifying ritual propriety and righteousness. They restored the cardinal bonds and constant virtues after their decline and revived the nine rules of governance after their neglect. The grandeur and far-reaching scope of his plans already equaled the flourishing achievements of Yao and Shun and the Three Dynasties. How could the mere Han dynasty merit comparison?

As for the words he uttered to leave instruction for posterity, whether expressed in discussions, proclaimed in edicts and commands, or committed to writing in his works, every statement and principle shone as brightly as the Six Classics. Thus, in expounding the hexagram The Family, he elucidated the way of sincerity and commanding dignity, making clear the profound meaning of Fu Xi and King Wen. In annotating the Great Plan, he revealed the mysteries of the August Ultimate and the enduring human relationships, bringing to light the categories discussed by Jizi and King Wu. His single edict inaugurating the dynasty embodied the stern distinctions of the Spring and Autumn Annals, which treated the Xia as insiders and the Yi as outsiders. The three compilations of the Grand Pronouncements embodied the gentleness and generosity of the Zhou proclamations and the Yin dynasty’s Pan Geng chapters.

Elsewhere, discussing rites and music, he said: “Rites guide reverence; music gives expression to harmony. Without reverence and harmony, how can there be good government?” Even Youzi’s discussion of rites and music could not surpass these words. Discussing schools, he said: “Among the essentials of government, moral transformation through education comes first. Moral transformation through education…”

translation_en:
…the way to bring about moral transformation rests upon schools.” Even Mencius’s discussion of kingly government could not improve upon these words. Discussing the rise and fall of former dynasties, he said: “The source of disorder and ruin lies in arrogance and indulgence.” Discussing the vast extent of the realm today, he said: “With territory so extensive and people so numerous, we must be especially watchful and apprehensive.” This, too, is an admonition to remain vigilant and diligent, attentive to circumstances and the first stirrings of change. He went so far as to say: “The government of emperors and kings never flourished more greatly than under Yao and Shun. Examining their transmission and reception of rule, we find that it rested solely upon holding to the Mean.” He also said: “The ruler’s mind alone is the foundation of government and moral transformation. If within him he lacks the mind of Yao and Shun, yet wishes to achieve their government in the administration of affairs, this is utterly impossible.” How great are these imperial words! Even the transmission of the divine sages of Tang and Yu, with their earnest injunctions beginning ‘Oh, you,’ amounted to no more than this. Here we may reverently discern the subtlety of the sage’s method of cultivating the mind, taking up a thread whose transmission had been broken for thousands of years.
Since this subtle method of cultivating the mind continues the transmission of the divine sages, all that he harbors within is the mind of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. Thus his words become canonical teachings: they are the very words of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. His actions become models: they are the very governance of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. What he hands down for his sagely sons and divine grandsons to carry forward is entirely the government of the Two Emperors and Three Kings. Your servant merely sees the myriad things coming into being, without understanding what makes the work of creation so wondrous; merely sees that even the smallest crevice is invariably illuminated, without understanding what makes the sun and moon so bright…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
維天下之勢存乎法持天下之法存乎人
甚矣天下之大也非法以維之則無以一
眾心統萬事而將有渙散潰亂之憂有其
法而無人以持之則徒法不能以自行抑
何以收治平之効也哉紀綱者維天下之
法也而常藉于人人君者主天下之治也
而必資于法有其法而又有人以持之則
治之成也無難矣請試陳之紀綱之說其
===
來尚矣見於五子之歌詠於棫樸假樂之
詩一家有一家之紀綱一國有一國之紀
綱天下有天下之紀綱存之則治失之則
亂如天之有日月星辰地之有山岳河海
所以經緯乎上下不可一日而亡者也韓
愈氏曰善醫者不視人之肥瘠察其脉之
病否而已矣善計天下者不視天下之安
危察其紀綱之理亂而已矣嗚呼紀綱之
理亂而天下安危隨之然則有國者可忽

translation_en:
Maintaining the order of the realm depends upon laws; upholding the laws of the realm depends upon people.

Vast indeed is the realm! Without laws to hold it together, there would be no means to unite the hearts of the multitude or bring all affairs under orderly direction, and disintegration and disorder would threaten. If laws exist but there are no people to uphold them, laws alone cannot put themselves into effect. How, then, could orderly and peaceful government be achieved? The governing framework is the body of laws that holds the realm together, yet it always depends upon people. The ruler presides over the government of the realm, yet he must rely upon laws. If there are laws and also people to uphold them, successful government presents no difficulty. Allow me to explain. The idea of a governing framework has a long history. It appears in the “Song of the Five Sons” and is celebrated in the poems “Clustering Oaks” (Yupu) and “Admirable Happiness” (Jiale). Each family has its own governing framework; each state has its own; and the realm has its own. Preserve it, and there is order; lose it, and there is disorder. Like the sun, moon, and stars in heaven, and the mountains, rivers, and seas on earth, it provides the warp and weft that order what is above and below, and cannot be absent for a single day. Han Yu said: “A skilled physician does not look at whether a person is stout or thin, but merely examines the pulse for signs of illness. One skilled in planning for the realm does not look at whether the realm is secure or imperiled, but merely examines whether its governing framework is orderly or disordered.” Alas! text:
乎哉古之君天下者若漢宣帝綜核名實
信賞必罰紀綱一振是以成中興之美夫
何孝元以降政令寖衰貂璫放恣外戚專
柄延及哀平疎斥英良而紀綱敝矣非紀
綱之敝也有所以敝乎紀綱者也唐太宗
刻厲矯揉萬目畢舉紀綱一布是以躋貞
觀之治夫何肅代以後政尚姑息舉措失
當藩鎮不庭至于懿宗堂陛陵夷而紀綱
壞矣非紀綱之壞也有所以壞夫紀綱者
===
也宋太宗沉謀英斷考功慎刑其紀綱可
謂過于近古子孫雖世守之可也夫何神
宗狹小制度妄意紛更任用匪人新法一
行海內騷動卒遺靖康之禍紀綱非不振
也失其所以振之之道也國之微也安足
恠乎洪惟我
太祖高皇帝天授聖神奄有海宇懲胡元之亂
紀綱之立兼統百王慶賞刑威之布禮樂
法度之施自

…could they neglect them? Among those who ruled the realm in antiquity, Emperor Xuan of the Han comprehensively examined the correspondence between names and actual performance, made rewards trustworthy and punishments certain, and reinvigorated the governing order. Thus he achieved the glory of a dynastic restoration. Why, then, from Emperor Xiaoyuan onward, did government commands gradually lose their force, eunuchs act without restraint, and imperial relatives monopolize power? By the reigns of Emperors Ai and Ping, worthy and capable men were estranged and dismissed, and the governing order had deteriorated. It did not deteriorate of itself: there were causes that brought about its deterioration.
Emperor Taizong of the Tang exerted himself rigorously to correct abuses, attending to every detail of government. Once the governing order was established, he attained the good government of the Zhenguan era. Why, then, after Emperors Suzong and Daizong, did government favor indulgence, measures become ill-judged, and regional military governors refuse allegiance to the court? By Emperor Yizong’s reign, the hierarchy between ruler and ministers had declined, and the governing order had collapsed. It did not collapse of itself: there were causes that brought about its collapse.
Emperor Taizong of the Song planned deeply and decided boldly, assessed merit, and exercised care in punishment. His governing order may be said to have surpassed that of the recent past; his descendants could well have preserved it from generation to generation. Why, then, did Emperor Shenzong regard the established institutions as too limited, recklessly conceive a multitude of changes, and employ unworthy men? Once the New Policies were put into effect, the entire realm was thrown into turmoil, ultimately bringing about the calamity of Jingkang. It was not that the governing order had not been vigorously asserted, but that the proper way of asserting it had been lost. How, then, could the dynasty’s decline occasion any surprise?
We reverently reflect upon our Emperor Taizu Gao, endowed by Heaven with sagely and divine qualities, who came to possess the entire realm. Taking warning from the disorder of the non-Han Yuan dynasty, he established a governing order that comprehensively united the practices of the hundred kings. title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
輦轂以及海徼由王公以逮甿庶事為之制
人為之防可謂至精至密而無以復加矣
百五十年來人知法守海內晏然俗美風
醇臻于至治有由然矣承平既乆人懷玩
愒法弛弊生執事謂紀綱有失其舊者愚
不敢謂其無也昔荀悅著申鑒論政治之
術有曰先屏四患乃崇五政所謂四患者
一曰偽二曰私三曰放四曰奢五政者興
農桑以養其性審好惡以正其俗宣文教
===
以彰其化立武備以秉其威明賞罰以統
其法悅之意以為偽亂俗私壞法放越軌
私敗制四患不除則五政不行故亟去之
去之誠是矣愚則以為紀綱風俗相因者
也紀綱弛于上斯風俗敝于下四患風俗
也五政紀綱也能行五政則四患自除而
何先後之云朱子謂綱紀在於辨賢否以
定上下之分核功罪以公賞罰之施固悅
審好惡明賞罰之說也自今觀之孰有要

punctuated:
輦轂以及海徼，由王公以逮甿庶，事為之制，人為之防，可謂至精至密而無以復加矣。百五十年來，人知法守，海內晏然，俗美風醇，臻于至治，有由然矣。承平既乆，人懷玩愒，法弛弊生。執事謂紀綱有失其舊者，愚不敢謂其無也。
昔荀悅著《申鑒》，論政治之術，有曰：「先屏四患，乃崇五政。」所謂四患者，一曰偽，二曰私，三曰放，四曰奢。五政者，興農桑以養其性，審好惡以正其俗，宣文教以彰其化，立武備以秉其威，明賞罰以統其法。悅之意，以為偽亂俗，私壞法，放越軌，私敗制。四患不除，則五政不行，故亟去之。去之誠是矣，愚則以為紀綱、風俗相因者也。紀綱弛于上，斯風俗敝于下。四患，風俗也；五政，紀綱也。能行五政，則四患自除，而何先後之云？朱子謂：「綱紀在於辨賢否，以定上下之分；核功罪，以公賞罰之施。」固悅審好惡、明賞罰之說也。自今觀之，孰有要
translation_en:
…from the imperial capital to the coastal frontiers, from princes and dukes to the common people, regulations were established for every affair and safeguards against wrongdoing for every person. These may be called supremely refined and meticulous, beyond any further improvement. For a hundred and fifty years, people have known to abide by the laws, and all within the seas has enjoyed peace. Customs have been admirable and manners wholesome: there is a reason why government has attained such excellence. Yet after prolonged peace, people have grown complacent and idle; laws have become lax and abuses have arisen. You gentlemen state that the governing order has lost something of its former character. I would not venture to deny it.
In former times, Xun Yue wrote in his Extended Reflections (Shenjian), discussing the art of government: “First eliminate the four evils; then promote the five policies.” The four evils are, first, deceit; second, selfishness; third, license; and fourth, extravagance. The five policies are to promote agriculture and sericulture to sustain the people's lives; to scrutinize what is approved and disapproved to rectify their customs; to spread cultural instruction to make its transforming influence manifest; to establish military preparedness to maintain authority; and to make rewards and punishments clear to coordinate the operation of the laws. Yue's meaning was that deceit disorders customs, selfishness undermines laws, license transgresses norms, and selfishness [?] ruins institutions. Unless the four evils are removed, the five policies cannot be implemented; hence his insistence on urgently eliminating them. Eliminating them is certainly right. In my humble view, however, the governing order and popular customs depend on one another. When the governing order grows lax above, customs deteriorate below. The four evils concern customs; the five policies concern the governing order. If the five policies can be implemented, the four evils will disappear of themselves. Why, then, speak of what must come first and what afterward? Master Zhu said: “The governing order consists in distinguishing the worthy from the unworthy to establish the proper distinctions between superiors and inferiors, and in examining merits and offenses to ensure fairness in dispensing rewards and punishments.” This is indeed Yue's argument for scrutinizing approval and disapproval and clarifying rewards and punishments. Viewed from the present, what could be more essential…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
于二者乎盖好惡審則聽言責事舉名察
實善無不顯惡無不彰而民志平矣賞罰
公則賞不僣刑不濫善知所勸惡知所懲
而國法立矣由是農桑可興文教可宣武
備可立紀綱振而民風善尚何政治之不
成邪雖然朱子又嘗言之矣紀綱之所以
振則以宰執秉持而不敢失臺諫補察而
無所私人主又以大公至正之心恭已于
上而照臨之愚之所謂存乎人者此也執
===
事俯于
經幄一陳焉則所以復
祖宗之舊而臻至治之風者在是矣豈非
宗社無疆之休哉
第三問
吳淮
同考試官教諭趙 批〔經與史本一道此策歷歷能言且於治經作史者之得失剖析明備非胷中會經史於一貫者不能噫脫穎而出者子其人乎〕

同考試官教諭趙　批
吴淮
經與史本一道此策歷
陳歷代經史得失剖析明備非負
于二者不能縱橫顏而出者子其人乎
punctuated:
于二者乎？盖好惡審，則聽言責事，舉名察實，善無不顯，惡無不彰，而民志平矣。賞罰公，則賞不僣，刑不濫，善知所勸，惡知所懲，而國法立矣。由是農桑可興，文教可宣，武備可立，紀綱振而民風善，尚何政治之不成邪？雖然，朱子又嘗言之矣：「紀綱之所以振，則以宰執秉持而不敢失，臺諫補察而無所私，人主又以大公至正之心恭已于上而照臨之。」愚之所謂存乎人者，此也。執事俯于經幄，一陳焉，則所以復祖宗之舊而臻至治之風者在是矣，豈非宗社無疆之休哉！

同考試官教諭趙批〔經與史本一道，此策歷歷能言，且於治經作史者之得失，剖析明備。非胷中會經史於一貫者不能。噫！脫穎而出者，子其人乎！〕
translation_en:
…more essential than these two? When approval and disapproval are carefully judged, words are heard and deeds held to account, reputations considered and realities examined. No good remains unrecognized and no evil remains unexposed, and the people’s minds are at peace. When rewards and punishments are impartial, rewards do not exceed what is deserved and punishments are not excessive. The good know what encourages them, and the wicked know what deters them; thus the laws of the state are established. Agriculture and sericulture can then flourish, cultural instruction can spread, and military preparations can be secured. With governing order restored and popular customs improved, what could remain unaccomplished in government?

Yet Master Zhu also once said: “Governing order is restored because the chief councilors uphold it and dare not let it lapse, while censorial and remonstrance officials correct omissions and scrutinize affairs without partiality. The ruler, with a mind of utmost impartiality and perfect rectitude, reverently conducts himself above and oversees all.” This is what I mean when I say that it depends upon the people entrusted with it. If you, sir, would once present this in attendance at the imperial lectures [?], herein would lie the means to restore the ancestral precedents and attain the conditions of perfect government. Would this not be an unbounded blessing for the imperial ancestral temple and the altars of soil and grain?

Examiner Li, Right Mentor, comments: From this candidate’s papers in the first two sessions, I already knew him to be exceptional. All five policy essays are composed and rich in implicit meaning, without indulging in flights of fancy. His response on the Classics and histories is particularly refined and sound. A fine scholar! How could anyone who rejects ornament and prizes substance fail to select him?

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-Waiting, comments: This candidate’s papers in all three sessions are thoroughly pure, proceeding entirely from rectitude [?]; their radiance, like that of gold and jade, cannot be concealed. His cultivation is profound indeed! The few words at the end of the policy essay also reveal considerable confidence in his own abilities. A fine scholar! A fine scholar!

If we consider the Classics and histories before their separation, learning throughout the world was one; if we consider them after their separation, learning throughout the world was divided in two. In antiquity, history was embodied in the Classics, and the names “Classics” and “histories” had not yet been established. Only when these names were established did the two begin to separate. Is this why the learning of ancient scholars proceeded from a single source, whereas later scholars could not avoid branching off and dividing it in two? You, honored examiners, have set policy questions in the examination compound of the capital and raised this matter to inquire of us students. This is precisely what I, an unworthy student, recite and study morning and evening, and what I have brought with me today to submit to examination. How could I dare offer no words in reply?

The Classics convey the Way, and histories record events: men of former times have indeed said this. Yet there have never been events in the world outside the Way, so the Classics are themselves histories; nor has there ever been a Way outside events, so histories are also Classics. title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
子謂聖人述史三焉其述書也帝王之制
備故索焉而皆獲其述詩也興衰之由顯
故究焉而皆得其述春秋也邪正之跡明
故考焉而皆當此三者同出於史而不可
雜也故聖人分焉蓋以尚書紀言春秋紀
事而詩明得失之故雖均為史而其體有
三者之異故曰不可雜者此也是固然矣
然而書者二帝三王之史也詩者周與列
國之史也春秋者東遷以降列侯五伯之
===
史也是其紀載之跡又有不同者焉斯時
也固未嘗有經史之名而亦安有所謂經
史之學哉故劉歆叙七畧王儉撰七志史
記以下皆附春秋蓋亦不為無見是則漢
魏以前經史猶未分也其後荀勗分四部
史記舊事入丙部阮孝緒七錄經典錄六
藝紀傳錄史傳而經與史至是始分矣後
之以學名者遂有二者之異若王安石以
經學稱司馬光以史學著是以三經字義

punctuated: 子謂：「聖人述史三焉：其述書也，帝王之制備，故索焉而皆獲；其述詩也，興衰之由顯，故究焉而皆得；其述春秋也，邪正之跡明，故考焉而皆當。此三者同出於史，而不可雜也，故聖人分焉。」蓋以《尚書》紀言，《春秋》紀事，而《詩》明得失之故，雖均為史，而其體有三者之異，故曰不可雜者，此也。是固然矣。然而《書》者，二帝三王之史也；《詩》者，周與列國之史也；《春秋》者，東遷以降列侯五伯之史也。是其紀載之跡，又有不同者焉。斯時也，固未嘗有經史之名，而亦安有所謂經史之學哉？故劉歆叙《七畧》，王儉撰《七志》，《史記》以下皆附《春秋》，蓋亦不為無見。是則漢魏以前，經史猶未分也。其後荀勗分四部，《史記》舊事入丙部；阮孝緒《七錄》，經典錄六藝，紀傳錄史傳，而經與史至是始分矣。後之以學名者，遂有二者之異。若王安石以經學稱，司馬光以史學著，是以三經字義
translation_en: …Master Wenzhong said: “The Sage set forth history in three forms. In his presentation of the Documents, the institutions of emperors and kings are fully preserved, so that all one seeks there may be found. In his presentation of the Odes, the causes of rise and decline are manifest, so that inquiry into them yields full understanding. In his presentation of the Spring and Autumn Annals, the traces of wrongdoing and rectitude are clear, so that examination of them yields sound judgments. These three all derive from history, yet cannot be mixed together; therefore the Sage distinguished them.” This is because the Book of Documents records words, the Spring and Autumn Annals records events, and the Odes makes clear the causes of success and failure. Although all are history, their forms differ in these three ways: this is what is meant by saying that they cannot be mixed together. This is certainly so. Yet the Documents is the history of the Two Emperors and Three Kings; the Odes is the history of Zhou and the various states; and the Spring and Autumn Annals is the history of the regional lords and the Five Hegemons from the eastward removal of the capital onward. Thus the historical matters they record also differ. At that time, the designations “classics” and “histories” had never existed; how, then, could there have been anything called the study of classics and the study of history? Thus, when Liu Xin compiled the Seven Summaries and Wang Jian composed the Seven Treatises, the Records of the Historian and subsequent works were all attached to the Spring and Autumn Annals. This arrangement was surely not without insight. It follows that before the Han and Wei, classics and histories were still undivided. Subsequently, Xun Xu established four divisions, placing the Records of the Historian and accounts of earlier events in Division C. In Ruan Xiaoxu’s Seven Catalogues, the Catalogue of Classics recorded the Six Arts, while the Catalogue of Annals and Biographies recorded histories and biographies. Only at this point did classics and histories become separate. Among later men renowned for learning, these consequently became two distinct fields. Wang Anshi, for example, was celebrated for his study of the classics, and Sima Guang was renowned for his study of history. Thus, the meanings of the Three Classics and of written characters [?]…

同考試官教諭魏批經術節義策博學士不
博者失於斷制狹者拘於所聞是篇識見卓偉抑揚予
奪曲中事理且歸重於節義而又要以至當之論子殆經
術中之有節義者歟
考試官右諭德李批評隲兩漢諸子得失皆為確
論蓋有得於春秋之學者是可以知子之所嚮矣
考試官侍讀學士汪批此卷前二場超然不羣策皆
善答而此篇尤贍整有條其學識之最優者乎
===
談經者貴有明道之功勵節者貴能見幾
之審見道不明則誦說雖勤徒事佔畢而
無益于實用知幾不審則忠憤雖切徒騰
論議而無補于國家持此可以論兩漢之
士矣請條陳之夫三代之後漢稱得士西
漢自武帝表章六經一時之士爭尚經術
然秉操履正以節義自勵者亦不能無焉
觀汲黯數好直諫而淮南為之寢謀蘇武
持節虜庭而匈奴以之奪氣朱雲借劍尚

楊春芳

同考試官教諭魏批《經術節義策》：博學士不博者失於斷制，狹者拘於所聞。是篇識見卓偉，抑揚予奪，曲中事理，且歸重於節義，而又要以至當之論。子殆經術中之有節義者歟！

考試官右諭德李批：評隲兩漢諸子得失，皆為確論，蓋有得於春秋之學者，是可以知子之所嚮矣。

考試官侍讀學士汪批：此卷前二場超然不羣，策皆善答，而此篇尤贍整有條，其學識之最優者乎！

談經者貴有明道之功，勵節者貴能見幾之審。見道不明，則誦說雖勤，徒事佔畢而無益于實用；知幾不審，則忠憤雖切，徒騰論議而無補于國家。持此可以論兩漢之士矣，請條陳之。夫三代之後，漢稱得士。西漢自武帝表章六經，一時之士爭尚經術，然秉操履正、以節義自勵者，亦不能無焉。觀汲黯數好直諫，而淮南為之寢謀；蘇武持節虜庭，而匈奴以之奪氣；朱雲借劍尚

Yang Chunfang

Associate Examiner Wei, Instructor, comments on the policy essay on classical learning and moral integrity: Scholars whose learning lacks breadth falter in judgment [?]; those of narrow outlook are confined by what they have heard. This essay displays outstanding insight. Its praise and censure, approval and disapproval, accord with the principles of affairs in every particular. Moreover, it gives primary weight to moral integrity, while grounding its conclusions in thoroughly sound judgments. You must surely be one who combines classical learning with moral integrity!

Examiner Li, Right Admonisher, comments: Your assessments of the merits and failings of the various men of the two Han dynasties are all well founded. You have evidently gained an understanding of the learning of the Spring and Autumn Annals. From this one can discern the direction of your aspirations.

Examiner Wang, Academician Reader-in-waiting, comments: This examination script stands far above the rest in its first two sessions. The policy questions are all well answered, and this essay is particularly rich, well composed, and orderly. Surely its author ranks highest in learning and discernment!

Those who discuss the Classics should be valued for their achievement in illuminating the Way; those who cultivate integrity should be valued for their accurate discernment of the first signs of change. If their understanding of the Way is unclear, then, however diligently they recite and expound, they merely pore over texts without contributing anything to practical use. If their discernment of incipient change is inexact, then, however ardent their loyal indignation, they merely stir up debate without benefiting the state. By these standards we may assess the scholars of the two Han dynasties. Allow me to set out the particulars.

After the Three Dynasties, the Han was renowned for obtaining worthy men. In the Western Han, from the time Emperor Wu gave prominence to the Six Classics, scholars of the age vied in esteeming classical learning. Yet there were also those who maintained their principles, acted uprightly, and spurred themselves on through moral integrity. Consider how Ji An repeatedly offered forthright remonstrance, causing the Prince of Huainan to shelve his plot; how Su Wu retained his envoy’s tally at the court of the northern captors, causing the Xiongnu to lose heart; and how Zhu Yun requested the loan of a sword from the imperial …

方攀檻大呼蕭望之職居師傅不肯就吏
印綬加身輒推不受龔勝恥事乎二姓安
車再聘堅卧不起薛方自託于巢由王章
却其妻牛衣之言抗疏下獄盖寛饒拒友
人蘧氏之喻上書自殞解劍無傷也雋不
疑則曰君子武備以衞身請不解而退免
冠隨俗也貢禹則曰冠一免安復可冠願
不免以去官之數子者清風勁節盖凛凛

方，攀檻大呼；蕭望之職居師傅，不肯就吏。印綬加身，輒推不受，龔勝恥事乎二姓；安車再聘，堅卧不起，薛方自託于巢由。王章却其妻牛衣之言，抗疏下獄；盖寛饒拒友人蘧氏之喻，上書自殞。解劍無傷也，雋不疑則曰：「君子武備以衞身。」請不解而退。免冠隨俗也，貢禹則曰：「冠一免，安復可冠？」願不免以去官。之數子者，清風勁節，盖凛凛乎其不可犯矣。人惟見夫仲舒、京房、匡衡、更生之流，懷經挾術，所在霧滃，遂以經術歸之，不知經術豈足以盡西漢之士邪？
東漢自光武率興教化，一時之人競崇節義，然負笈抱策而經術是事者，亦未嘗少焉。觀伏湛之篤信好古，經為人師；桓譚之徧習五經，剖析疑異；樊儵刪定《公羊》嚴氏《春秋》章句，世號曰「樊侯學」；鄭玄因考論圖緯，請益辭歸，其師嘆曰：「吾道東！」兄弟習《魯詩》而為學士所推者，則魯恭、魯丕；父子明左
translation_en:
…the imperial sword, clinging to the balustrade and crying out loudly; Xiao Wangzhi, holding the position of imperial tutor, refused to submit to the judicial officers. When seals and ribbons of office were conferred upon him, Gong Sheng pushed them away and refused them, deeming it shameful to serve two ruling houses. Twice summoned with a carriage in which he could ride seated, Xue Fang steadfastly remained reclining and would not rise, invoking the examples of Chao Fu and Xu You. Wang Zhang rejected his wife’s words when they lay under an ox-coverlet, submitted a remonstrance, and was imprisoned. Gai Kuanrao rejected his friend’s admonition invoking Qu Boyu, submitted a memorial, and took his own life. There would have been no harm in removing his sword, yet Jun Buyi said, “A gentleman keeps weapons ready to defend himself.” He requested leave to withdraw without removing it. Removing one’s cap would have accorded with custom, yet Gong Yu said, “Once the cap is removed, how could I put it on again?” He preferred to leave office without removing it. These men’s pure conduct and firm integrity were indeed so awe-inspiring that none could violate them. People see only the likes of Zhongshu, Jing Fang, Kuang Heng, and Gengsheng, bearing the classics and possessing scholarly learning, gathering everywhere like thick mist. They consequently characterize Western Han scholars in terms of classical learning, failing to understand: how could classical learning alone encompass all the scholars of the Western Han?
In the Eastern Han, after Guangwu took the lead in promoting moral instruction, men of the age competed in honoring integrity and righteousness. Yet there were also no few who carried book-baskets and texts and devoted themselves to classical learning. Consider Fu Zhan, steadfast in conviction and devoted to antiquity, who taught others the classics; Huan Tan, who studied all the Five Classics and analyzed doubtful passages and divergent interpretations; and Fan Shu, who edited and established the Yan school’s chapter-and-sentence commentary on the Gongyang tradition of the Spring and Autumn Annals, known in his day as “Lord Fan’s learning.” Zheng Xuan examined and discussed prophetic diagrams and apocryphal texts, sought further instruction, and took leave to return home. His teacher sighed, “My Way goes east!” The brothers who studied the Lu tradition of the Book of Odes and won the esteem of scholars were Lu Gong and Lu Pi; the father and son who mastered the Zuo…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
氏而為羣儒所宗者則鄭興鄭衆絳帳設
教生徒千人馬融名重于關西正定五經
刻石太學蔡邕儒崇于靈帝之數子者博
古名家盖彬彬乎其盛矣人唯見夫八俊
八顧八及八厨之輩危言激論所在風生
遂以節義許之不知節義豈足以盡東漢
之士邪經術所以致用明易如張禹藉經
飾詐來持禄保位之譏擬易如揚雄畏禍
取容有劇秦美新之作谷永欲阿王鳳則
===
引申伯以稱其忠劉歆欲附新莽則獻符
命以逢其惡數子非不經術之是究也然
出口入耳無講學明道之功繪句揣章乏
體驗擴充之實是以諛佞成習風節罔聞
規避苟安士氣掃地豈經術之罪哉節義
將以建功有清世之志如陳蕃幾事不密
而功隳羣小負王佐之才如王允氣溢志
驕而身殘餘孽李膺被枉戮姦其事偉矣
無何而名陷黨議范滂登車攬轡其志雄

氏而為羣儒所宗者，則鄭興、鄭衆。絳帳設教，生徒千人，馬融名重于關西；正定五經，刻石太學，蔡邕儒崇于靈帝。之數子者，博古名家，盖彬彬乎其盛矣！人唯見夫八俊、八顧、八及、八厨之輩，危言激論，所在風生，遂以節義許之。不知節義豈足以盡東漢之士邪？

經術所以致用。明易如張禹，藉經飾詐，來持禄保位之譏；擬易如揚雄，畏禍取容，有劇秦美新之作；谷永欲阿王鳳，則引申伯以稱其忠；劉歆欲附新莽，則獻符命以逢其惡。數子非不經術之是究也，然出口入耳，無講學明道之功；繪句揣章，乏體驗擴充之實。是以諛佞成習，風節罔聞，規避苟安，士氣掃地，豈經術之罪哉？

節義將以建功。有清世之志如陳蕃，幾事不密，而功隳羣小；負王佐之才如王允，氣溢志驕，而身殘餘孽。李膺被枉戮姦，其事偉矣，無何而名陷黨議；范滂登車攬轡，其志雄
translation_en:
…Those who mastered the Zuo Commentary and were revered by the assembled scholars were Zheng Xing and Zheng Zhong. Teaching behind a crimson curtain, with a thousand students, Ma Rong enjoyed great renown west of the passes. Establishing the correct texts of the Five Classics and engraving them on stone at the Imperial University, Cai Yong was esteemed for his classical learning under Emperor Ling. These men were distinguished masters of ancient learning: how splendidly cultivated and flourishing their company was! Yet people see only such groups as the Eight Eminent Men, the Eight Supporters, the Eight Exemplars, and the Eight Providers, whose forthright words and impassioned arguments stirred the air wherever they went, and consequently praise them for integrity and righteousness. Do they not realize that integrity and righteousness alone cannot encompass all the scholars of the Eastern Han?

Classical learning is intended for practical application. Zhang Yu understood the Book of Changes, yet used the classics to cloak deceit, inviting criticism for clinging to his stipend and preserving his position. Yang Xiong modeled his writing on the Book of Changes, yet feared disaster and sought acceptance, composing his Censure of Qin and Praise of Xin. When Gu Yong wished to flatter Wang Feng, he invoked the Earl of Shen to praise Wang’s loyalty. When Liu Xin wished to attach himself to Wang Mang’s Xin regime, he presented auspicious tokens of Heaven’s mandate to gratify Wang’s wicked ambitions. These men certainly investigated classical learning. Yet their learning merely passed into the ears and out of the mouth, without the work of studying and discussing it to illuminate the Way. They embellished phrases and pondered passages, but lacked the substance of personally realizing and extending their learning. Thus flattery and sycophancy became habitual, while moral character and integrity went unheard of; evading responsibility and seeking mere security, they brought the spirit of scholars utterly low. Could this be the fault of classical learning?

Integrity and righteousness are intended to accomplish worthy deeds. Chen Fan aspired to cleanse his age, yet failed to keep his crucial plans secret, and his achievement was frustrated by a host of petty men. Wang Yun possessed the talents to assist a sovereign, yet his spirit grew overbearing and his ambition arrogant, and he was killed by the surviving evil faction. Li Ying suffered injustice and executed evildoers [?]: his deeds were magnificent, yet before long his name became entangled in accusations of factionalism. Fan Pang mounted his carriage and took up the reins; his ambition was heroic…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
惠甚渥也愚也敢不悉心以對夫學必師
孔孟治必法三代自宋儒著爲定論學者
守爲家法而
國朝養士於學校取士於科目尊崇六經罷
黜百家一以程朱之說爲主其道德固已
一而風俗固已同矣執事過慮恐爲學者
有近於佛老而爲政者或流於申韓愚也
亦不敢謂無其人也夫自王者之迹熄而
聖人之道不明於是申韓于秦黃老于漢
===
而大壞于晉宋齊梁之間彼秦用法令以
收富疆之效而遂并天下申商若可用矣
然徒文具而無惻隱之實二世之敗天下
土崩以爲可用者見其利未見其害也漢
用清淨以脩玄默之化而致黎民醇厚黃
老若可用矣然禁網疎闊豪強莫制七國
之變漢事幾殆以爲可用者見其得未見
其失也儒者必深斥之不少假借者非以
此歟韓非論法術謂人主之大物非法則

punctuated: 惠甚渥也。愚也敢不悉心以對？夫學必師孔孟，治必法三代，自宋儒著爲定論，學者守爲家法。而國朝養士於學校，取士於科目，尊崇六經，罷黜百家，一以程朱之說爲主，其道德固已一，而風俗固已同矣。執事過慮，恐爲學者有近於佛老，而爲政者或流於申韓，愚也亦不敢謂無其人也。夫自王者之迹熄，而聖人之道不明，於是申韓于秦，黃老于漢，而大壞于晉宋齊梁之間。彼秦用法令以收富疆之效，而遂并天下，申商若可用矣。然徒文具而無惻隱之實，二世之敗，天下土崩，以爲可用者，見其利未見其害也。漢用清淨以脩玄默之化，而致黎民醇厚，黃老若可用矣。然禁網疎闊，豪強莫制，七國之變，漢事幾殆，以爲可用者，見其得未見其失也。儒者必深斥之，不少假借者，非以此歟？韓非論法術，謂人主之大物，非法則
translation_en:
…Your kindness is most generous. How could I, ignorant though I am, dare not devote my whole mind to answering? In learning, one must take Kongzi and Mengzi as teachers; in governing, one must take the Three Dynasties as models. Since the Song Confucians established this as a settled judgment, scholars have upheld it as their inherited rule. Our dynasty nurtures scholars in schools and recruits them through the examinations, venerates the Six Classics and rejects the Hundred Schools, taking the teachings of Cheng and Zhu as its sole guide. Its moral principles are thus already unified, and its customs already shared. You, sir, are deeply concerned, fearing that students may approach the teachings of the Buddha and Laozi, and that those who govern may drift toward those of Shen Buhai and Han Fei. Ignorant though I am, I too dare not claim that no such people exist.

Once the traces of the true kings had vanished and the Way of the sages was no longer clear, the teachings of Shen Buhai and Han Fei prevailed under the Qin, and those of Huangdi and Laozi under the Han; the Way then suffered grievous ruin during the Jin, Song, Qi, and Liang dynasties. The Qin employed laws and commands to achieve wealth and strength, and ultimately united all under Heaven. The teachings of Shen Buhai and Shang Yang thus appeared usable. Yet they provided only formal instruments, without the substance of compassion. With the fall of the Second Emperor, the realm crumbled. Those who considered these teachings usable had seen their benefits but not their harm. The Han employed purity and tranquility to cultivate the transforming influence of profound stillness, bringing the common people to simplicity and sincerity. The teachings of Huangdi and Laozi thus appeared usable. Yet the net of prohibitions was loose and wide, and no one restrained the powerful. During the Rebellion of the Seven Kingdoms, the Han state almost came to ruin. Those who considered these teachings usable had seen their gains but not their losses. Is this not why Confucians must condemn them vigorously and allow them no indulgence?

Han Fei, discussing law and administrative techniques, says that the great instruments of a ruler are either law or…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
術法者編著之圖籍設之於官府而布之
於百姓者也術者藏之胷中以偶衆端而
潛御羣臣者也法莫如顯而術不欲見又
曰申不害言術公孫鞅爲法則其爲用有
異矣儒者雖或有所不廢而所謂以不忍
人之心行不忍人之政者彼盖未之聞也
道家稱無爲又曰無不爲以虛無爲本以
因應爲用其言似亦幾矣然大易不言有
無言有無者皆諸子之陋也今之學者溺
===
於訓詁詞章之習既不足以知大道之要
而脫去凡近以求高明者又多流於異學
而不自知爲政者玩於苟且偷惰之風既
不足以宣至治之澤而專事操切以急近
功者又多傷於刻核而不之反執事之憂
非過也愚也不敏請熟誦伊洛關閩之書
而敬守之則庶乎其不悖矣

punctuated:
術。法者，編著之圖籍，設之於官府而布之於百姓者也。術者，藏之胷中，以偶衆端而潛御羣臣者也。法莫如顯，而術不欲見。又曰：「申不害言術，公孫鞅爲法。」則其爲用有異矣。儒者雖或有所不廢，而所謂以不忍人之心行不忍人之政者，彼盖未之聞也。

道家稱無爲，又曰無不爲，以虛無爲本，以因應爲用，其言似亦幾矣。然大易不言有無，言有無者，皆諸子之陋也。今之學者溺於訓詁詞章之習，既不足以知大道之要，而脫去凡近以求高明者，又多流於異學而不自知。爲政者玩於苟且偷惰之風，既不足以宣至治之澤，而專事操切以急近功者，又多傷於刻核而不之反。執事之憂，非過也。愚也不敏，請熟誦伊洛關閩之書而敬守之，則庶乎其不悖矣。
translation_en:
…or techniques of rule. Laws are what is compiled and written in documents, established in government offices, and promulgated among the common people. Techniques are what is concealed within the breast, used to meet the manifold contingencies of affairs and secretly control the assembled ministers. Laws are best made manifest, whereas techniques should not be revealed. He further says: “Shen Buhai advocated techniques; Gongsun Yang established laws.” Thus their applications differ. Although there may be aspects that Confucians do not entirely reject, these men presumably never heard of what is called carrying out government that cannot bear to harm others with a heart that cannot bear their suffering.

The Daoists speak of nonaction, but also say that nothing is left undone. They take emptiness and nonbeing as their foundation, and adaptation and response as their practical application. Their words, too, seem to come close to the Way. Yet the great Book of Changes does not speak of being and nonbeing: discourse on being and nonbeing belongs entirely to the limitations of the various philosophical masters. Scholars today are immersed in the habits of textual glossing and literary composition, and so are incapable of grasping the essentials of the Great Way. Those who cast off the ordinary and familiar to seek what is lofty and luminous, moreover, often drift into heterodox learning without realizing it. Those who govern grow heedless amid a prevailing habit of expediency and indolence, and so are incapable of extending the beneficence of consummate government. Those who devote themselves exclusively to coercive measures in their haste for immediate results, moreover, often fall into harmful severity and minute scrutiny without turning back. Your concern, sir, is not excessive. Dull-witted as I am, I propose to recite thoroughly the writings of the masters of Yi, Luo, Guan, and Min and reverently abide by them; then perhaps I shall avoid departing from the Way.

translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Yingtian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the autumn, in the eighth month of the jimao year of the Zhengde reign [1519], the time had come for the Provincial Examination throughout the empire. The officials of Yingtian Prefecture requested that it be held according to precedent. His Majesty commanded your servant Jun, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, and your servant Shi, Right Mentor, to go and preside over the examination. The following day, we took leave of His Majesty; after twenty-five more days, we arrived. Scholars bearing ancient books and writings had gathered like clouds in the capital to sit the examination. In accordance with the prescribed regulations, we examined them in three sessions; 135 men passed. Their names, together with a selection of the finest essays, were engraved for printing as a record to be presented to His Majesty. It fell to your servant Shi to write its postface.

Reverently considering [?] how our sagely progenitor, the Gao Emperor, received Heaven’s great mandate and came to possess all the central lands…

title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
金陵寔肇迹之地一時佐命
武臣瑰竒偉雋又皆東南之
英得人之盛靡可及矣
聖子神孫飾治弘化保有丕基則
唯文儒是賴而東南之才亦
往往過於他省顧創業之時
其用也出于招延守成之際
===
非科舉則有莫能得者科舉
之設其来尚矣成周以三物
賓興賢能後之選舉實昉焉
然其為法或廣而靡精或狹
而近陋或繁而過猥或泥而
難通是以得才之效代有不
同而政治因之

金陵寔肇迹之地，一時佐命武臣，瑰竒偉雋，又皆東南之英，得人之盛靡可及矣。聖子神孫飾治弘化，保有丕基，則唯文儒是賴，而東南之才亦往往過於他省。顧創業之時，其用也出于招延；守成之際，非科舉則有莫能得者。

科舉之設，其来尚矣。成周以三物賓興賢能，後之選舉實昉焉。然其為法，或廣而靡精，或狹而近陋，或繁而過猥，或泥而難通。是以得才之效，代有不同，而政治因之
translation_en:
…Jinling was indeed the place where his rise began. The military officials who assisted in founding the dynasty were extraordinary and outstanding men, all eminent talents of the southeast. Such abundance in securing worthy men could scarcely be matched. His sagely sons and divine grandsons have refined governance, extended moral transformation, and preserved the great dynastic foundation, relying solely upon men of Confucian learning. The talents of the southeast, moreover, have often surpassed those of other provinces. Yet, when the dynasty was being founded, men were brought into service through invitations and recruitment; when preserving its achievements, there are men who cannot be obtained except through the civil-service examinations.

The institution of the civil-service examinations has a long ancestry. In the Zhou dynasty, the worthy and capable were honored as guests and recommended for service on the basis of the three categories of instruction. Later systems of selection and recommendation truly originated here. Yet their methods were sometimes broad without being discriminating, sometimes narrow and bordering on the inadequate, sometimes elaborate and excessively cumbersome, and sometimes rigid and difficult to apply. Thus their effectiveness in securing talent differed from age to age, and political governance varied accordingly…

…At the great court, ceremonial dress distinguishes official ranks [?]: the Three Dukes and Three Solitaries, the Grand Guardians and Grand Preceptors; officials of the central departments and courts, censorial and remonstrance officials; provincial administrators and local governors. Responsibilities as the sovereign’s limbs and the charge of the people and their altars are entrusted only to scholars. Such is the weight accorded to employing scholars. For more than a hundred and fifty years, government has flourished, moral transformation has spread throughout the realm, and all within the seas has enjoyed peace and order. Surely there is a reason for this! You scholars are casting off your moorings and setting your wheels in motion. You will all have duties concerning these responsibilities as the sovereign’s limbs and these charges over the people and their altars. Should you not reflect upon them?
His Majesty nurtures us through rectitude. When you assume office and accept responsibility, let your words always be upright and your actions always correct; do not distort learning to curry favor with the world. His Majesty selects us impartially. You must put the state before your family and public duty before private interest; do not form factions with like-minded men and betray the public good. His Majesty places great weight upon employing us. You must discharge your offices diligently and reverently. title: 正德十四年應天府鄉試錄
text:
國家作養選舉之意庶幾其不
負矣俾我
朝文德與武功並稱守成與創
業同美曰唯東南之才豈不
休哉諸士生長
王化首被之地漸漬涵濡于斯
三者必槩于其中矣〔時〕于其
===
始進也故特言之若夫援經
述史形諸較論颯颯乎
昭代之風一洗六朝之舊固諸
士之所優為而或藉以為它
日希崇陟峻之階者又諸士
之所不屑為也〔時〕皆得而畧
云

punctuated: 國家作養選舉之意，庶幾其不負矣。俾我朝文德與武功並稱，守成與創業同美，曰：「唯東南之才！」豈不休哉！諸士生長王化首被之地，漸漬涵濡于斯三者，必槩于其中矣。〔時〕于其始進也，故特言之。若夫援經述史，形諸較論，颯颯乎昭代之風，一洗六朝之舊，固諸士之所優為；而或藉以為它日希崇陟峻之階者，又諸士之所不屑為也。〔時〕皆得而畧云。
translation_en:
…the state's intentions in nurturing and selecting talent might thus be fulfilled without being betrayed. Let our dynasty's civil virtue be acclaimed alongside its military achievements, and its preservation of the inheritance be as admired as its founding, so that people say, “It is thanks to the talent of the southeast!” Would this not be glorious! You gentlemen were born and raised in the region first to receive the transforming influence of royal rule. Steeped and nourished in these three things, you must surely be moved by them in your hearts. I, Shi 〔時〕, therefore speak of them particularly as you first embark upon advancement.

As for drawing upon the Classics and recounting history, expressing these in comparative argument, with the vigorous spirit of this illustrious age sweeping away the old habits of the Six Dynasties—these are certainly things in which you gentlemen excel. Yet using such abilities as steps toward lofty rank and high promotion in the future is something you would disdain to do. I, Shi 〔時〕, may therefore pass over all this with only a brief mention.
